On Hopf Ideals, Integrality, and Automorphisms of Quantum Groups at Roots of 1
Matthew Harper and Thomas Kerler

Abstract
. We consider skew-commutative subalgebras in Drinfeld-Jimbo quantum groups at a root of unity ζ \zeta generated by primitive power elements. We classify the centrality and commutativity of these skew-polynomial algebras depending on the Lie type and the order of ζ \zeta modulo 8. We describe Hopf ideals in the quantum group induced from ideals in these subalgebras, including the non-commutative cases. Among these, we construct and analyze a family of Hopf ideals that depend on the choice of an element in the Weyl group. We show that they arise naturally both in the construction of (partial) R R -matrices and as vanishing ideals of Bruhat subgroups. Specialization to the maximal element yields a rigorous construction of restricted quantum groups as pre-triangular Hopf algebras, independent of any choices. Our treatment also includes even orders of ζ \zeta , non-simply laced Lie types, and minimal ground rings. Consequently, we extend some results of De Concini-Kac-Procesi, whose work focuses on odd orders of ζ \zeta , which forces the subalgebra to be strictly central, and complex ground fields. This includes the identification of the subalgebras for Lie types 𝖠 n \mathsf{A}_{n} and 𝖡 2 \mathsf{B}_{2} with the coordinate rings of associated algebraic groups in the commutative cases, even if ζ \zeta has even order. Our descriptions are computationally explicit and do not utilize Poisson structures. As technical preparations, we discuss PBW bases over minimal rings, dependencies on choices of convex orderings, as well as various new constructions of, and relations among, automorphisms on quantum groups. The latter include formulae for the Garside element in the Lustzig-Artin group action and the family of Che-transformations.



1.
Introduction

One of the original motivations for this monograph was to provide accessible constructions and computational tools for quantum groups at roots of unity. Although initially aimed at practitioners engaged in newer developments in quantum topology, the topics and theorems presented here focus exclusively on the quantum algebra side, introducing several new results and perspectives. Keeping the intended audience in mind, algebraic background material will be selectively introduced.

Broadly speaking, a quantum group
U
is a Hopf algebra associated to a simple Lie algebra
\mathfrak{g}
over a ground ring
\Lambda
. In the original definitions by Drinfeld and Jimbo
[
25
,
37
]

\Lambda
is naturally given as
\mathbb{Q}(q)
, where
q
is viewed as a formal “deformation parameter” relating
U
to the standard universal enveloping algebra of
\mathfrak{g}
. In many variants of the original definition
\Lambda
can be chosen as a subring of
\mathbb{Q}(q)
or an extension of scalars of such a subring. Analogous to the universal envelope of
\mathfrak{g}
, any relevant version of
U
has a decomposition
U=U^{+}\,U^{0}\,U^{-}
into subalgebras with generating sets typically of the form
\{E_{i}\}
,
\{K_{i}\}
, and
\{F_{i}\}
, respectively, where the indices enumerate a set of simple roots of
\mathfrak{g}
.

Quantum groups play a central role in low-dimensional and quantum topology thanks to their associated
R
-matrices, which give rise to solutions of the Yang Baxter equation. The latter yield representations of braid groups and invariants of knots, links, and 3-manifolds. Early
constructions of 3-manifold invariants and TQFTs, inspired by quantum field theories in physics,
start from a Hopf algebra
H

[
30
,
40
]
, its representation theory
[
62
]
,
or, more generally, certain types of tensor categories
[
73
,
38
]
. An important requirement
for these constructions is that
H
is effectively finite-dimensional, to assure the existence of integrals, well-defined and finite Kirby colors, or certain coends (which are all essentially equivalent).

The so-called
small quantum groups
provide the quintessential examples of finite dimensional Hopf algebras in our context. Lusztig
[
46
,
47
]
obtains these by first defining a divided power algebra
{\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{L}$}}{U}
version of
U
over
\Lambda=\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]
, and then extending this ring to
\mathbb{Z}[\zeta]
, where
q
is specialized to a primitive
\mathscr{k}
-th root of unity
\zeta
. The small quantum group appears then as the subalgebra generated by the original
\{E_{i},F_{i},K_{i}\}
in
{\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{L}$}}{U}
. The construction is, thus, independent of further choices and may also be formulated as the kernel of a Frobenius homomorphism. An important caveat is that
\mathrm{Spec}(U^{0})
is, of course, finite and discrete for these algebras, a feature that is not easily circumvented in this construction due to extra generators required in
{\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{L}$}}{U}^{0}
.

More recently, invariants constructed from quantum groups with
continuous

\mathrm{Spec}(U^{0})
have gained considerable interest as they establish connections to classical topological invariants. Typically, parameters associated with
\mathrm{Spec}(U^{0})
are identified with formal variables that appear in algebraic topology constructions. For generic
q
, one obtains
R
-matrix representations of braid groups for which the continuous weights of the
K_{i}
correspond to deck transformation parameters of homological representations
[
35
,
33
,
5
,
48
]
.

At roots of unity
U
admits finite-dimensional representations and a rigidity structure, while retaining continuity of
\mathrm{Spec}(U^{0})
. Invariants of knots and links are obtained by extending to modified quantum traces on the braid representations derived from
R
-matrices.
In this setting of non-semisimple
U
and modified traces,
the continuous parameters supplied by
\mathrm{Spec}(U^{0})
often imply that the quantum invariants
subsume
classical invariants
as special cases.
Among the first such examples is the Alexander Polynomial, for which highest weights yield the
indeterminate variable
[
54
,
55
,
59
]
. For the more involved Akutsu-Deguchi-Ohtsuki (ADO) invariant
[
1
]
, the continuous weights have similar homological interpretations
[
34
,
6
]
.

All the examples mentioned thus far assume the simplest Lie type
\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{sl}_{2}
. A higher rank example, leading to non-commutative properties of the knot invariant,
has been studied in
[
29
]
. In

[
19
,
12
]
quantum groups at roots of unity (in rank one) are used to define infinitely graded categories from which 3-manifold invariants and TQFTs are constructed. These, in turn, extend both the Reshetikhin-Turaev (RT) invariants and the classical Turaev-Reidemeister torsion. The invariant depends on a 1-cohomology class
\omega\in H^{1}(M,\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z})
whose coefficients stem again from the continuous spectrum of
K
. Specifically, the torsion map assigns the meridian homology generators of a surgery link to
\zeta^{\lambda}
, where
\zeta
is a fourth root of unity and
\lambda
a complex weight. Constructions for more general categories, such as those in
[
23
]
, are, thus, likely candidates to admit similar connections to more involved classical geometric invariants.

The
restricted quantum groups
underlying these invariants may be characterized by the conditions that
U^{-}
and
U^{+}
are finite-dimensional, that
U^{0}=\Lambda[\{K_{i}^{\pm 1}\}]
, and that there is at least a quasi-
R
-matrix. Their construction typically starts from the specialization of the full (unrestricted) quantum to a root of unity
\zeta
, sometimes also called the De Concini-Kac-Procesi (DCKP) algebra over
\mathbb{Q}(\zeta)
. The allowed restrictions to subrings
\Lambda
in
\mathbb{Q}(\zeta)
heavily depend on renormalizations of generators and the condition that the algebra is stable under the Artin group action defined by Lusztig.

The restricted quantum group, for some given
\mathfrak{g}
and
\zeta
, is then commonly written as the quotient of the DCKP algebra by an ideal generated by a collection of elements
X_{\alpha}=E_{\alpha}^{\ell_{\alpha}}
and
Y_{\alpha}=F_{\alpha}^{\ell_{\alpha}}
, which we refer to as
primitive power generators
. Here
\alpha
ranges over the set of positive roots
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
and
E_{\alpha}
is defined via the Artin group action, depending on the choice of a convex ordering of
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
. The exponent
\ell_{\alpha}
is the order of
\zeta^{(\alpha|\alpha)}
, thus depending on the length of
\alpha
.

Although it is clear that this definition yields continuous
\mathrm{Spec}(U^{0})
as desired, it does not immediately imply that the constructed quotient is indeed a Hopf algebra with finite-dimensional
U^{\pm}
. To illustrate the involved subtleties, assume that
\mathfrak{g}
is of type
\mathsf{B}
,
\mathsf{C}
, or
\mathsf{F}
and the order
\mathscr{k}
of
\zeta
is a multiple of 4. In this case, there exists
no
(uniform)
\ell
for which
\{E_{\alpha}^{\ell},F_{\alpha}^{\ell}\}
generates a Hopf ideal.
Hence, the quotient fails to be a Hopf algebra for any
\ell
.

A basic computation shows that the
X_{i}=X_{\alpha_{i}}
are
skew-primitive
for simple roots
\alpha_{i}
, meaning
\Delta(X_{i})=X_{i}\otimes L_{i}+1\otimes X_{i}
with
L_{i}=K_{i}^{\ell_{i}}
group-like. One easily infers from this that the set
\{X_{i},Y_{i}:i=1,\ldots,n\}
indeed generates a Hopf ideal. However, the quotient algebra by this ideal yields
infinite
dimensional
U^{\pm}
in ranks greater than 1. Finally, for non-simple roots
\alpha\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\setminus\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}
, the
X_{\alpha}
are far from skew-primitive.
Consequently, the ideal generated by an arbitrary subset of these elements is generally also
not
a Hopf ideal.

Computationally explicit and self-contained proofs that the
X_{\alpha}
and
Y_{\alpha}
generate Hopf ideals for all Lie types and roots of unity tend to be difficult to locate in the existing literature. For the
\mathsf{A}_{n}
Lie type one such treatment can be found in
[
9
]
, relying on recursions that are considerably more complicated for other Lie types. For
\zeta
of odd order
\mathscr{k}
, respective statements can be inferred indirectly from the differential methods developed in
[
20
]
.
Our initial aim at the onset of this project has been the clarification of these points, which
has led us to the exploration of numerous other directly related questions.

One of them is, which subsets of the
X_{\alpha}
generate Hopf ideals. The answer we give here is in terms of the inversion sets
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)={\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\cap s({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}})
(and unions thereof), where
s\in\mathscr{W}
is an element of the Weyl group. The associated ideals
\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(s)$}}
also occur naturally in the iterative construction of quasi-
R
-matrices, in the sense that intertwining relations for partial
R
-matrices hold on the (partial) quotients by the
\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(s)$}}
. Like the generators themselves, the
\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(s)$}}
ideal
a priori
depends on the choice of a total convex ordering or, equivalently, a reduced word presentation of
s
. We show independence of the latter so that, in particular, the fully restricted quantum groups are also independent of these choices and admit unique quasi-
R
-matrices.

Another source of classical parameter spaces inherent to quantum groups at roots of unity and, thus, potential starting points for quantum invariants extending classical invariants, are Lie groups associated to central subalgebras. Assign to a connected, reductive algebraic group
G
a solvable group
G^{\#}<G\times G
of the same dimension by choosing Borel subgroups
B^{+}<G
and
B^{-}<G
for which
H=B^{+}\cap B^{-}
is a maximal torus in
G
and denote

(1.1)

G^{\#}\,=\,\ker\!\left(m\circ(\pi^{-}\times\pi^{+}):B^{-}\times B^{+}\rightarrow H\right)\,=\,\left\{(g,h)\in B^{-}\times B^{+}\,:\,\pi^{-}(g)\cdot\pi^{+}(h)=1\right\}\;,

where
\pi^{\pm}:B^{\pm}\rightarrow H
are the usual abelianization maps. This group naturally appears in various contexts, such as the study of flag varieties, compactifications of algebraic groups, and Poisson Lie groups.

The algebra
\mathcal{Z}
generated by the
X_{\alpha}
,
Y_{\alpha}
, and
L_{i}
is in the center of the DCKP algebra for
odd
orders
\mathscr{k}
and is complementary to the generic Harish-Chandra center. In
[
20
]
De Concini, Kac, and Procesi establish an isomorphism of Poisson groups between
\mathrm{Spec}(\mathcal{Z}\otimes\mathbb{C})
and
G^{\#}
, or, equivalently, a Poisson Hopf isomorphism between
\mathcal{Z}\otimes\mathbb{C}
and the coordinate ring of
G^{\#}
. The construction relies on differential Poisson structures that reduce the proofs to the comparison of skew-primitive elements for simple roots and, therefore, side-steps explicit assignments of the
X_{\alpha}
generators for non-simple roots and comparisons of those coproducts.

For even
\mathscr{k}
, the algebra
\mathcal{Z}
is generally only a
skew-commutative
(commutative up to sign or unit factor) Hopf algebra. In
[
72
]
Tanisaki defines the Frobenius center as the intersection of
\mathcal{Z}
with the center of
U
, which is generally no longer a Hopf subalgebra. He shows it is isomorphic to the coordinate ring of the quotient
G^{\#}
/
\mathscr{G}
as an algebraic variety for a finite group
\mathscr{G}
, utilizing similar techniques as in
[
20
]
.

In this paper, we provide Hopf algebra isomorphisms from
\mathcal{Z}\otimes\mathbb{C}
to
\mathbb{C}[G^{\#}]
with
explicit
assignments of
all

X_{\alpha}
generators for Lie type
\mathsf{A}_{n}
with
\mathscr{k}\not\equiv 2\mod 4
and type
\mathsf{B}_{2}
for any
\mathscr{k}
. Our computations directly compare the coalgebra structures
of
\mathcal{Z}

with those of
\mathbb{C}[\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})^{\#}]
and
\mathbb{C}[\mathrm{SO}(5,\mathbb{C})^{\#}]
, and do not rely on Poisson structures. The concrete forms of these identifications make them more suitable for applications in quantum topology.

The congruence restriction above for
\mathsf{A}_{n}
is imposed solely to assure that
\mathcal{Z}
is commutative. For
\mathscr{k}\equiv 2\mod 4
, the full
\mathcal{Z}
algebra is isomorphic to
a non-commutative Artin-Schelter-Tate central extension
[
7
]
of classical matrix algebras. For this case, we suggest modifications of the Hopf algebra structures on
\mathbb{C}[G^{\#}]
via
\mathscr{G}
weights. We provide a concrete description of
\mathscr{G}
and the isomorphism of
\mathbb{C}[G^{\#}/\mathscr{G}]
with the Frobenius center, as proven abstractly in
[
72
]
.

Our calculations for the
\mathsf{B}_{2}
algebra illustrate further that, for
\mathscr{k}
a multiple of four, the group
G^{\#}
needs to be replaced by
\breve{G}^{\#}
. Here, the Langlands dual group
\breve{G}
is the algebraic group associated to the coroot system
\breve{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}}
, reflecting the fact that long and short roots are exchanged for the primitive power generators
X_{\alpha}
.
In both examples, we also show the ideals
\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(s)$}}
in
\mathcal{Z}
encountered above are
isomorphically mapped to the vanishing ideals on the Bruhat subgroups. The latter are defined here as

(1.2)

B(s)=B\cap\dot{s}B\dot{s}^{-1}\;,

where
\dot{s}
is a lift from the geometric Weyl group to
G
.

An additional important feature of many quantum invariants is that they are valued in integral polynomial rings, since one may expect integer coefficients to relate to topological information. For example, RT-type invariants of homology spheres are valued in
\mathbb{Z}[\zeta]
with coefficients giving rise to so-called finite type invariants of homology 3-spheres
[
57
,
58
,
59
]
, which are, in turn,
often related to geometric invariants.
In a more direct approach, the Hennings invariant of a 3-manifold is valued in the ground ring of the Hopf algebra chosen for the construction, assuming adequate properties of (co)integrals
[
30
,
26
,
27
]
.

Among the different versions of quantum groups, we consider here the original Jimbo normalization with generators
\{E_{i},F_{i},K_{i}\}
as well as elements obtained from these via the Artin group action. We write
U_{q,\mathbb{Q}}
for the rational form of the quantum group with these generators. It is easy to see that the minimal ground ring for the Hopf subalgebra
U^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}
generated by
\{E_{i},K_{i}\}
must contain
\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1},[\mathsf{e}]^{-1}]
. Here
[n]
indicates the usual quantum number and
\mathsf{e}=1
for Lie types
\mathsf{ADE}
,
\mathsf{e}=2
for types
\mathsf{BCF}
, and
\mathsf{e}=3
for type
\mathsf{G}
.

We prove that a PBW theorem holds for this minimal ring with respect to
appropriate monomial bases.
For the full quantum group with the described standard generators
\{E_{i},F_{i},K_{i}\}
the ring over which the algebra is defined also includes
(q-q^{-1})^{-1}
. Minimal ground rings for quantum algebras with differently normalized generators are discussed as well.

Throughout this project, (anti)automorphisms of quantum groups are an important tool for generating and relating monomial basis elements. In addition to the Artin group action, symmetries are generated by numerous (anti)involutions as well as an infinite family of so-called
Che transformations

\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{\mathsfit h}_{u}
. The latter act on generators via multiplication with Cartan generators and scalars and appear in numerous calculations, particularly, relations and expressions involving the antipode.

We carefully organize the catalog of relations between all types of automorphisms, allowing us to derive explicit expressions for other automorphisms, most notably, the action of the Garside element with respect to the Artin group action. The study of these automorphisms serves to provide insights into symmetries of quantum invariants.

1.1.
Organization and Summary of Main Results

Section
2
introduces basic background on spherical Artin and Coxeter groups as well as their actions on roots systems. In Sections
2.3
,
2.4
, and
2.5
we present numerous properties of inversion sets
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)
and discuss relations between reduced word expressions, weak Bruhat orders, as well as convex orderings of roots. We introduce root sums for inversion sets and a relation
v\dualmap w
for reduced words, which is later used to describe involutions of basis elements. The notion of symmetric root lattice maps, discussed in Section
2.6
, prepares the definition of Che transformations. We further compile formulae for rank 2 root systems in Section
2.7
, as they will be frequently used in later proofs.

Section
3
covers the basic definitions of the Drinfeld-Jimbo quantum groups, which will be the focus of the paper as the most commonly used version. The section includes discussions of their various minimal ground rings, extensions of scalars, basic Hopf algebra structures, and pointedness. Specifically, the subalgebras
U_{q}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}
generated by
E_{i}
and
K_{i}
are defined over
\Lambda_{q,{\mathsf{e}^{*}}}
, which is the extension of
\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]
by
([\mathsf{e}]!)^{-1}\,
, where
[n]!
is the usual quantum factorial and
\mathsf{e}\in\{1,2,3\}
depends on the Lie type as above. The full algebra
U_{q}
is defined over
\Lambda_{q,{\mathsf{e}^{*}}}^{\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{0.87694pt}{\scalebox{.47}{$\blacktriangledown$}}}
, which is obtained by further extending
\Lambda_{q,{\mathsf{e}^{*}}}
by
(q-q^{-1})^{-1}
.

In addition to the standard integer root lattice grading of quantum groups, we introduce in Section
4.1
an independent
\mathbb{F}_{2}=\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}
root lattice grading, which is useful for the derivation and structure analysis of the skew-commutative subalgebras at roots of unity. We assign to each

\mathsf{\Phi}

-symmetric lattice map
\mathsfit h
and homomorphism
u:\mathbb{Z}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}\rightarrow\Lambda^{\star}
a Che automorphism
\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{\mathsfit h}_{u}
in Section
4.2
. We also introduce in that subsection (anti)involutions, such as
\Omega
,
\mho
,
\Upsilon
,
\Pi
, and
\amalg
, and list numerous relations between them, including a formula for the antipode.

Lusztig’s action of the Artin group
\mathscr{A}
on
U
and its relations with the other automorphisms is explored in Section
4.3
. Our convention differs slightly as we use instead the automorphisms
\mathit{\Gamma}_{b}=T_{\iota(b)}\,
, where
b\in\mathscr{A}
and
\iota
the inversion automorphism on
\mathscr{A}
.

In Section
5
we construct families of bases for
U
, starting in Section
5.1
with the definition of elements
E_{w}
and
F_{w}
assigned to any reduced word
w
of the underlying Weyl group. There we show that
E_{w}=E_{k}
if the standard degree of
E_{w}
is a simple root
\alpha_{k}
, extending the proof in
[
45
]
to all Lie types. As an application, we derive in Section
5.2
the formula

\mathit{\Gamma}_{\boldsymbol{\partial}}=\mbox{\hskip-12.80373pt
I}\circ\Pi\circ\mho\circ S

for the Lusztig-Artin action
\mathit{\Gamma}_{\boldsymbol{\partial}}
of the Garside element
\boldsymbol{\partial}\in\mathscr{A}
in terms of the automorphisms from Section
4
as well as the involution

I
given by symmetries of the Dynkin diagram. In the remainder of the subsection, we provide a dictionary between generators in Lusztig’s and our convention in the rank 2 case via the
\mho
-involution. Aside from facilitating the translation of results and formulae, it serves to show that later definitions of ideals and quotients are independent of which of the two
\mathscr{A}
-actions is chosen.

Section
5.3
develops a formalism for PBW-style monomial elements
{E}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 25.90247pt}
and
{E}\mkern 1.3mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}w$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-16.46146pt}{\hskip-11.75818pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 26.7191pt}\,
, depending on reduced words
w
as well as an exponent functions
\psi:\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(w)\rightarrow\mathbb{N}_{0}
. We derive explicit formulae for the actions of automorphisms from Section
4
and introduce notations for spanning sets and spans. Various commutation relations between these monomials are gathered in Section
5.4
for later use.

In Sections
5.5
and
5.6
we adapt Lusztig’s proof of a PBW basis for the divided power algebras from
[
45
,
46
]
to produce a PBW theorem for
U_{q}^{+}
and
U_{q}
over respective minimal extensions of
\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]
for one particular convex ordering. In Section
5.7
we state criteria for subsets of exponent functions from which one can deduce that their respective spans are independent of the choice of a reduced word expression for a given Weyl element. The results are combined in Section
5.8
to yield Proposition
5.17
and Theorem
5.18
. They are restated in less formal terms as follows.

Theorem A
.

Assume
\mathfrak{g}
to be of any simple Lie type and let
z
be any reduced word of maximal length.
Then
\{{E}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle z\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-24.82289pt}{\hskip-24.82289pt}{\hskip-14.99458pt}{\hskip-10.71045pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 24.82289pt}\}
and
\{{E}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle z\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-24.82289pt}{\hskip-24.82289pt}{\hskip-14.99458pt}{\hskip-10.71045pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 24.82289pt}\cdot K^{\mu}\}
are
\Lambda_{q,{\mathsf{e}^{*}}}
-bases of
U_{q}^{+}
and
U_{q}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}\,
, respectively.

Moreover, the set
\{{E}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle z\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-24.82289pt}{\hskip-24.82289pt}{\hskip-14.99458pt}{\hskip-10.71045pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 24.82289pt}\cdot{F}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi^{\prime}$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-5.97253pt}{\hskip-5.97253pt}{\hskip-3.83766pt}{\hskip-3.15903pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle z\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-24.82289pt}{\hskip-24.82289pt}{\hskip-14.99458pt}{\hskip-10.71045pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 24.82289pt}\cdot K^{\mu}\}
is a
\Lambda_{q,{\mathsf{e}^{*}}}^{\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{0.9289pt}{\scalebox{.47}{$\blacktriangledown$}}}
-basis of the Hopf subalgebra
U_{q}\subset U_{q,\mathbb{Q}}
.

The exponents are integer functions
\psi,\psi^{\prime}\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{{{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}}}
and
\mu\in\mathbb{Z}^{{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}}
on the positive and simple roots, respectively. Analogous statements hold for bases obtained from the monomials
{E}\mkern 1.3mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}z$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-24.85338pt}{\hskip-24.85338pt}{\hskip-15.31584pt}{\hskip-10.9399pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 24.85338pt}
defined with respect to the reverse direction of multiplication.
We discuss a few less commonly used normalizations of generators that yield smaller ground rings.

In Section
6
we turn to the root of unity case, beginning in Section
6.1
with the introduction of various rings related to
\mathbb{Z}[\zeta]=\Lambda_{\zeta}
, notation for various orders, and formulae for multinomial coefficients. In Section

we derive skew-commutation relations involving the primitive power generators
X_{w}=E_{w}^{\ell_{w}}
,
Y_{w}=F_{w}^{\ell_{w}}
, and
L_{i}=K_{i}^{\ell_{i}}
in terms of special functions
({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}})^{2}\rightarrow\{\pm 1\}
. The discussion is extended in Section
6.3
to monomials, where we also introduce unital algebras such as
\mathcal{Z}^{+}_{w}
,
\mathcal{Z}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}_{w}
, and
\mathcal{Z}_{w}
, generated over
\Lambda_{\zeta,{\mathsf{e}^{*}}}
or
\Lambda_{\zeta,{\mathsf{e}^{*}}}^{\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{0.87694pt}{\scalebox{.47}{$\blacktriangledown$}}}
by
X_{u}
,

, and
L^{\mu}
with
u\leq_{R}w
. We conclude the section with a full classification of Lie types and
\mathscr{k}
congruences for which these algebras are central as subalgebras of
U_{\zeta}
and for which they are commutative. For
{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}\in\{+,-,0,{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}},{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\leq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\leq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\leq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\leq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}\}
and a given reduced word

, they give rise to the ideal
\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(w)$}}^{{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}}
in a maximal
\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}
generated by the augmentation ideal
A_{w}^{+}
of
\mathcal{Z}^{+}_{w}
.

For each rank 2 type
\mathsf{A}_{2}
,
\mathsf{B}_{2}
,
\mathsf{G}_{2}
there are two possible convex orderings, each of which is represented by a maximal reduced word. In Section
6.4
we compute explicit formulae that express the
X_{w}
from one ordering in terms of those of the other ordering, with the exception of words of length 3 and 4 in type
\mathsf{G}_{2}
. Drawing on the results in previous section, the implied closure under the
\mho
-action entails that the algebras above do not depend on the word
w
representing an element
s
of the Weyl group, but only on
s
itself. Summarizing Theorem
6.19
, Corollary
6.21
, Theorem
6.22
, and Corollary
6.26
this observation results in the following.

Theorem B
.

Assume a Lie type different from
\mathsf{G}_{2}
and
\zeta
of any order
\mathscr{k}\not\in\{1,2,\mathsf{e},2\mathsf{e}\}
. Suppose
w
is a reduced word and
s
the Weyl group element it represents. For
{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}\in\{+,-,0,{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}},{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\leq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\leq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\leq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\leq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}\}
we have the following.

i)

The algebra
\mathcal{Z}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}_{w}
depends only on
s
.

ii)

The maximal skew-commutative algebra
\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}^{{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}}
is defined independently of the choice of ordering.

iii)

\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}
is invariant under the Artin group action.

iv)

The augmentation ideal
\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(w)$}}^{{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}}
in
\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}
is only dependent on
s
.

In Section
6.5
we consider the action of an elementary abelian 2-group
\mathscr{G}
on
\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}
and induce for any
\mathscr{G}
-stable ideal
J
in
\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}
a two-sided ideal

in

. We introduce notations for special and extended cases of the resulting
\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(s)$}}
and discuss various examples.

Sections

are devoted to the identifications of the
\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}
algebras with coordinate rings of algebaric groups in the basic

collects background on algebraic groups and their coordinate rings, with emphasis on the correspondence between subgroups and Hopf ideals, and a discussion of relevant elementary examples.

Generators, commutation relations, and coproducts are computed for the quantum algebras for

and
\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{sl}_{n}
in Section

. Specializing to a root of unity of order

, we identify in Section

the respective
\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}
algebra with the AST algebra over
\Lambda_{\zeta}

[
7
]
. For

the extension is trivial, resulting in a Hopf algebra isomorphism to the coordinate ring of the group of upper triangular matrices over
\mathbb{k}=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta)
or

. In Section
7.4
the full
\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}
algebra for
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}
over

and the augmentation ideals
\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(s)$}}
with vanishing ideals of Bruhat subgroups
B(s)
defined in
loc. cit
. The section concludes with a discussion of potential interpretations of the skew-commutative case.

We start our treatment of the
\mathsf{B}_{2}
case with a complete description of the Hopf algebra structure of
\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}
in Section
8.1
, deferring the detailed computations of the coproducts to Section

and Appendix

. The required replacement of the root system by the coroot system, as mentioned above, is achieved by the choice of an isomorphism between the
\mathsf{B}_{2}
and

algebras.

In Section
8.3
we use a specific complex parametrization of
\mathrm{SO}(5,\mathbb{C})^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}
to derive formulae for the coalgebra structure of its coordinate ring. Using its Lie-Kolchin form, the vanishing ideals of the Bruhat subgroups are readily identified. Comparing the coalgebra structures obtained in Section
8.2
and
8.3
, we obtain Hopf algebra isomorphisms between the central subalgebra and the coordinate ring in Section
8.4
. The involved Hopf algebras fit into parametrized families of abstract weighted Hopf algebras, which are classified in the same sections.

The theorem below summarizes the main results from Lemma
7.18
, Theorem
7.16
, and Theorem
8.10
. The field
\mathbb{k}
can be chosen as either
\mathbb{Q}(\zeta)
or
\mathbb{C}
. The notation
G^{\#}
,
B
, and
B(s)
for an algebraic group
G
is as in (
1.1
) and (
1.2
). The isomorphisms are given as explicit assignments of polynomial generators.

Theorem C
.

Suppose
\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}
is the full commutative subalgebra for
\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{gl}_{n}
with
\mathscr{k}\not\equiv 2\mod 4
or
\mathfrak{g}
of type
\mathsf{B}_{2}
for any
\mathscr{k}
. Let
G=\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{k})
or
G=\mathrm{SO}(5,\mathbb{k})
respectively. Then

i)

There is a Hopf algebra isomorphism from
\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}\otimes\mathbb{k}
to
\mathbb{k}[G^{\#}]
, which restricts to an isomorphism between
\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}\otimes\mathbb{k}
and
\mathbb{k}[B]
.

ii)

The isomorphism maps the augmentation ideal
\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(s)$}}\subseteq\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}
exactly to the vanishing ideal in
\mathbb{k}[B]
of the Bruhat subgroup
B(s)<B
.

Section
9
is mainly concerned with the construction of
R
-matrices and quasi-triangular structures. We review relevant algebra completions as well as Tanisaki’s axioms for pre-triangular bialgebras in Section
9.1
. The algebraic properties of elementary and partial quasi-
R
-matrices for generic

are discussed in Sections
9.2
and
9.3
. We consider their relations with the Artin group action, introduce the Taniski automorphism

L
for the pre-triangular structure, and define coefficients related to the Tanisaki-Lusztig pairings. Specialized at a root of unity, the latter is used in Section
9.4
to define the full quotient into the restricted quantum group, where maximal ideals are identified with null spaces.

The technical core result of Section
9.5
is a set of intertwining relations via truncated partial
R
-matrices between the coproduct
\Delta(x)
and a twisted coproduct
\Delta^{s}(x)
, modulo ideals derived from the ideals
\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(w)$}}
introduced in Section
6
. Here
\Delta^{s}(x)
is the coproduct conjugated by
\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}
and the underlying quantum group
U_{\zeta,\ell}
is now over the ring
\Lambda_{\zeta,\ell}^{\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{0.87694pt}{\scalebox{.47}{$\blacktriangledown$}}}\,
, which also includes
([\ell-1]!)^{-1}
. The rather involved computations for generators are deferred to Appendix
A
. An important consequence of these relations is that the two-sided ideals
\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(w)$}}
depend only on the Weyl elements represented by
w
and are Hopf for all cases, including
\mathsf{G}_{2}
. The following combines the statements in Theorem
9.20
and Proposition
9.21
.

Theorem D
.

Let
\zeta
be of any order
\mathscr{k}\not\in\{1,2,\mathsf{e},2\mathsf{e}\}
and
U_{\zeta,\ell}
of any simple Lie type. Suppose
w
is a reduced word representing a Weyl element
s
. Let
\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(w,w)$}}
be the two-sided ideal generated by all
X_{u}
and
Y_{u}
with
u\leq_{R}w
. Then

i)

\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(w,w)$}}
is a Hopf ideal depending only on
s
so that the quotient
U_{\zeta,\ell}^{[s]}
by this ideal is a well-defined Hopf algebra over
\Lambda_{\zeta,\ell}^{\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{0.9289pt}{\scalebox{.47}{$\blacktriangledown$}}}
.

ii)

PBW bases of
U_{\zeta,\ell}^{[s]}
are given by the set of exponents with
\psi(\alpha)<\ell_{\alpha}\,
for all
\alpha\in\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)
.

iii)

For any reduced word
u
representing some
t\leq_{R}s
there is a partial quasi-
R
-matrix
\mathcal{P}^{\scalebox{.75}{$\star$}}_{\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}{u}}
such that

\Delta^{[t]}(x)\cdot\mathcal{P}^{\scalebox{.75}{$\star$}}_{\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}{u}}\,=\,\mathcal{P}^{\scalebox{.75}{$\star$}}_{\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}{u}}\cdot\Delta(x)\;,

where
x\in U_{\zeta,\ell}^{[s]}
and
\Delta^{[t]}
is the coproduct on
U_{\zeta,\ell}^{[s]}
obtained by conjugation with
\mathit{\Gamma}_{t}
.

In Section
9.6
we consider the specialization to the maximal length element

{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}
in the Weyl group, defining the restricted quantum group as
U_{\zeta,\ell}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.93}{$\mkern 1.0mu\mathsf{rest}$}}{\scalebox{.93}{$\mkern 1.0mu\mathsf{rest}$}}{\scalebox{.62}{$\mkern 1.0mu\mathsf{rest}$}}{\scalebox{.62}{$\mkern 1.0mu\mathsf{rest}$}}}=U_{\zeta,\ell}^{[{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}]}
. Using our formula for the Garside element, we identify
\Delta^{[{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}]}
with the Tanisaki-Lusztig conjugate
\raise 7.20001pt\hbox{\rule{5.12149pt}{0.76823pt}}\mkern-10.6mu\Delta
and show the maximal
\mathcal{P}^{\scalebox{.75}{$\star$}}_{\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}{z}}
is independent of the chosen word. A slightly less formal statement of Theorem
9.25
is as follows, which now encompasses also the
\mathsf{G}_{2}
case.

Theorem E
.

For any Lie type and root of unity as in Theorem
D
, the triple
(U_{\zeta,\ell}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.93}{$\mkern 1.0mu\mathsf{rest}$}}{\scalebox{.93}{$\mkern 1.0mu\mathsf{rest}$}}{\scalebox{.62}{$\mkern 1.0mu\mathsf{rest}$}}{\scalebox{.62}{$\mkern 1.0mu\mathsf{rest}$}}},\mathcal{P}^{\scalebox{.75}{$\star$}},\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
L})
is a pre-triangular Hopf algebra over
\Lambda_{\zeta,\ell}^{\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{0.9289pt}{\scalebox{.47}{$\blacktriangledown$}}}
. Its construction is independent of any choices, it has the properties of a restricted quantum group, and it admits the actions of the Artin group and all involutions.

2.
Root Systems and Weyl Groups

This section combines a general review of basic notions of
root systems, Coxeter groups, and Artin groups with a discussion of
several more specialized lemmas and concepts. The latter serve as technical tools in later sections, but
are typically not treated in standard textbooks on Coxeter groups. Examples of such topics
are various properties of inversion sets, complementary words, as well as

\mathsf{\Phi}

-symmetric lattice maps.

2.1.
Root Systems and Weyl Reflections

Let

\mathsf{\Phi}

be an irreducible root system of rank
n
in some Euclidean space
E
. For a choice of simple roots
\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}=\{\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{n}\}
denote by
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
and
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}}
the sets of positive and negative roots, with
\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}={\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\cup{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}}\,
. Although it is not dependent on the choice of

\mathsf{\Delta}

, we will frequently denote the root lattice of

\mathsf{\Phi}

in
E
by
\mathbb{Z}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}\,
.

The Weyl group
\mathscr{W}
is, by definition, generated by the reflections
s_{\alpha}
of
E
along roots
\alpha\in\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}
, which are
expressed as
s_{\alpha}(x)=x-\mathchoice{\left\langle{\alpha,x}\right\rangle}{\langle{\alpha,x}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha,x}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha,x}\rangle}\alpha
. The form
\mathchoice{\left\langle{\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,}\right\rangle}{\langle{\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,}\rangle}{\langle{\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,}\rangle}{\langle{\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,}\rangle}
is linear in the second entry
and gives rise to the Cartan matrix
A
associated to

\mathsf{\Phi}

via
A_{ij}=\mathchoice{\left\langle{{\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j}}}\right\rangle}{\langle{{\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j}}}\rangle}{\langle{{\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j}}}\rangle}{\langle{{\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j}}}\rangle}\,
. The convention for
A
chosen here conforms with that in
[
21
,
46
]
but is transposed to that of textbooks such as
[
13
]
. Clearly,

\mathscr{W}
also acts on
\mathbb{Z}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}\,
as an invariant subspace of
E
.

For a given Cartan matrix, we may find integers
d_{i}\in\{1,2,3\}
that symmetrize the Cartan matrix in the sense that
C_{ij}=d_{i}A_{ij}
is symmetric. Accordingly, we set
d_{\alpha}=d_{i}
if
\alpha
has the same length as
\alpha_{i}
or, equivalently, if
\alpha
is in the
\mathscr{W}
-orbit of
\alpha_{i}\,
. We will use the following convention and notation,

(2.1)

\min_{i}\{d_{i}\}=1\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\mathsf{e}=\max_{i}\{d_{i}\}\,\in\{1,2,3\}\,.

Thus, in the simply laced cases
ADE
we have
\mathsf{e}=1
, meaning all
d_{i}=1
. We have
\mathsf{e}=2
for
doubly laced Lie types
\mathsf{BCF}
and
\mathsf{e}=3
for type
\mathsf{G}\,
.
The renomalization leads to the definition of an inner form

(2.2)

\mathchoice{\left(\,\cdot\,|\,\cdot\,\right)}{(\,\cdot\,|\,\cdot\,)}{(\,\cdot\,|\,\cdot\,)}{(\,\cdot\,|\,\cdot\,)}\,:\mathbb{Z}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}\times\mathbb{Z}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}\,

by setting
\mathchoice{\left(\alpha_{i}|\alpha_{j}\right)}{(\alpha_{i}|\alpha_{j})}{(\alpha_{i}|\alpha_{j})}{(\alpha_{i}|\alpha_{j})}=C_{ij}=d_{i}A_{ij}\,
for the basis roots vectors. It is readily verified that the Weyl group
\mathscr{W}
acts by isometries with respect to this form, meaning
\mathchoice{\left(s(\alpha)|s(\beta)\right)}{(s(\alpha)|s(\beta))}{(s(\alpha)|s(\beta))}{(s(\alpha)|s(\beta))}=\mathchoice{\left(\alpha|\beta\right)}{(\alpha|\beta)}{(\alpha|\beta)}{(\alpha|\beta)}\,
for any
s\in\mathscr{W}
and
\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{Z}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}\supset\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}\,
. So
\mathchoice{\left(\,\cdot\,|\,\cdot\,\right)}{(\,\cdot\,|\,\cdot\,)}{(\,\cdot\,|\,\cdot\,)}{(\,\cdot\,|\,\cdot\,)}
is a scalar multiple of the standard Euclidean inner product on
E
for an irreducible root system

\mathsf{\Phi}

. Specifically, it coincides with the canonical inner product for the realizations in the appendix of
[
13
]
when the Lie type is
one of
\mathsf{ACDEG}
, and it is twice the canonical inner product given there if the Lie type is
\mathsf{B}
or
\mathsf{F}\,
.
The integer from (
2.1
) may thus also be understood as the lower bound on inner products of positive roots,

(2.3)

\mathsf{e}=\max_{i,j}\{-C_{ij}\}=\max_{i,j}\{-\mathchoice{\left(\alpha_{i}|\alpha_{j}\right)}{(\alpha_{i}|\alpha_{j})}{(\alpha_{i}|\alpha_{j})}{(\alpha_{i}|\alpha_{j})}\}=\max\{-\mathchoice{\left(\alpha|\beta\right)}{(\alpha|\beta)}{(\alpha|\beta)}{(\alpha|\beta)}:\alpha,\beta\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\}\,.

In these conventions we also find
\mathchoice{\left(\alpha|\alpha\right)}{(\alpha|\alpha)}{(\alpha|\alpha)}{(\alpha|\alpha)}=2d_{\alpha}
by choosing some
s\in\mathscr{W}
and
\alpha_{i}\in\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}

with
\alpha=s(\alpha_{i})
and, hence,
d_{i}=d_{\alpha}
. As usual, for a fixed root system, we will call
\alpha
a
short
root if
d_{\alpha}=1
and, in the non-simply laced case, we say
\alpha
is a
long
root if
d_{\alpha}=\mathsf{e}>1\,
. The initial integral pairing is recovered from
\mathchoice{\left(\,\cdot\,|\,\cdot\,\right)}{(\,\cdot\,|\,\cdot\,)}{(\,\cdot\,|\,\cdot\,)}{(\,\cdot\,|\,\cdot\,)}
via

(2.4)

\mathchoice{\left\langle{\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,}\right\rangle}{\langle{\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,}\rangle}{\langle{\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,}\rangle}{\langle{\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,}\rangle}:\,\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}\times\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}\qquad\mbox{with}\quad\mathchoice{\left\langle{\alpha,\beta}\right\rangle}{\langle{\alpha,\beta}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha,\beta}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha,\beta}\rangle}\,=\,\frac{1}{d_{\alpha}}\mathchoice{\left(\alpha|\beta\right)}{(\alpha|\beta)}{(\alpha|\beta)}{(\alpha|\beta)}\quad\in\mathbb{Z}\,.

For later notational convenience we also introduce

(2.5)

{\mathsf{e}^{*}}=\mathsf{e}+1\in\{2,3,4\}\,.

That is,
{\mathsf{e}^{*}}=2
for Lie types
ADE
,
{\mathsf{e}^{*}}=3
for the
BCF
types, and
{\mathsf{e}^{*}}=4
for
\mathsf{G}_{2}
.

2.2.
Coxeter Systems, Reduced Words, and Bruhat Orders

Recall that
(\mathscr{W},\mathscr{S})
forms a Coxeter system, where the set of generators
\mathscr{S}=\{s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}\}
consists of the simple reflections
s_{i}=s_{\alpha_{i}}\,
. The relations for a presentation of
\mathscr{W}
in generators
\mathscr{S}
are given by the involution
s_{i}^{2}=1
and the Artin-Tits relations. They are given for each pair
(i,j)
with
i\neq j
by

(2.6)

{s_{i}s_{j}\ldots}={s_{j}s_{i}\ldots}

with
m_{ij}
reflections terms on each side with alternating indices. Here
m_{ij}=2,3,4,\mbox{or }6
depending on whether the edge number
\max(|A_{ij}|,|A_{ji}|)
is 0, 1, 2, or 3, respectively.

As usual, the length
l(s)
of an element
s\in\mathscr{W}
is the smallest number
k
such that
s=s_{i_{1}}\ldots s_{i_{k}}
can be expressed as a product of
k
simple reflections.
A
reduced word
is a formal word expression
w_{i_{1}}\ldots w_{i_{k}}
in the letters

w_{1},\ldots,w_{n}\,
such that the respective product
s=s_{i_{1}}\ldots s_{i_{k}}

in
\mathscr{W}
is of minimal length
k=l(a)\,
. We use the separate notation
\mathscr{W}^{*}
for the set of reduced words, since several objects in the article will explicitly depend on words rather than just elements in
\mathscr{W}
.

An obvious surjection
\mathscr{r}:\mathscr{W}^{*}\twoheadrightarrow\mathscr{W}
is obtained by replacing each letter
w_{i}
by the respective
s_{i}
and mapping the empty word

\emptyset

to the identity element
1\in\mathscr{W}
. We say
s\in\mathscr{W}
is represented by a word
w\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
if
w
maps to
s
so that, by definition,
l(s)
is the number of letters in
w
. Denote by
\mathscr{A}
the
Artin group
associated to the same Coxeter data as
\mathscr{W}
. That is,
\mathscr{A}
shares the same generator set
\mathscr{S}
and the relations in (
2.6
) but lacks the relations
s_{i}^{2}=1
. Also denote by
\mathscr{A}^{+}
the
Artin monoid
, defined as the subset of elements in
\mathscr{A}
that are a product of generators with positive powers.

Matsumoto’s Theorem states that there is a well-defined map
\mathscr{s}:\mathscr{W}\rightarrow\mathscr{A}^{+}\subset\mathscr{A}
such that
\mathscr{s}\circ\mathscr{r}:\mathscr{W}^{*}\rightarrow\mathscr{A}^{+}
is given as the assignment of letters
w_{i}
to the respective Artin generators (see Part IV, §1.5 in
[
13
]
or
[
49
]
). The more practical formulation is as follows.

Corollary 2.1

(Matsumoto)
.

Suppose two words in
\mathscr{W}^{*}
represent the same element in
\mathscr{W}
. Then they are related by a sequence of Artin relations given in (
2.6
).

Given a reduced word
w=w_{i_{1}}\ldots w_{i_{k}}\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
, we write
w[a,b]=w_{i_{a}}\ldots w_{i_{b}}
for the subword between indices
a
and
b
with
1\leq a\leq b\leq k
. Further, denote
w^{*}=w_{i_{k}}\ldots w_{i_{1}}
the word with letters multiplied in the opposite direction so that
\mathscr{r}(w^{*})=\mathscr{r}(w)^{-1}\,
.

The
weak Bruhat orders
on
\mathscr{W}
and
\mathscr{W}^{*}
are defined in terms of smaller elements occurring as subwords. For our purposes, the most relevant is the weak right Bruhat order
\leq_{R}
. For two words
w,u\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
we say
u\leq_{R}w
if there exists
v\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
such that
w=u\cdot v
or, equivalently, if
u=w[1,j]
for some
j
. Similarly, for two elements
s,t\in\mathscr{W}
we have
s\leq_{R}t
if
t
and
s
are represented by words
w
and
u
, respectively, with
u\leq_{R}w
.

To define the left weak Bruhat order, replace
u=w[j,k]
in the above definition. If
{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}\in\mathscr{W}
is the unique longest element, then
{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}
is also the unique maximal element for any of the Bruhat orders, including
\leq_{R}
(e.g., Proposition 3.1.2 in
[
11
]
).

Correspondingly, we write
\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}=\mathscr{r}^{-1}({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}})
for the set of reduced words of maximal length. The set will be used to bijectively label all convex orders on
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\,
. See, for example,
[
68
]
for formulae for the size and rapid growth of
|\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}|\,
.

Note that any reduced word
u\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
can be written as the initial subword of some word in
\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}
. Explicitly, let
s=\mathscr{r}(u)
, set
s^{\prime}=s^{-1}{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}
, and choose any
u^{\prime}\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
representing
s^{\prime}
. Since
s\leq_{R}{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}
we have
l(u^{\prime})=l(s^{\prime})=l({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}})-l(s)=l({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}})-l(u)
by the same proposition in
[
11
]
. Now,
w=u\cdot u^{\prime}
represents
{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}
and, since
l(u)+l(u^{\prime})=l({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}})
, it is a reduced expression so that
w\in\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}
.

Similarly, the element
\boldsymbol{\partial}=\mathscr{s}({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}})\in\mathscr{A}^{+}
plays an important role as the fundamental element that renders
(\mathscr{A}^{+},\boldsymbol{\partial})
a Garside monoid (see, for example, Proposition 1.29 in
[
24
]
). In particular, Lemma 5.2 in
[
14
]
asserts that for all

b\in\mathscr{A}^{+}\,
the commutation relation

(2.7)

\boldsymbol{\partial}\cdot b=\sigma(b)\cdot\boldsymbol{\partial}

holds, where
\sigma
is an involutive automorphism of
\mathscr{A}^{+}
. Since
\sigma
needs to map generators to themselves, we may rewrite (
2.7
) as the relation

\boldsymbol{\partial}\cdot w_{i}\cdot\boldsymbol{\partial}^{-1}=w_{\sigma(i)}\,
in
\mathscr{A}\,
, with
\sigma
redefined as an involution on
\{1,\ldots,n\}\,
.

For example, for type
\mathsf{A}_{n}
the Artin-Tits monoid is the set of positive braids
B_{n}^{+}
in the braid group in
n
strands, and
\boldsymbol{\partial}
is the full positive half-twist. In this situation, relation (
2.7
) is readily visualized by moving a single positive neighbor crossing through this twist resulting in a crossing in reflected position, implying that
\sigma(w_{i})=w_{n+1-i}\,
. For other types, the involution coincides with the respective ones in the Coxeter or Weyl group situation as in Section
2.4
.

Note that relation (
2.7
) can also be derived directly from the presentations of
{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}
for other Lie types given in Section
5.5
below, essentially following the methods for relative Garside elements developed in
[
2
]
.

2.3.
Inversion Root Sets and Convex Orderings

In numerous calculations with words, it will be convenient to formally denote the index of the last letter as well as the word with the last letter deleted. That is, for a non-empty (
k\geq 1
) word

(2.8)

w=w_{i_{1}}\ldots w_{i_{k}}\in\mathscr{W}^{*}\qquad\mbox{set}\qquad w^{\flat}=w_{i_{1}}\ldots w_{i_{k-1}}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\tau(w)=i_{k}\,.

These components naturally enter the statement of the following lemma, which asserts an assignment of a positive root to any reduced word.

Lemma 2.2
.

Suppose
w=w_{i_{1}}\ldots w_{i_{k}}\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
is a non-empty reduced word. Then we have

\gamma(w)=w^{\flat}(\alpha_{\tau(w)})=w_{i_{1}}\ldots w_{i_{k-1}}(\alpha_{i_{k}})\quad\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\,,

where
w
acts on roots by its respective element in
\mathscr{W}
.

To see this, note that
s(\beta)\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
if and only of
l(s\cdot s_{\beta})>l(s)
by Proposition 4.4.6 in
[
11
]
, where
s_{\beta}
denotes the reflection along
\beta\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
. The lemma follows by specializing to
s=\mathscr{r}(w^{\flat})
and
\beta=\alpha_{i_{k}}\,
.
Next, define for any element
s\in\mathscr{W}
the
inversion set
of
s
as

(2.9)

\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)=\,\{\alpha\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}:s^{-1}(\alpha)\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}}\}\,=\,{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\cap s({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}})\,.

For a type
\mathsf{A}_{n-1}
root system realized as
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}=\{\alpha_{i,j}=\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{j}:\,1\leq i<j\leq n\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}
with
\mathscr{W}=S_{n}
, the symmetric group in
n
letters,
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)
is indeed given by the literal inversion set of the permutation
s^{-1}
.
Proposition 3.6 in
[
31
]
or Corollary 2 in Chapter VI §1.6 of
[
13
]
show that for any reduced word
w\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
as in (
2.8
) with
s=\mathscr{r}(w)\in\mathscr{W}
this set can be enumerated as

(2.10)

\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)=\{\beta_{m}=\gamma(w[1,m]):1\leq m\leq k\}\qquad\mbox{where}\quad\beta_{m}=s_{i_{1}}\ldots s_{i_{m-1}}(\alpha_{i_{m}})

and
k=l(w)=l(s)
. Thus, any word representing
s
imposes a total ordering on
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)

given by

\beta_{p}\preceq_{w}\beta_{j}
if
p\leq j\,
, writing also
\beta_{p}\prec_{w}\beta_{j}
if
p<j\,
.
Clearly,
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(1)=\emptyset
,
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s_{i})=\{\alpha_{i}\}
, and

\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(w)=\{\gamma(u):u\leq_{R}w\}
if the notation is extended to words. Additional immediate
consequences of the above are

(2.11)

l(s)\,=\,|\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)|\;,\quad s^{-1}\left({\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)}\right)=-\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s^{-1})\;,\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}})={\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\;.

We next explain how these sets determine the defect in length additivity for composites of Weyl group elements. In the first observation, we denote for an arbitrary subset
A\subseteq\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}

two subsets of
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\,
as

A^{+}=A\cap{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad A^{-}=-(A\cap{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}})=(-A)\cap{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\,,

so that
A=A^{+}\sqcup-A^{-}\,
. Also write
B\setminus A
for the complement of
A
in
B
.

Lemma 2.3
.

Suppose
s=a\cdot b
for
a,b\in\mathscr{W}
. Then
\,\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a)\cap a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b))=\emptyset\,
and

(2.12)

\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)\;=\;a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b))^{+}\,\sqcup\,\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a)\setminus a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b))^{-}\,.

Moreover,

(2.13)

l(s)\,=\,l(a)+l(b)\,-\,2\varsigma(a,b)\qquad\mbox{where}\quad\varsigma(a,b)=|a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b))^{-}|=|\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b)\cap\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a^{-1})|\,.

Proof.

The disjointness statement is clear since
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b)\subseteq{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
and
a^{-1}(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a))\subseteq{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}}\,
. For (
2.12
) we may split
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)

according to the partition
\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}=a({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}})\sqcup a({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}}\,)
. Then

a({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}})\cap\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)=a({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\cap a^{-1}(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)))=a({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\cap a^{-1}({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}})\cap b({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}}))=a(a^{-1}({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}})\cap\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b))={\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\cap a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b))=a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b))^{+}\,
.

Now, from
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}=b({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}})\cap{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\sqcup b({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}})\cap{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
we see that
b({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}})\cap{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}={\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\setminus\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b)\,
and, hence,
b({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}})\cap{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}}={\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}}\setminus(-\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b))\,
. Applying
a
to this we get

s({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}})\cap a({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}})=a({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}})\setminus(-a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b)))\,
, and intersecting this with

{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
we find
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)\cap a({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}})=\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a)\setminus((-a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b)))\cap{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}})=\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a)\setminus a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b))^{-}\,
.

Note that
-a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b))^{-}=a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b))\cap{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}}=a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b)\cap a^{-1}({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}}))=a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b)\cap\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a^{-1})
as
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b)\subseteq{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
. This readily implies the equality of the two expressions for
\varsigma(a,b)\,
. Clearly,
|a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b))^{+}|=|a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b))|-|a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b))^{-}|=|\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b)|-\varsigma(a,b)=l(b)-\varsigma(a,b)\,
. Now,
a^{-1}(a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b))^{-})=(-\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b))\cap a^{-1}({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}})=-(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b)\cap a^{-1}({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}})=-(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b)\cap\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a^{-1}))\,
. Thus, using also (
2.11
),

|\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a)\setminus a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b))^{-}|=|a^{-1}(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a))\setminus a^{-1}(a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b))^{-})|=|(-\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a^{-1}))\setminus-(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b)\cap\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a^{-1}))|=|\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a^{-1})|-|\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b)\cap\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a^{-1})|=l(a^{-1})-\varsigma(a,b)\,
. Using
l(a^{-1})=l(a)
and adding these expressions yields the length defect equation in (
2.13
).
∎

The following criteria for exact additivity and monotonicity are now easily derived from Lemma
2.3
. For example, if
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a)\subseteq\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)
we have
\varsigma(a^{-1},s)=|\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)\cap\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a)|=|\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a)|=l(a)\,
.
So, for
b=a^{-1}s
(
2.13
) implies
l(b)=l(a^{-1})+l(s)-2l(a)=l(s)-l(a)\,
or
l(s)=l(a)+l(b)\,
. The latter and
s=a\cdot b
now imply
a\leq_{R}s\,
as claimed in (
2.14
).

Corollary 2.4
.

For two elements
a,b\in\mathscr{W}
the following conditions are equivalent.

i)

l(a\cdot b)=l(a)+l(b)

ii)

\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a\cdot b)=a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b))\sqcup\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a)

iii)

a(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b))\subseteq{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}

iv)

\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b)\cap\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a^{-1})=\emptyset

Moreover, we have for elements
a,b,s\in\mathscr{W}
that

(2.14)

a\leq_{R}s\;\Leftrightarrow\;\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a)\subseteq\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\qquad b\leq_{L}s\;\Leftrightarrow\;\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(b^{-1})\subseteq\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s^{-1})\,.

In particular,
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)=\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(a)
implies
s=a\,
.

The fact that the longest element of
\mathscr{W}
yields all of
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
implies that any reduced word of maximal length
w\in\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}
imposes a total order
\prec_{w}
on the set of positive roots via
\,{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}=\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(w)\,
. Specifically, if we denote

\beta_{j}=\gamma(w[1,j])
we have
\beta_{1}\prec_{w}\beta_{2}\prec_{w}\ldots\prec_{w}\beta_{L}
where
L=l(w)\,
. We
write
\preceq_{w}
if equality is included.

The result of Papi in
[
60
]
states that the assignment
w\mapsto\preceq_{w}
establishes a bijection between elements in
\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}
and the (total)
convex
orders on
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
. Here convexity means that if for two roots
