\alpha,\beta\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
we have
\alpha\prec_{w}\beta
and

\alpha+\beta\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
, then
\alpha\prec_{w}\alpha+\beta\prec_{w}\beta\,
.

Let
s=\mathscr{r}(w)
and observe that, since the
\beta_{j}
as above are distinct and
L=|\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)|
, we have that the map
[1,L]\rightarrow\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s):\,j\mapsto\beta_{j}
is a bijection.
Thus, to each
\alpha\in\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)
we can assign a unique
j_{\alpha}
such that

\alpha=\beta_{j_{\alpha}}\,
. It is convenient to also introduce the inverse map from the root set to words,

(2.15)

\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)\rightarrow\{u\in\mathscr{W}^{*}:u\leq_{R}w\}\,:\;\alpha\mapsto w[\alpha]\,,

where we denote
w[\alpha]=w[1,j_{\alpha}]\,
so that
\alpha=\mathscr{r}(w[\alpha])\,
. In particular, if
w\in\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}
the correspondence (
2.15
) assigns to any positive root a reduced word
\leq_{R}w\,
.

For non-simply laced root systems (types
\mathsf{BCFG}
) with
\mathsf{e}>1
it is useful to distinguish the short and long roots portions of the various root sets.
That is, we have
\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}=\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}_{L}\sqcup\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}_{S}
where
\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}_{L}=\{\alpha\in\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}:d_{\alpha}=\mathsf{e}\}
and

\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}_{S}=\{\alpha\in\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}:d_{\alpha}=1\}
.
Correspondingly, denote

(2.16)

\displaystyle{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}_{L}}

\displaystyle={\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\cap\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}_{L}\,,\qquad

\displaystyle{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}_{L}}

\displaystyle={\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}}\cap\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}_{L}\,,\qquad

\displaystyle\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)_{L}

\displaystyle=\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)\cap{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}_{L}}\,,

\displaystyle{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}_{S}}

\displaystyle={\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\cap\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}_{S}\,,\qquad

\displaystyle{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}_{S}}

\displaystyle={\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}}\cap\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}_{S}\,,\qquad

\displaystyle\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)_{S}

\displaystyle=\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)\cap{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}_{S}}\,.

Since
s(\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}_{L})=\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}_{L}
and
s(\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}_{S})=\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}_{S}
for any
s\in\mathscr{W}
, we also have

\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)_{L}=s({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}_{L}})\cap{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}_{L}}
and
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)_{S}=s({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}_{S}})\cap{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}_{S}}\,
. Thus, for example, the relations between root sets in Lemma
2.3
will hold for the respective long root and short root portions separately. Furthermore, introduce the following subsets of the Weyl group.

(2.17)

\mathscr{W}_{S}=\left\{{s\in\mathscr{W}\,:\,\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)_{S}=\emptyset}\right\}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\mathscr{W}_{L}=\left\{{s\in\mathscr{W}\,:\,\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)_{L}=\emptyset}\right\}

Lemma 2.5
.

Suppose

\mathsf{\Phi}

is a non-simply laced root system with
\mathsf{e}>1\,
. Then
\mathscr{W}_{S}
and
\mathscr{W}_{L}
are the subgroups of
\mathscr{W}
generated by
\{s_{i}:d_{i}=\mathsf{e}\}
and
\{s_{i}:d_{i}=1\}
respectively.

Thus, for type
\mathsf{B}_{n}
, we have that
\mathscr{W}_{S}\cong S_{n-1}
is the canonical
\mathsf{A}_{n-1}
-subgroup and
\mathscr{W}_{S}\cong\mathbb{F}_{2}
the
\mathsf{A}_{1}
-subgroup. The assignments are reversed for
\mathsf{C}_{n}
.
For
\mathsf{F}_{4}
they are the respective
\mathsf{A}_{2}
-subgroups and for
\mathsf{G}_{2}
the respective
\mathsf{A}_{1}
-subgroups.

Proof.

\mathscr{W}_{S}
is readily identified with the stabilizer
\{s:s({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}_{S}})={\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}_{S}}\}
and thus a subgroup of
\mathscr{W}
.
If
d_{i}=\mathsf{e}
we also have
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s_{i})=\{\alpha_{i}\}
so that
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s_{i})_{S}=\emptyset
and, hence,
s_{i}\in\mathscr{W}_{S}
,
implying that
\mathscr{W}_{S}
contains the subgroup generated by
\{s_{i}:d_{i}=\mathsf{e}\}
. For the converse inclusion, assume

s=\mathscr{r}(w)\in\mathscr{W}_{S}
is given by a reduced expression
w=w_{i_{1}}\ldots w_{i_{k}}
. Then
\beta_{m}=\gamma(w[1,m])=t(\alpha_{i_{m}})
where
t=\mathscr{r}(w[1,m-1])
so that
\beta_{m}
has the same length as
\alpha_{i_{m}}
.
Hence,
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)_{S}=\emptyset
if and only if
d_{i_{1}}=\ldots=d_{i_{k}}=\mathsf{e}
, implying that
s
is in the subgroup generated by
s_{i}
with
d_{i}=\mathsf{e}\,
. The arguments for
\mathscr{W}_{L}
are analogous.
∎

We will need the following observation about root decompositions later only in the
\mathsf{A}
case. The elementary argument, though, extends to all classical types. The exceptional types are not discussed here.

Lemma 2.6
.

Let

\mathsf{\Phi}

be a root system of classical type
\mathsf{ABCD}\,
. Assume that
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
is equipped with any convex ordering
\prec_{w}\,
. Suppose
\beta=\beta_{1}+\ldots+\beta_{k}

with
\beta,\beta_{i}\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
for
i=1,\ldots,k\,
with
k>1\,
. Then

i)

There exists
j
for which
\beta-\beta_{j}\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
.

ii)

There exists
r
for which
\beta_{r}\prec_{w}\beta\,
.

Proof.

Consider the same numbering of simple roots as in
[
13
, Plate I-IV]
so that
\alpha_{1}
is opposite the special roots. The formulae in

[
13
]
imply that every positive root is of the form
\beta_{a,b}=\sum_{s=a}^{b}\alpha_{\mathscr{c}(s)}
, where

\mathscr{c}:\{1,\ldots,N\}\rightarrow\{1,\ldots,n\}\,
is a
numbering sequence depending on Lie type,
n=|\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}|\,
, and
1\leq a\leq b\leq N
.

For
\beta=\sum_{i}c_{i}\alpha_{i}
set
\,0pt(\beta)=\sum_{i}c_{i}\,
and

\,r(\beta)=\min\{i:c_{i}\neq 0\}\,
. The formulae
0pt(\beta_{a,b})=b-a+1\,

and
r(\beta_{a,b})=\min\{\mathscr{c}(a),\mathscr{c}(b)\}\,
are readily checked for all cases below.
We use this notation to prove the statement
i)
for each Lie type separately.

For type
\mathsf{A}_{n}
set
N=n
and
\mathscr{c}(i)=i
. Then any positive root is of the form
\beta=\beta_{a,b}
. Now, for
\beta
as in the lemma, at least one
\beta_{j}
must have non-zero coefficient for
\alpha_{a}
and no
\beta_{i}
can have
\alpha_{s}
with
s<a
as a summand. Thus, we must have
r(\beta_{j})=a

for at least one
j
, which implies
\beta_{j}=\beta_{a,c}
for some
c\leq b
and, with
k>1
, also
c<b
. Then

\beta-\beta_{j}=\beta_{a,b}-\beta_{a,c}=\beta_{c+1,b}\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\,
.

Next consider type
\mathsf{C}_{n}\,
, setting
N=2n-1
and
(\mathscr{c}(1),\ldots,\mathscr{c}(N))=(1,\ldots,n-1,n,n-1,\ldots,1)\,
.
It follows by inspection that all positive roots are of the form
\beta_{a,b}\,
and all
\beta_{a,b}\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\,
. In fact,
(a,b)\mapsto\beta_{a,b}
defines a bijection between
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
and the set of pairs
(a,b)
for which
a\leq\min(n,b)
and
\mathscr{c}(a)\leq\mathscr{c}(b)\,
. Let
\beta=\beta_{a,b}
with these constraints so that
a=r(\beta)\,
. As before,
we can pick
\beta_{j}
such that
a=r(\beta_{j})
and, hence,
\beta_{j}=\beta_{a,c}
for some
c<b\,
. Then,

\beta-\beta_{j}=\beta_{c+1,b}
which is again in
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
by previous remarks.

For
\mathsf{B}_{n}
we set
N=2n
and
(\mathscr{c}(1),\ldots,\mathscr{c}(N))=(1,\ldots,n-1,n,n,n-1,\ldots,1)\,
. As opposed to previous Lie types, not all
\beta_{a,b}
are roots. Specifically,
\beta_{a,b}\not\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
if and only if

a\neq b
but
\mathscr{c}(a)=\mathscr{c}(b)\,
. This case has to be excluded to establish
a one-to-one correspondence,
as in the
\mathsf{C}_{n}
case. We may thus assume
\beta=\beta_{a,b}
with
a=r(\beta)\leq n
and
\mathscr{c}(a)<\mathscr{c}(b)\,

since
k>1
implies
a\neq b\,
. Then, as before, we have
\beta_{j}=\beta_{a,c}
for some
c<b
so that

\gamma=\beta-\beta_{j}=\beta_{c+1,b}\,
. If either
c+1=b
or
\mathscr{c}(c+1)\neq\mathscr{c}(b)
we are done since

\beta_{c+1,b}\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\,
. In case
c+1<b
and
\mathscr{c}(c+1)=\mathscr{c}(b)
we have
\gamma=2\sum_{c<i\leq n}\alpha_{i}=\sum_{t\neq j}\beta_{t}\,
so that there has to be an
s\neq j
with
\beta_{s}=\beta_{c+1,d}
with
d<b
.
With
\mathscr{c}(N+1-i)=\mathscr{c}(i)
,
b=N-c
, and
d^{\prime}=N-d
we have
\beta_{s}=\beta_{d^{\prime}+1,b}
. Now,
\beta-\beta_{s}=\beta_{a,d^{\prime}}
which is in
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
since
\mathscr{c}(a)<\mathscr{c}(d^{\prime})\,
.

For type
\mathsf{D}_{n}
we may choose
N=2n-2
and
(\mathscr{c}(1),\ldots,\mathscr{c}(N))=(1,\ldots,n-2,n-1,n,n-2,\ldots,1)\,
. A second sequence
\mathscr{c}^{\prime}
may be defined via
\mathscr{c}^{\prime}(i)=\mathscr{c}(N+1-i)=\eta(\mathscr{c}(i))
, where

\eta=(n-1,n)
is the non-trivial involution of the Dynkin diagram. All positive roots are of the form
\beta_{a,b}
or

\beta^{\prime}_{a,b}
defined via the respective sequences and
\beta_{\mathscr{c}(a),\mathscr{c}(b)}=\beta^{\prime}_{a,b}

if
\{a,b\}\cap\{n-1,n\}=\emptyset\,
. As for
\mathsf{B}_{n}
,
\beta_{a,b}\not\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
if and only if

a\neq b
and
\mathscr{c}(a)=\mathscr{c}(b)\,
. The argument now proceeds as in the
\mathsf{D}_{n}
case, except that a subsequence
may be chosen from either
\mathscr{c}
or
\mathscr{c}^{\prime}\,
.

Item
ii)
follows now by induction in
k\,
. That is, if
\beta=\beta_{1}+\ldots+\beta_{k}

and
j
such that
\beta^{\prime}=\beta-\beta_{j}=\sum_{i\neq j}\beta_{i}\,\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\,
, convexity implies that
either
\,\beta_{j}\prec_{w}\beta\prec_{w}\beta^{\prime}\,
or
\,\beta^{\prime}\prec_{w}\beta\prec_{w}\beta_{j}\,
.
In the former case we are done. In the latter, the induction hypothesis implies
\beta_{i}\prec_{w}\beta^{\prime}

for some
i
(
i\neq j
) so that, by transitivity, also
\beta_{i}\prec_{w}\beta\,
.
∎

2.4.
Longest Elements, Involutions, and Complementary Words

The longest element
{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}\in\mathscr{W}
is an involution by uniqueness. Its respective involutive action on the root system maps
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
isometrically to
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}}
(e.g., Corollary 3 in
[
13
, VI.1.6]
) and is thus of the form

{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}(\alpha_{i})=-\alpha_{\eta(i)}
for an involution
\eta
of the Dynkin diagram associated to

\mathsf{\Phi}

.

As specified in Item XI of each plate in the appendix of
[
13
]
,
\eta
is the non-trivial involution for
\mathsf{A}_{n}
,
\mathsf{D}_{2k+1}
, and
\mathsf{E}_{6}
, and it is identity in all other cases. Mapping the
\mathscr{A}
-version of (
2.7
) to
\mathscr{W}
then implies that
\sigma=\eta\,
. We use the same notation
\eta
for the conjugation action of
{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}
on
\mathscr{W}
. Since
s_{i}
is given by reflection along
\alpha_{i}
we, thus, find

(2.18)

\eta(s_{i})=s_{\eta(i)}\qquad\mbox{where}\quad\eta(t)={{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}}t{{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}}^{-1}={{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}}t{{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}}\,.

We use the same notation for the obvious extension of
\eta
to the set of
reduced words
\mathscr{W}^{*}\,
. We will frequently use the involution

(2.19)

w^{\dagger}=\eta(w)^{*}=\eta(w^{*})

on
\mathscr{W}^{*}
, explicitly given as
(w_{i_{1}}\ldots w_{i_{N}})^{\dagger}=w_{\eta(i_{N})}\ldots w_{\eta(i_{1})}\,
for reduced expressions. Clearly,
l(w^{\dagger})=l(w)
and
s^{\dagger}=\gamma(w^{\dagger})=\eta(s)^{-1}\,
. A related involutive map on
\mathscr{W}
is given by right multiplication with the longest element by

(2.20)

t\,\mapsto\,t^{\llcorner}=t\cdot{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}\,.

Lemma 2.7
.

Suppose
t\in\mathscr{W}
and
t^{\llcorner}
is as in (
2.20
). Then

i)

t=t^{\llcorner}{}^{\llcorner}\,,

ii)

{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}\cdot t=\eta(t^{\llcorner})=\eta(t)^{\llcorner}\,,

iii)

l(t^{\llcorner})=l({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}})-l(t)\,,

iv)

t\leq_{R}u\;\Leftrightarrow\;u^{\llcorner}\leq_{R}t^{\llcorner}\,,

v)

\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(t^{\llcorner})={\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\setminus\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(t)={\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\cap t({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}})\,,

vi)

t^{\llcorner}\left({\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(t^{\dagger})}\right)=\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(t)\,.

Proof.

Items
i)
,
ii)
, and
iii)
are immediate from the definitions. See also Proposition 2.3.2 in
[
11
]
.
For Item
iv)

assume
t\leq_{R}t
, meaning
u=t\cdot a
with
l(u)=l(t)+l(a)
. Using (
2.18
) this yields the decomposition
t^{\llcorner}=u^{\llcorner}\cdot\eta(a)^{-1}\,
.
Further, using
iii)
,
l(t^{\llcorner})-l({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}})-l(t)=l(u^{\llcorner})+l(a)=l(u^{\llcorner})+l(\eta(a)^{-1})\,
. So,
u^{\llcorner}\leq_{R}t^{\llcorner}\,
. For Item
v)
note that

\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(t^{\llcorner})={\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\cap t^{\llcorner}({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}})={\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\cap t({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}}))={\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\cap t({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}})={\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\setminus\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(t)\,
. Finally,
Item
iv)
follows from

t^{\llcorner}\left({\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(t^{\dagger})}\right)=t{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\cap t^{\dagger}({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}}))=t({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}})\cap{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}t^{\dagger}({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}}))=t({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}}\cap t^{-1}{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}}))=t({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}}\cap t^{-1}({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}))=t({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{-}})\cap{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}=\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(t)\,
.
∎

For the description of involutive automorphisms on quantum groups, the related notion of
complementary words
will be relevant. Given a non-empty reduced word
w\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
, we say that
v\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
is complementary to
w
, writing
v\dualmap w
, if the following two conditions hold.

(2.21)

v\dualmap w\qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad\tau(v)=\eta(\tau(w))\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\mathscr{r}(v)^{\llcorner}=\mathscr{r}(w^{\flat})\,.

If we write
s=\mathscr{r}(w^{\flat})
,
t=\mathscr{r}(v^{\flat})
,
j=\tau(w)
, and
k=\tau(v)
the condition in (
2.21
) can be rephrased more symmetrically as
k=\eta(j)
and

(2.22)

t^{-1}\cdot s=q_{j}\qquad\mbox{where}\quad q_{j}={s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}\cdot s_{j}=s_{\eta(j)}\cdot{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}\,.

Note, with
N=l({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}})
, these imply
l(w)+l(v)=N+1
or
l(t)+l(s)=N-1
.

Lemma 2.8
.

Suppose
v\dualmap w
for non-empty, reduced words
v,w\in\mathscr{W}^{*}\,
. Then

i)

w\dualmap v\,,

ii)

\gamma(v)=\gamma(w)\,,

iii)

\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(w)\cap\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(v)=\{\gamma(w)\}\,,

iv)

{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}=\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(w)\cup\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(v)\,.

Moreover, if
z\in\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}
is a reduced word of maximal length
N=l(z)
and
y=z^{\dagger}
, then

(2.23)

z[1,r]\dualmap z[r,N]^{\dagger}=y[1,N+1-r]\,.

Proof.

Symmetry in
i)
is immediate from (
2.22
) together with

q_{j}^{-1}=q_{\eta(j)}
and
\eta^{2}=\mathrm{id}\,
. Note further that
q_{j}(\alpha_{j})={s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}(s_{j}(\alpha_{j}))={s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}(-\alpha_{j})=\alpha_{\eta(j)}\,
. So, with notation as in (
2.22
),
\gamma(w)=s(\alpha_{j})=t(q_{j}(\alpha_{j}))=t(\alpha_{\eta(j)})=\gamma(v)\,
. For
iii)
and
iv)
note that
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(w)=\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(w^{\flat})\sqcup\{\gamma(w)\}
by
Corollary
2.4
, and
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(w^{\flat})={\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\setminus\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(v)
by (
2.21
) and Lemma
2.7

v)
.

For the last statement, let
z=w_{i_{1}}\ldots w_{i_{N}}
so that
y=w_{\eta(i_{N})}\ldots w_{\eta(1)}\,
. Denote further

w=z[1,r]=w_{i_{1}}\ldots w_{i_{r}}\,
and
v=z[r,N]^{\dagger}=\eta(w_{i_{r}}\ldots w_{i_{N}})^{*}=w_{\eta(i_{N})}\ldots w_{\eta(i_{r})}=y[1,N+1-r\,]
. Clearly,
\eta(\tau(w))=\eta(i_{r})=\tau(v)
, and
z=z[1,r-1]z[r,N]=w^{\flat}\eta(v^{*})\,
.
The latter implies
{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}=\mathscr{r}(w^{\flat})\mathscr{r}(\eta(v)^{*})=\mathscr{r}(w^{\flat})\mathscr{r}(\eta(v))^{-1}
and hence
\mathscr{r}(w^{\flat})={s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}\cdot\eta(\mathscr{r}(v))=\mathscr{r}(v)\cdot{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}=\mathscr{r}(v)^{\llcorner}\,
as desired.
∎

Combining Item
ii)
and (
2.23
) the following order reversal relation is an immediate consequence for the total ordering
\prec_{z}
on
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
depending on a maximal length reduced word
z\in\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}
as introduced in Section
2.3
.

Corollary 2.9
.

Suppose
z\in\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}
and
y=z^{\dagger}\,
. Then
\,\alpha\prec_{z}\beta\,
if and only if

\,\beta\prec_{y}\alpha\,
.

Relation (
2.23
) provides explicit constructions of complementary words that imply a partitioning of
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
into two totally ordered sets, which have only their maximal elements in common. That is, for a given
w\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
find

z\in\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}
with
z\geq_{R}w
and hence
w=z[1,r]
. Set then
v=y[N+1-r]
with
y=z^{\dagger}\,
.
Setting
\beta_{i}=\gamma(z[1,i])
and
\mu_{i}=\gamma(y[1,i])
, the sets
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(w)
and

\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(v)
are then given by the elements in respective maximal chains
\beta_{1}\prec_{z}\beta_{2}\prec_{z}\ldots\prec_{z}\beta_{r}
and
\mu_{1}\prec_{y}\mu_{2}\prec_{y}\ldots\prec_{y}\mu_{N+1-r}
, with
\beta_{r}=\mu_{N+1-r}
but

\beta_{i}\neq\mu_{j}
otherwise.

For example, consider the reduced word
w=w_{2}w_{3}w_{2}w_{1}
in a type
\mathsf{A}_{3}
Coxeter system. A maximal length reduced word

z\in\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}
with
w\leq_{R}z
is then given by
z=w_{2}w_{3}w_{2}w_{1}w_{2}w_{3}\,
so that
w=z[1,4]\,
. With
\eta(1)=3
we find

y=\eta(z)^{*}=w_{1}w_{2}w_{3}w_{2}w_{1}w_{2}
, which implies that
v=y[1,3]=w_{1}w_{2}w_{3}
is a complementary word
w\dualmap v\,
. Then
the ordered elements of
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(w)
are
\alpha_{2}\prec_{z}\alpha_{2}+\alpha_{3}\prec_{z}\alpha_{3}\prec_{z}\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+\alpha_{3}
and those of
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(v)
are
\alpha_{1}\prec_{y}\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}\prec_{y}\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+\alpha_{3}\,
. Complementary words can also be constructed directly from the conditions in (
2.22
) by choosing a presentation for
t=\mathscr{r}(w^{\flat})q_{j}^{-1}
and adjoining
w_{\tau(w)}\,
.

In the rank 2 case, complementary words are unique. A complete discussion of this situation is provided in Section
2.7
below.

2.5.
Root Lattices and Special Elements

Let
J({s})\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}
be the set of indices
J({s})=\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{M}\}
occurring in a reduced expression
s=s_{i_{1}}\ldots s_{i_{M}}\,
. It is clear by either Matsumoto’s theorem or properties of parabolic subgroups in Section 2.4 of
[
11
]
(or the lemma below) that
J({s})
does not depend on the choice of this presentation.

Denote also by
\,\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}(s)=\langle\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)\rangle_{\mathbb{Z}}\subset\mathbb{Z}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}
the sublattice of the root lattice generated by roots in the inversion set
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)
. It admits the following simple description in terms of the set
J({s})\,
.

Lemma 2.10
.

The subset
\{\alpha_{i}\in\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}\,:\,i\in J({s})\}
is a basis for

\,\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}(s)\,
.

Proof.

Proceeding by induction in
l(s)
, we note that for
s=s_{j}
we have

\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}(s)=\langle\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s_{j})\rangle_{\mathbb{Z}}=\langle\{\alpha_{j}\}\rangle_{\mathbb{Z}}=\mathbb{Z}\alpha_{j}\,
as desired.
Suppose now
\,t=s_{k}\cdot s\,
with
l(t)=l(s)+1
and assume the claim holds for
s\,
.
By Corollary
2.4
we then have

\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(t)=s_{k}\left({\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)}\right)\sqcup\{s_{k}\}
and, hence,

\,\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}(t)=s_{k}\left({\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}(s)}\right)+\mathbb{Z}\alpha_{k}\,
.
By induction hypothesis
\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}(s)
is spanned by all
\alpha_{i}
with
i\in J({s})
so that the first summand is spanned by all

s_{k}(\alpha_{i})=\alpha_{i}-A_{ki}\alpha_{k}
with
i\in J({s})
. Hence,

\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Xi}$}}}(t)
is spanned as a lattice by all
\alpha_{i}
with

i\in J({s})\cup\{k\}=J({t})
as desired.
∎

For later use in computations, we introduce the sum of roots
\theta(s)
and sum of coroots

\breve{\theta}(s)
as elements of lattices in
E
, namely,

(2.24)

\theta(s)=\sum_{\alpha\,\in\,\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)}\!\alpha\;\;\in\mathbb{Z}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\breve{\theta}(s)=\sum_{\alpha\,\in\,\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)}\tfrac{1}{d_{\alpha}}\alpha=\sum_{\alpha\,\in\,\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)}\breve{\alpha}\;\;\in\tfrac{1}{\mathsf{e}}\mathbb{Z}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}\;.

Here
\breve{\alpha}=d^{-1}_{\alpha}\alpha
are the usual coroots.
Observe also that, by (
2.4
), the pairings
\mathchoice{\left(\breve{\theta}(s)|\beta\right)}{(\breve{\theta}(s)|\beta)}{(\breve{\theta}(s)|\beta)}{(\breve{\theta}(s)|\beta)}
are integers for any
\beta\in\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}
and any
s\in\mathscr{W}
. Corollary
2.4
and
\mathscr{W}
-invariance of
d_{\alpha}
readily imply that for elements
t_{1},t_{2}\in\mathscr{W}
and
s=t_{1}\cdot t_{2}
with
l(s)=l(t_{1})+l(t_{2})
we have

(2.25)

\theta(s)\,=\,\theta(t_{1})\,+\,t_{1}\!\left({\theta(t_{2})}\right)\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\breve{\theta}(s)\,=\,\breve{\theta}(t_{1})\,+\,t_{1}\!\left({\breve{\theta}(t_{2})}\right)\,.

The following mirror relations for both roots sets and root sums are immediate from (
2.9
) and (
2.24
).

(2.26)

\displaystyle s^{-1}(\theta(s))=-\theta(s^{-1})\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad s^{-1}(\breve{\theta}(s))=-\breve{\theta}(s^{-1})

Finally, the vectors
\theta(s)
and
\breve{\theta}(s)
can be expressed more directly using the usual half sums of positive roots or coroots via the formulae,

(2.27)

\displaystyle\theta(s)

\displaystyle=\rho-s(\rho)\qquad\mbox{and}

\displaystyle\quad\breve{\theta}(s)

\displaystyle=\breve{\rho}-s(\breve{\rho})\,,

\displaystyle\mbox{where}\qquad\rule{0.0pt}{14.22636pt}

\displaystyle\rho

\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}}\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2}\theta({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}})\qquad\mbox{and}

\displaystyle\quad\breve{\rho}

\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}}\breve{\alpha}=\tfrac{1}{2}\breve{\theta}({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}})\,.

The formula for
\theta(s)
is proved in Proposition 21.15 in
[
15
]
and the proof for the one for
\breve{\theta}(s)
is analogous using also invariance
d_{s(\alpha)}=d_{\alpha}\,
. Applying a simple reflection to (
2.27
), a standard argument shows that
\mathchoice{\left(\rho|\alpha_{i}\right)}{(\rho|\alpha_{i})}{(\rho|\alpha_{i})}{(\rho|\alpha_{i})}=\frac{1}{2}\mathchoice{\left(\alpha_{i}|\alpha_{i}\right)}{(\alpha_{i}|\alpha_{i})}{(\alpha_{i}|\alpha_{i})}{(\alpha_{i}|\alpha_{i})}=d_{i}
and
\mathchoice{\left(\breve{\rho}|\alpha_{i}\right)}{(\breve{\rho}|\alpha_{i})}{(\breve{\rho}|\alpha_{i})}{(\breve{\rho}|\alpha_{i})}=1
for all
\alpha_{i}\in\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}\,
.

The latter allows us to express the height function
0pt
, given as
0pt(\beta)=\sum_{i}b_{i}
for a root vector
\beta=\sum_{i}b_{b}\alpha_{i}
, as
0pt(\beta)=\mathchoice{\left(\breve{\rho}|\beta\right)}{(\breve{\rho}|\beta)}{(\breve{\rho}|\beta)}{(\breve{\rho}|\beta)}\,
. Thus, together with
(
2.27
) we can write

(2.28)

\mathchoice{\left(\breve{\theta}(s)|\beta\right)}{(\breve{\theta}(s)|\beta)}{(\breve{\theta}(s)|\beta)}{(\breve{\theta}(s)|\beta)}\,=\,0pt(\beta)-0pt(s^{-1}(\beta))\quad\in\mathbb{Z}\,.

Finally, we note that
\rho
is an element of the weight lattice

\mathsf{\Sigma}

and that

\breve{\rho}\in\tfrac{1}{\mathsf{e}}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Sigma}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Sigma}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Sigma}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Sigma}$}}}\,
.

2.6.

\mathsf{\Phi}

-Symmetric Lattice Maps

In preparation for the construction
of a large family of automorphisms on quantum groups in Section
4.2
, we generalize some classical notions of root systems to non-canonical integral inner products on
E
.

We say that a lattice homomorphism
\mathsfit h:{\mathbb{Z}}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}\rightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}

is

\mathsf{\Phi}

-symmetric
if
\mathchoice{\left(\mathsfit h(\mu)|\nu\right)}{(\mathsfit h(\mu)|\nu)}{(\mathsfit h(\mu)|\nu)}{(\mathsfit h(\mu)|\nu)}=\mathchoice{\left(\mu|\mathsfit h(\nu)\right)}{(\mu|\mathsfit h(\nu))}{(\mu|\mathsfit h(\nu))}{(\mu|\mathsfit h(\nu))}
for all
\mu,\nu\in\mathbb{Z}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}\,
, that is,
\mathsfit h
is symmetric with respect to an underlying Euclidean space
E\,
. Denote also
{\mathbb{S}}(\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}})
the space of such

\mathsf{\Phi}

-symmetric maps, which, thus, forms a sublattice of
\,\mathrm{End}({\mathbb{Z}}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}})
of
rank
\binom{n+1}{2}\,
. Note that the quotient
\mathrm{End}({\mathbb{Z}}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}})/{\mathbb{S}}(\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}})
will, generally, contain torsion.

Clearly, orthogonality of the Weyl group action implies that for any
s\in\mathscr{W}
and

\mathsf{\Phi}

-symmetric map
\mathsfit h
also
s{\mathsfit h}s^{-1}
is

\mathsf{\Phi}

-symmetric. Note that for any
\alpha\in\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}
, the Weyl reflection
s_{\alpha}\in{\mathbb{S}}(\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}})
since
s_{\alpha}=s_{\alpha}^{-1}
. Hence, any integer combination of such reflections
\sum_{\alpha}c_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}
is also

\mathsf{\Phi}

-symmetric.
Generalizing the element
\rho
from (
2.27
), we define for
a given

\mathsf{\Phi}

-symmetric lattice map
\mathsfit h
the vector
\rho_{\mathsfit h}
in
E
via the condition

(2.29)

\mathchoice{\left(\rho_{\mathsfit h}|\alpha_{i}\right)}{(\rho_{\mathsfit h}|\alpha_{i})}{(\rho_{\mathsfit h}|\alpha_{i})}{(\rho_{\mathsfit h}|\alpha_{i})}\,=\,\tfrac{1}{2}\mathchoice{\left(\alpha_{i}|\mathsfit h(\alpha_{i})\right)}{(\alpha_{i}|\mathsfit h(\alpha_{i}))}{(\alpha_{i}|\mathsfit h(\alpha_{i}))}{(\alpha_{i}|\mathsfit h(\alpha_{i}))}\,.

While the concept of

\mathsf{\Phi}

-symmetric maps does not depend on the choice of a simple root system, the definition of
\rho_{\mathsfit h}
strongly depends on a choice of

\mathsf{\Delta}

.
We, further, generalize formula (
2.27
) for the sum
\theta(s)
above by setting for any
s\in\mathscr{W}

(2.30)

\theta_{\mathsfit h}(s)\,=\,\rho_{s{\mathsfit h}s^{-1}}\,-\,s(\rho_{\mathsfit h})\,.

Several basic properties of these objects are summarized in the following lemma, where

\mathsf{\Sigma}

is the weight lattice associated to

\mathsf{\Phi}

and
\mathsfit i\!d:\mathbb{Z}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}
is the identity map, which is obviously

\mathsf{\Phi}

-symmetric.

Lemma 2.11
.

For any

\mathsf{\Phi}

-symmetric lattice maps
\mathsfit h,\mathsfit k\in{\mathbb{S}}(\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}})
, any root vector
\beta\in\mathbb{Z}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}
, any Weyl group elements
s,t\in\mathscr{W}
, and any
m\in\mathbb{Z}
the following hold:

i)

\rho_{\mathsfit h+\mathsfit k}=\rho_{\mathsfit h}+\rho_{\mathsfit k}\,,

ii)

\rho_{\mathsfit h}\in\frac{1}{2}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Sigma}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Sigma}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Sigma}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Sigma}$}}}\,,

iii)

\rho_{m\cdot\mathsfit i\!d}=m\cdot\rho\,,

iv)

\mathchoice{\left(\beta|\mathsfit h(\beta)\right)}{(\beta|\mathsfit h(\beta))}{(\beta|\mathsfit h(\beta))}{(\beta|\mathsfit h(\beta))}-2\mathchoice{\left(\rho_{\mathsfit h}|\beta\right)}{(\rho_{\mathsfit h}|\beta)}{(\rho_{\mathsfit h}|\beta)}{(\rho_{\mathsfit h}|\beta)}\;\in\;2\mathbb{Z}

v)

\theta_{\mathsfit h+\mathsfit k}(s)=\theta_{\mathsfit h}(s)+\theta_{\mathsfit k}(s)\,,

vi)

\mathchoice{\left(\theta_{\mathsfit h}(s)|\beta\right)}{(\theta_{\mathsfit h}(s)|\beta)}{(\theta_{\mathsfit h}(s)|\beta)}{(\theta_{\mathsfit h}(s)|\beta)}\;\in\;\mathbb{Z}\,,

vii)

\theta_{m\cdot\mathsfit i\!d}(s)=m\cdot\theta(s)\,,

viii)

\theta_{\mathsfit h}(ts)=\theta_{s{\mathsfit h}s^{-1}}(t)+t\left({\theta_{\mathsfit h}(s)}\right)\,.

Proof.

Items
i)
,
iii)
,

v)
,
vii)
, and
viii)
are immediate from the definitions in (
2.29
) and (
2.30
) as well as the formulae for
\theta(s)
and
\rho
in (
2.27
).
For the statement in
ii)
note that
\mathchoice{\left(\rho_{\mathsfit h}|\breve{\alpha}_{i}\right)}{(\rho_{\mathsfit h}|\breve{\alpha}_{i})}{(\rho_{\mathsfit h}|\breve{\alpha}_{i})}{(\rho_{\mathsfit h}|\breve{\alpha}_{i})}=d_{i}^{-1}\mathchoice{\left(\rho_{\mathsfit h}|\alpha_{i}\right)}{(\rho_{\mathsfit h}|\alpha_{i})}{(\rho_{\mathsfit h}|\alpha_{i})}{(\rho_{\mathsfit h}|\alpha_{i})}=\frac{1}{2}d_{i}^{-1}\mathchoice{\left(\alpha_{i}|{\mathsfit h}(\alpha_{i})\right)}{(\alpha_{i}|{\mathsfit h}(\alpha_{i}))}{(\alpha_{i}|{\mathsfit h}(\alpha_{i}))}{(\alpha_{i}|{\mathsfit h}(\alpha_{i}))}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j}d_{i}^{-1}\mathchoice{\left(\alpha_{i}|\alpha_{j}\right)}{(\alpha_{i}|\alpha_{j})}{(\alpha_{i}|\alpha_{j})}{(\alpha_{i}|\alpha_{j})}{\mathsfit h}_{ji}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j}A_{ij}{\mathsfit h}_{ji}\in\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}
, where
\breve{\alpha}_{i}=d^{-1}_{i}\alpha_{i}
is the usual coroot,
A_{ij}
the Cartan data, and
{\mathsfit h}_{ji}
are the matrix coefficients of
\mathsfit h
in the

\mathsf{\Delta}

-basis.

For
\beta=\sum_{i}b_{i}\alpha_{i}
and using symmetry of
n_{ij}=\mathchoice{\left(\alpha_{i}|\mathsfit h(\alpha_{j})\right)}{(\alpha_{i}|\mathsfit h(\alpha_{j}))}{(\alpha_{i}|\mathsfit h(\alpha_{j}))}{(\alpha_{i}|\mathsfit h(\alpha_{j}))}
the expression in
iv)
can be worked out as
2\sum_{i>j}b_{i}b_{j}n_{ij}\,+\,\sum_{i}(b_{i}^{2}-b_{i})n_{ii}\,
, which is clearly in
2\mathbb{Z}\,
. For Item

vi)
, note that both terms
\mathchoice{\left(s^{-1}(\beta)|\mathsfit h(s^{-1}(\beta))\right)}{(s^{-1}(\beta)|\mathsfit h(s^{-1}(\beta)))}{(s^{-1}(\beta)|\mathsfit h(s^{-1}(\beta)))}{(s^{-1}(\beta)|\mathsfit h(s^{-1}(\beta)))}-2\mathchoice{\left(\rho_{\mathsfit h}|s^{-1}(\beta)\right)}{(\rho_{\mathsfit h}|s^{-1}(\beta))}{(\rho_{\mathsfit h}|s^{-1}(\beta))}{(\rho_{\mathsfit h}|s^{-1}(\beta))}=\mathchoice{\left(\beta|(s\mathsfit hs^{-1})(\beta)\right)}{(\beta|(s\mathsfit hs^{-1})(\beta))}{(\beta|(s\mathsfit hs^{-1})(\beta))}{(\beta|(s\mathsfit hs^{-1})(\beta))}-2\mathchoice{\left(s(\rho_{\mathsfit h})|\beta\right)}{(s(\rho_{\mathsfit h})|\beta)}{(s(\rho_{\mathsfit h})|\beta)}{(s(\rho_{\mathsfit h})|\beta)}
and
\mathchoice{\left(\beta|(s\mathsfit hs^{-1})(\beta)\right)}{(\beta|(s\mathsfit hs^{-1})(\beta))}{(\beta|(s\mathsfit hs^{-1})(\beta))}{(\beta|(s\mathsfit hs^{-1})(\beta))}-2\mathchoice{\left(\rho_{s{\mathsfit h}s^{-1}}|\beta\right)}{(\rho_{s{\mathsfit h}s^{-1}}|\beta)}{(\rho_{s{\mathsfit h}s^{-1}}|\beta)}{(\rho_{s{\mathsfit h}s^{-1}}|\beta)}
are in
2\mathbb{Z}
by
iv)
. Thus, also their difference
2\mathchoice{\left(\theta_{\mathsfit h}(s)|\beta\right)}{(\theta_{\mathsfit h}(s)|\beta)}{(\theta_{\mathsfit h}(s)|\beta)}{(\theta_{\mathsfit h}(s)|\beta)}
has to be in
2\mathbb{Z}\,
.
∎

For an illustration of these notions, we briefly discuss the rank 2 root systems. We assume
A_{12}=\mathsf{e}\in\{1,2,3\}
depending on whether

\mathsf{\Phi}

is of type
\mathsf{A}_{2}
,
\mathsf{B}_{2}
, or
\mathsf{G}_{2}
, as well as
A_{21}=-1\,
. A
\mathbb{Z}
-basis for
{\mathbb{S}}(\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}})
for any type is given by
\{\mathsfit i\!d,s_{1},s_{2}\}
where
s_{i}=s_{\alpha_{i}}
are the usual reflections along the simple roots.
Note that
s_{12}=s_{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}=s_{2}s_{1}s_{2}=(\mathsf{e}-2)s_{2}-s_{1}
. So,
\{\mathsfit i\!d,s_{1},s_{12}\}
would be an alternate basis for
\mathsf{e}\in\{1,3\}
but not for
\mathsf{e}=2\,
.
It follows from elementary calculations that
\,\mathrm{End}({\mathbb{Z}}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}})/{\mathbb{S}}(\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}})
is
\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{F}_{2}\,
for
\mathsf{e}=2
but only
\mathbb{Z}
for
\mathsf{e}\in\{1,3\}\,
.

Since
\rho_{\mathsfit h}
is additive in
{\mathsfit h}
is suffices to compute the vector for the basis elements
\{\mathsfit i\!d,s_{1},s_{2}\}
, for which we already know that
\rho_{\mathsfit i\!d}=\rho\,
. The other two elements are computed as

\displaystyle\rho_{s_{1}}

\displaystyle=-\tfrac{1}{2}(1+(\mathsf{e}-1)(2\mathsf{e}-3))\alpha_{1}\,-\,\tfrac{1}{2}(\mathsf{e}-1)^{2}\alpha_{2}\,,

\displaystyle\rho_{s_{2}}

\displaystyle=-(\mathsf{e}-1)^{2}\alpha_{1}-\tfrac{1}{2}(1+(\mathsf{e}-1)^{2})\alpha_{2}\,.

Thus, even in the
\mathsf{e}=1
(
\mathsf{A}_{2}
) case we have
\rho_{s_{i}}=-\tfrac{1}{2}\alpha_{i}\not\in\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Sigma}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Sigma}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Sigma}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Sigma}$}}}\,
, as opposed to
\rho\,
. Similarly, for the
\theta_{\mathsfit h}(s)
is suffices to consider
\mathsfit h\in\{s_{1},s_{2}\}\,
. The values
\theta_{s_{i}}(s_{j})
are explicitly computed below:

\displaystyle\theta_{s_{1}}(s_{1})

\displaystyle=s_{1}(\alpha_{1})=-\alpha_{1}\,,

\displaystyle\theta_{s_{1}}(s_{2})

\displaystyle=s_{1}(\alpha_{2})=\mathsf{e}\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}\,,

\displaystyle\rule{0.0pt}{8.53581pt}\theta_{s_{2}}(s_{2})

\displaystyle=s_{2}(\alpha_{2})=-\alpha_{2}\,,

\displaystyle\theta_{s_{1}}(s_{2})

\displaystyle=s_{2}(\alpha_{1})+\mbox{${\binom{\mathsf{e}}{2}}$}\alpha_{1}=\tfrac{1}{2}(\mathsf{e}^{2}-\mathsf{e}+2)\alpha_{1}+\mathsf{e}\alpha_{2}\,.

From these one can obtain
\theta_{s_{i}}(s)
using the
recursion in Item
viii)
of Lemma
2.11
together with the explicit formulae
s_{i}s_{j}s_{i}=(\mathsf{e}-2)s_{i}-s_{j}
for
i\neq j
for the adjoint action of
\mathscr{W}
on
\langle s_{1},s_{2}\rangle\subset{\mathbb{S}}(\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}})\,
. In particular, we see that in this example

\theta_{\mathsfit h}(s)\in\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}\,
for all
s\in\mathscr{W}
and
\mathsfit h\in{\mathbb{S}}(\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}})\,
.
Consider the case
\mathsf{e}=1
(
\mathsf{A}_{2}
) , for which
\theta_{s_{j}}(s_{i})=s_{i}(\alpha_{j})=s_{j}(\alpha_{i})
, suppose
\mathsfit h=n_{1}s_{1}+n_{2}s_{2}\,
, and set
\beta=n_{1}\alpha_{1}+n_{2}\alpha_{2}\,
. The suggested computation then yields that

\displaystyle\theta_{\mathsfit h}(s)=s(\beta)\quad\mbox{if $\,l(s)\,$ is odd}\qquad\mbox{and }\qquad\theta_{\mathsfit h}(s)=0\quad\mbox{if $\,l(s)\,$ is even.}

We defer further discussion of

\mathsf{\Phi}

-symmetric maps to future work. Open questions include whether one can always find a subset
\mathscr{T}\subset{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
such that
\{s_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\mathscr{T}\}
is a
\mathbb{Z}
-basis for
{\mathbb{S}}(\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}})
and how to use this to efficiently compute the
\rho_{\mathsfit h}
and

\theta_{\mathsfit h}(s)
in generality. Other questions are whether
\theta_{\mathsfit h}(s)\in\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}
also for higher ranks and what the possible torsion factors of
\,\mathrm{End}({\mathbb{Z}}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}})/{\mathbb{S}}(\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}})
are.

2.7.
Rank 2 Subsystems

As a simple but useful example, consider the Coxeter subsystem for the generator set
\{s_{i},s_{j}\}\,
, given two distinct but fixed indices
i,j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\,
. The respective Weyl subgroup
\mathscr{W}\mkern-4.0mu\raise-0.39993pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle(i,j)$}
is a dihedral group of order
2m_{ij}\in\{4,6,8,12\}\,
. The longest element
\mathchoice{{s}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{s}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{s}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{s}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}}
is given by the expressions in (
2.6
) and, hence, of length
l(\mathchoice{{s}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{s}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{s}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{s}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}})=m_{ij}
.
The element of maximal length has two word presentations given by

(2.31)

\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}\mkern-2.5mu\raise-0.59998pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle(i,j)$}=\{\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}},\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ji$}}\}=\mathscr{r}^{-1}(\mathchoice{{s}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{s}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{s}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{s}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}})\,,

where the words with
m_{ij}
letters are
\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}}=w_{i}w_{j}\ldots
and
\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ji$}}=w_{j}w_{i}\ldots\,
.
Thus, Matsumoto’s Theorem says that two reduced
w,w^{\prime}\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
represent the same

s=\mathscr{r}(w)=\mathscr{r}(w^{\prime})
if
w^{\prime}
is obtained from
w
by successively swapping sub words
\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}}\leftrightharpoons\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ji$}}\,
.

For any element
s\in\mathscr{W}\mkern-4.0mu\raise-0.39993pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle(i,j)$}
with
l(s)<m_{ij}
there is exactly one reduced word
in
\mathscr{r}^{-1}(s)\subset\mathscr{W}^{*}\mkern-4.0mu\raise-0.59998pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle(i,j)$}
representing
s
. To simplify notation here and in later applications, let
m=m_{ij}
as well as

(2.32)

a_{r}=\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}}[1,r]=\begin{cases}(w_{i}w_{j})^{\frac{r}{2}}&r\mbox{ even}\\
(w_{i}w_{j})^{\frac{r-1}{2}}w_{i}&r\mbox{ odd}\end{cases}\qquad b_{r}=\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ji$}}[1,r]=\begin{cases}(w_{j}w_{i})^{\frac{r}{2}}&r\mbox{ even}\\
(w_{j}w_{i})^{\frac{r-1}{2}}w_{j}&r\mbox{ odd}\end{cases}\;

for
0\leq r\leq m
, so,
a_{m}=\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}}
and
b_{m}=\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ji$}}\,
and
l(a_{r})=l(b_{r})=r\,
. The
a_{r}
and
b_{r}
provide a distinct enumeration of elements in
\mathscr{W}^{*}\mkern-4.0mu\raise-0.59998pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle(i,j)$}
with the exception of the empty word
a_{0}=b_{0}=\scalebox{.9}{$\emptyset$}\,
. This organization
of words provides a succinct way of expressing the complementary word relations introduced in
Section
2.4
.

Lemma 2.12
.

With notation as above, (non-empty) complementary words are uniquely given for all finite Coxeter types by

a_{r}\dualmap b_{m+1-r}\;.

Proof.

Note that for
m=3
we have
\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}}^{*}=\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}}
and

\eta(\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}})=\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ji$}}
, whereas for
m\in\{4,6\}
we have

\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}}^{*}=\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ji$}}
and
\eta(\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ji$}})=\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ji$}}\,
. Thus,
\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}}^{\dagger}=\eta(\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}}^{*})=\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ji$}}
for all Lie types, which implies the statement by
(
2.23
). Uniqueness is also clear since
b_{m+1-r}
is the only word matching the length constraint and the constraint on the final letter index.
∎

In order to describe the total orders on rank 2 root systems implied by the two words
\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}}
and

\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ji$}}
we choose

to be the shorter and
\alpha_{j}
to be the longer root. Thus, in the conventions from

, the Cartan data is given as
-A_{ji}=d_{i}=1
and

depending on Lie type. Following the definitions in
