\displaystyle\left({(s_{*}\boldsymbol{\iota})\cdot\boldsymbol{\iota}^{-1}\cdot\mathchoice{\vartheta^{\mathsfit i\!d}\mkern-9.0mu\raisebox{-1.7pt}{$\scriptstyle s$}\mkern 2.7mu}{\vartheta^{\mathsfit i\!d}\mkern-9.0mu\raisebox{-1.7pt}{$\scriptstyle s$}\mkern 2.7mu}{\vartheta^{\mathsfit i\!d}\mkern-9.0mu\raisebox{-1.7pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle s$}\mkern 2.7mu}{\vartheta^{\mathsfit i\!d}\mkern-3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle s}}}\right)(\beta)

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\iota}(s^{-1}(\beta))\boldsymbol{\iota}(\beta)^{-1}\mathchoice{\vartheta^{\mathsfit i\!d}\mkern-9.0mu\raisebox{-1.7pt}{$\scriptstyle s$}\mkern 2.7mu}{\vartheta^{\mathsfit i\!d}\mkern-9.0mu\raisebox{-1.7pt}{$\scriptstyle s$}\mkern 2.7mu}{\vartheta^{\mathsfit i\!d}\mkern-9.0mu\raisebox{-1.7pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle s$}\mkern 2.7mu}{\vartheta^{\mathsfit i\!d}\mkern-3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle s}}(\beta)

\displaystyle=(-1)^{\mathchoice{\left(\breve{\rho}|s^{-1}(\beta)\right)}{(\breve{\rho}|s^{-1}(\beta))}{(\breve{\rho}|s^{-1}(\beta))}{(\breve{\rho}|s^{-1}(\beta))}}(-1)^{-\mathchoice{\left(\breve{\rho}|\beta\right)}{(\breve{\rho}|\beta)}{(\breve{\rho}|\beta)}{(\breve{\rho}|\beta)}}q^{-\mathchoice{\left(\theta_{\mathsfit i\!d}(s)|\beta\right)}{(\theta_{\mathsfit i\!d}(s)|\beta)}{(\theta_{\mathsfit i\!d}(s)|\beta)}{(\theta_{\mathsfit i\!d}(s)|\beta)}}

\displaystyle=(-1)^{\mathchoice{\left(s(\breve{\rho})|\beta\right)}{(s(\breve{\rho})|\beta)}{(s(\breve{\rho})|\beta)}{(s(\breve{\rho})|\beta)}-\mathchoice{\left(\breve{\rho}|\beta\right)}{(\breve{\rho}|\beta)}{(\breve{\rho}|\beta)}{(\breve{\rho}|\beta)}}q^{-\mathchoice{\left(\theta(s)|\beta\right)}{(\theta(s)|\beta)}{(\theta(s)|\beta)}{(\theta(s)|\beta)}}

\displaystyle=(-1)^{\mathchoice{\left(\breve{\theta}(s)|\beta\right)}{(\breve{\theta}(s)|\beta)}{(\breve{\theta}(s)|\beta)}{(\breve{\theta}(s)|\beta)}}q^{-\mathchoice{\left(\theta(s)|\beta\right)}{(\theta(s)|\beta)}{(\theta(s)|\beta)}{(\theta(s)|\beta)}}\qquad=\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{s}(\beta)\,.

The following verification of the first identity invokes the expression in (

) for the antipode, the commutation rule from Proposition

, the conjugation with
\mho
from (

), homomorphy from Proposition

, and the above relation for

.

\displaystyle S\circ(\mathit{\Gamma}_{s})^{-1}

\displaystyle=\mho\circ\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{\mathsfit i\!d}_{\boldsymbol{\iota}}\circ(\mathit{\Gamma}_{s})^{-1}

\displaystyle=\mho\circ(\mathit{\Gamma}_{s})^{-1}\circ\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{\mathsfit i\!d}_{(s_{*}\boldsymbol{\iota})\cdot\mathchoice{\vartheta^{\mathsfit i\!d}\mkern-9.0mu\raisebox{-1.7pt}{$\scriptstyle s$}\mkern 2.7mu}{\vartheta^{\mathsfit i\!d}\mkern-9.0mu\raisebox{-1.7pt}{$\scriptstyle s$}\mkern 2.7mu}{\vartheta^{\mathsfit i\!d}\mkern-9.0mu\raisebox{-1.7pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle s$}\mkern 2.7mu}{\vartheta^{\mathsfit i\!d}\mkern-3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle s}}}

\displaystyle=\mathit{\Gamma}_{(s^{-1})}\circ\mho\circ\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{\mathsfit i\!d}_{(s_{*}\boldsymbol{\iota})\cdot\mathchoice{\vartheta^{\mathsfit i\!d}\mkern-9.0mu\raisebox{-1.7pt}{$\scriptstyle s$}\mkern 2.7mu}{\vartheta^{\mathsfit i\!d}\mkern-9.0mu\raisebox{-1.7pt}{$\scriptstyle s$}\mkern 2.7mu}{\vartheta^{\mathsfit i\!d}\mkern-9.0mu\raisebox{-1.7pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle s$}\mkern 2.7mu}{\vartheta^{\mathsfit i\!d}\mkern-3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle s}}}

\displaystyle=\mathit{\Gamma}_{(s^{-1})}\circ S\circ(\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt

Ch}^{0}_{\boldsymbol{\iota}^{-1}\cdot(s_{*}\boldsymbol{\iota})\cdot\mathchoice{\vartheta^{\mathsfit i\!d}\mkern-9.0mu\raisebox{-1.7pt}{$\scriptstyle s$}\mkern 2.7mu}{\vartheta^{\mathsfit i\!d}\mkern-9.0mu\raisebox{-1.7pt}{$\scriptstyle s$}\mkern 2.7mu}{\vartheta^{\mathsfit i\!d}\mkern-9.0mu\raisebox{-1.7pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle s$}\mkern 2.7mu}{\vartheta^{\mathsfit i\!d}\mkern-3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle s}}}

\displaystyle=\mathit{\Gamma}_{(s^{-1})}\circ S\circ\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{0}_{\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{s}}

The second identity can be derived from the first by replacing

with
s^{-1}
and (
4.31
). Specifically,

S\circ(\mathit{\Gamma}_{(s^{-1})})^{-1}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}\circ S\circ\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{0}_{\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{(s^{-1})}}
implies

(\mathit{\Gamma}_{s})^{-1}\circ S=S\circ\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{0}_{\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{(s^{-1})}}\circ\mathit{\Gamma}_{(s^{-1})}=S\circ\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt

The character
\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{s}
also appears in commutation relations of the Artin-Tits groups action with the conjugation anti-automorphism
\Upsilon\,
.

Proposition 4.5
.

For any element
s\in\mathscr{W}
we have

(4.33)

\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}\circ\Upsilon\,=\,\Upsilon\circ\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}\circ\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{0}_{\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{(s^{-1})}}\,=\,\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{0}_{\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{s}}\circ\Upsilon\circ\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}\,.

Proof.

The second equality follows from
\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}\circ\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{0}_{\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{(s^{-1})}}=\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{0}_{s_{*}\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{(s^{-1})}}\circ\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}=\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{0}_{\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{s}^{-1}}\circ\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}
by (
4.29
) and (
4.31
) as well as (
4.15
).
For
s=s_{i}
equation (
4.33
) applied to a generator
E_{j}
reads

\displaystyle\mathit{\Gamma}_{i}(E_{j})

\displaystyle=\Upsilon(\mathit{\Gamma}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{s_{i}}(\alpha_{j})E_{j}))=\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{s_{i}}(\alpha_{j})^{-1}\Upsilon(\mathit{\Gamma}_{i}(E_{j}))

\displaystyle=(-1)^{\mathchoice{\left(\breve{\alpha}_{i}|\alpha_{j}\right)}{(\breve{\alpha}_{i}|\alpha_{j})}{(\breve{\alpha}_{i}|\alpha_{j})}{(\breve{\alpha}_{i}|\alpha_{j})}}q^{\mathchoice{\left(\alpha_{i}|\alpha_{j}\right)}{(\alpha_{i}|\alpha_{j})}{(\alpha_{i}|\alpha_{j})}{(\alpha_{i}|\alpha_{j})}}\Upsilon(\mathit{\Gamma}_{i}(E_{j}))=(-1)^{A_{ij}}q_{i}^{A_{ij}}\Upsilon(\mathit{\Gamma}_{i}(E_{j}))\,.

This is readily verified for both the
i=j
and
i\neq j
cases from (
4.18
), (
4.20
), and (
4.12
). Since
\Omega
commutes with both
\mathit{\Gamma}_{i}
and
\Upsilon
and, furthermore, inverts
q
the relation for
s=s_{i}
also holds on
F_{i}
. As it is also trivially true on
K_{i}
we proved (
4.33
) for
s=s_{i}
.
Suppose now (
4.33
) holds for two elements
s,t\in\mathscr{W}
with
l(s)\,,l(t)\geq 1
and
l(ts)=l(t)+l(s)
. Then

\displaystyle\mathit{\Gamma}_{ts}\circ\Upsilon

\displaystyle=\mathit{\Gamma}_{t}\circ\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}\circ\Upsilon=\mathit{\Gamma}_{t}\circ\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{0}_{\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{s}}\circ\Upsilon\circ\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}=\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{0}_{t_{*}(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{s})}\circ\mathit{\Gamma}_{t}\circ\Upsilon\circ\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}

\displaystyle=\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{0}_{t_{*}(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{s})}\circ\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{0}_{\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{t}}\circ\Upsilon\circ\mathit{\Gamma}_{t}\circ\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}=\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{0}_{t_{*}(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{s})\cdot\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{t}}\circ\Upsilon\circ\mathit{\Gamma}_{ts}=\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{0}_{\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{ts}}\circ\Upsilon\circ\mathit{\Gamma}_{ts}\,,

where we used (
4.29
) and (
4.31
). The assertion now follows by induction.
∎

5.
Generators, Bases, and Integrality

Ponicaré-Birkhoff-Witt (PBW) bases have been established for quantum deformations of Lie algberas in many settings. These typically consider quantum algebras defined over a field such as
\mathbb{Q}(q)
or
\mathbb{C}
and assume specific fixed choices with respect to which the quantum analogs of the
E_{\alpha}
operators are defined. See, for example,
[
65
,
16
,
36
,
63
,
47
]
.

Lusztig describes the algebras
{\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{L}$}}{U}^{{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}}
of divided powers as free modules over
\Lambda_{q}
in
[
45
,
46
]
for specific choices of
E_{\alpha}\,
. In
[
47
]
explains independence of some of these choices for respective bases over
\mathbb{Q}(q)\,
. Specifically,
certain spanning sets

{\mathfrak{B}}\mkern-1.0mu

\scriptstyle+\hskip-3.01389pt
\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}
of monomial expressions, to be defined below, will depend on the choice of a maxiaml reduced word
w\in\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}\,
.

Corollary 40.2.2 in
[
47
]
implies that

{\mathfrak{B}}\mkern-1.0mu

\scriptstyle+\hskip-3.01389pt
\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}
is a basis of
U_{q,\mathbb{Q}}^{+}
over the field
\mathbb{Q}(q)\,
for all Lie types and all choices of
w
, which also implies that

{\mathfrak{B}}\mkern-1.0mu

\scriptstyle+\hskip-3.01389pt
\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}
is a linearily independent set of generators for the
\Lambda_{q,{\mathsf{e}^{*}}}
-module
U_{q}^{+}\,
and that
its span

{\mathfrak{S}}\mkern-1.0mu

\scriptstyle+\hskip-3.01389pt
\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}
is a free
\Lambda_{q,{\mathsf{e}^{*}}}
-module. The
\mathbb{Q}(q)
-basis does, however, not exclude the possibility that

\mathcal{T}_{w}=U_{q}^{+}/{\scalebox{.96}{${\mathfrak{S}}\mkern-1.0mu$}}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle+\hskip-3.01389pt$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-3.77936pt}{\hskip-3.77936pt}{\hskip-2.70573pt}{\hskip-2.45294pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 25.90247pt}
is a non-zero torsion module and, thus, does not imply that

{\mathfrak{B}}\mkern-1.0mu

\scriptstyle+\hskip-3.01389pt
\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}
is also a
\Lambda_{q,{\mathsf{e}^{*}}}
-basis.

For versions of
U_{q}^{+}
for classical Lie types, bases over
\Lambda_{q}
are obtained from iterated
q
-brackets in
[
70
]
for specific lexicographic orderings. In the formalism and constructions of generators used there, however, it is difficult to describe quasi-triangular Hopf algebra structures or braid actions for reordering. Still, the example provided in Proposition 5.6 in the same paper illustrates the delicate dependence of integrality of bases on the chosen orders.

Specifically, Takeuchi shows for an algebra
\bar{\mathscr{B}}_{3}^{\circ}\,
, which can be roughly understood as a quotient of
U_{q}^{+}
for Lie type
\mathsf{B}_{3}\,
, that the analog of the torsion module
\mathcal{T}_{w}
is indeed zero for a convex ordering but contains non-zero torsion summands such
as
\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]/\langle q^{3}-q^{2}+1\rangle
for a non-convexly ordered monomial basis. A careful treatment of orderings will thus have to be a crucial component in the derivation of integral PBW bases.

The plan of this section is to adapt arguments in
[
45
,
46
]
and related references to infer PBW bases that generate the algebras
U_{q}^{\pm}
and
U_{q}
as free
\Lambda_{q,{\mathsf{e}^{*}}}
and
\Lambda_{q,{\mathsf{e}^{*}}}^{\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{0.87694pt}{\scalebox{.47}{$\blacktriangledown$}}}
modules respectively. Generators
E_{w}
depending on reduced words
w\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
are constructed in Section
5.1
and some of their basic properties discussed. From these monomial expressions that, in addition, depend on exponent functions are introduced, their relations with the two anti-involutions
\Omega
and
\mho
are explained in Section
5.3
. A formalism for the spanning sets associated to the monomials is laid out in Section
5.7
, where a general criterion for order independence is derived.

The relations between the box pre-orderings introduced by Lusztig, convex orderings, and words representing the longest elements in
\mathscr{W}
are explained in Section
5.5
. Lusztig’s proof of PBW bases is adapted to the
U_{q}
-algebras in Section
5.6
and the general theorem for integral PBW bases for general orders is stated in Section
5.8
.

5.1.
Generators Associated to Words

In a series of articles, Lusztig defines of a generator
\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{\alpha}
for each
\alpha\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
, starting with a
presentation
\alpha=s_{i_{1}}\ldots s_{i_{k-1}}(\alpha_{i_{k}})
obtained from a maximal reduced word. The simple root
\alpha_{j}
is replaced by
E_{j}\,
and each
s_{i}
by an automorphism
T_{i}
described in Section
4.3
.
We will adopt and adjust the definition here by replacing the
T_{i}
by their inverses

\mathit{\Gamma}_{i}\,
and explicitly retain the dependence on words in the notation. That is, for a non-empty
reduced word
w=w_{i_{1}}\ldots w_{i_{k}}
and using the notation in (
2.8
) we set

(5.1)

E_{w}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{w^{\flat}}(E_{\tau(w)})=\mathit{\Gamma}_{i_{1}}\ldots\mathit{\Gamma}_{i_{k-1}}(E_{i_{k}})\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad F_{w}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{w^{\flat}}(F_{\tau(w)})\,.

As remarked in Section
4.3
, we may write
E_{w}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}(E_{j})
where
s=\mathscr{r}(w^{\flat})
and
j=\tau(w)\,
,
implying that
E_{w}
only depends on the pair
(s,j)\,
. Further redundancies in the labeling are implied by Proposition
5.1
below, from which one can easily obtain examples of distinct pairs
(s,j)\neq(s^{\prime},j^{\prime})
with
\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}(E_{j})=\mathit{\Gamma}_{s^{\prime}}(E_{j^{\prime}})\,
. For computations with specific words
w=w_{i_{1}}\ldots w_{i_{k}}
it is often convenient to also use the index notation

(5.2)

E_{w}=E_{(i_{1}\ldots i_{k})}\,.

Given a
fixed
reduced word
z\in\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}
of
maximal
length or, equivalently, a convex order
\preceq_{w}
on
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
, we will sometimes also use the abbreviated notation

(5.3)

E_{\alpha}=E_{z[\alpha]}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad F_{\alpha}=F_{z[\alpha]}

for an
\alpha\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
and with
z[\alpha]
as defined in (
2.15
). On occasion, we may also use the analogous notation for the respectively defined Cartan element
K_{w}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{w^{\flat}}(K_{\tau(w)})=K^{\nu}\,
, where
K^{\nu}
is as defined above (
4.2
) with
\nu=\gamma(w)\,
.
For most applications in this article the word labeling is, however, the preferred one
as we often consider orderings depending on choices of words.
We list next several immediate properties of these generators.

Suppose
w=u\cdot v
for non-empty reduced words
u,v\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
with
l(w)=l(u)+l(v)
and let
s=\mathscr{r}(u)
. Then (
5.1
) and (
4.22
) imply

(5.4)

E_{w}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}(E_{v})\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad F_{w}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}(F_{v})\,.

Furthermore, commutation of the
\mathit{\Gamma}_{i}
with
\Omega
yields the identity

(5.5)

\Omega(E_{w})=F_{w}\qquad\mbox{and }\qquad\Omega(F_{w})=E_{w}\;.

The generators from (
5.1
) as well as the Cartan element
K^{\nu}
are homogeneous elements,
for which gradings follow immediately from (
4.25
) and
(
4.26
) with notation from Lemma
2.2
.

(5.6)

\displaystyle\mathbb{w}(E_{w})

\displaystyle=\gamma(w)

\displaystyle\mathbb{w}(F_{w})

\displaystyle=-\gamma(w)

\displaystyle\mathbb{w}(K_{\nu})

\displaystyle=0

(5.7)

\displaystyle\mathbb{o}^{+}(E_{w})

\displaystyle=\gamma(w)\mod 2

\displaystyle\mathbb{o}^{+}(F_{w})

\displaystyle=0

\displaystyle\mathbb{o}^{+}(K_{\nu})

\displaystyle=\nu\mod 2

Extending the definition in (
5.1
) to non-reduced words leads to elements outside the respective Borel subalgebra, such as
E_{w_{i}\cdot w_{i}}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{i}(E_{i})\not\in U_{q}^{+}\,
. The proposition below states that this does not happen for reduced words. The statement is proved for simply laced Lie types

\mathsf{ADE}
in
[
45
]
. In our proof below, we extend the arguments from
[
45
]
to all Lie types
and the regular power quantum algebras
U_{q}^{\pm}
over
\Lambda_{q,{\mathsf{e}^{*}}}\,
. The second assertion on the uniqueness of generators graded by simple roots will be used in later computation of braid automorphisms.

Proposition 5.1
.

Suppose
w\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
is any non-empty reduced word. Then
E_{w}\in U_{q}^{+}
and
F_{w}\in U_{q}^{-}
.

Moreover, if
\gamma(w)=\alpha_{k}\in\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}\,
, then
E_{w}=E_{k}
and
F_{w}=F_{k}\,
.

Proof.

We first provide the proof of the statement for a rank 2 subalgebra
{U}_{\ \mkern-9.0muq}\mkern-1.5mu\raise 0.80002pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle(i,j)$}
generated by
\{E_{i},E_{j},F_{i},F_{j},K_{i},K_{j}\}
for some fixed pair of indices
i\neq j\,
. The notations
{U}_{\ \mkern-9.0muq}\mkern-1.5mu\raise 0.80002pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle(i,j)$}^{\pm}
and minimal ground rings are chosen analogous to those for
U_{q}\,
.
Omitting the trivial
A_{1}\times A_{1}
case, we thus consider the Lie types
\mathsf{A}_{2}
,
\mathsf{B}_{2}=\mathsf{C}_{2}
, and
\mathsf{G}_{2}\,
. As in Section 39.2 of
[
47
]
assume that
\alpha_{i}
is the shorter root. So,
A_{ji}=-1
and
A_{ij}=-\mathsf{e}
with
\mathsf{e}\in\{1,2,3\}\,
, as well as
d_{i}=1
and
d_{j}=\mathsf{e}\,
.

The respective sets of reduced words
\mathscr{W}^{*}\mkern-4.0mu\raise-0.59998pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle(i,j)$}
are given by alternating sequences of
w_{i}
and
w_{j}
of length at most
m_{ij}\in\{3,4,6\}
have been described in Section
2.7
and subject to (
2.6
).

Note that the automorphisms
\mathit{\Gamma}_{i}
from (
4.18
) through (
4.21
) coincide with the
T^{\prime}_{i,-1}

operators defined in Section 37.1.3 of
[
47
]
. There, Lusztig computes the
E_{z}
explicitly for every non-empty reduced word
z\in\mathscr{W}^{*}\mkern-4.0mu\raise-0.59998pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle(i,j)$}
in Section 39.2.2 for
\mathsf{e}=3
, in Section 39.2.3 for
\mathsf{e}=2
, and in Section 39.2.4 for
\mathsf{e}=1
. The (a) sequences in each section contain all words
z
with
\tau(z)=j
, that is, ending in the long root generator, and the (b) sequences correspond to words
z
starting in
\tau(z)=i
.

For
\mathsf{e}=1
or
2
, each
E_{z}
is expressed as an element
x_{1,m;-1}
or
x^{\prime}_{1,m;-1}
in the subalgebra generated by
E_{i}
and
E_{j}
over
\Lambda_{q,m+1}\,
. In the
\mathsf{e}=3
case, additional elements
\hat{x}
and
\hat{x}^{\prime}
are included, which are easily seen to be elements of the subalgebra over
\Lambda_{q,4}\,
. Hence, each
E_{z}
is in
{U}_{\ \mkern-9.0muq}\mkern-1.5mu\raise 0.80002pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle(ij)$}^{+}\,
defined over
\Lambda_{q,{\mathsf{e}^{*}}}
as desired.

For a word
w\in\mathscr{W}^{*}\mkern-4.0mu\raise-0.59998pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle(i,j)$}
of maximal length
l(w)=m_{ij}
, the formulae in Section 39.2 in
[
47
]
imply the identity

E_{w}=E_{k}
where
k\in\{i,j\}
such that
\gamma(w)=\alpha_{k}\,
.
So, for example, we have
\mathit{\Gamma}_{i}\mathit{\Gamma}_{j}(E_{i})=E_{j}
in the
\mathsf{e}=1
case and

\mathit{\Gamma}_{i}\mathit{\Gamma}_{j}\mathit{\Gamma}_{i}(E_{j})=E_{j}
in the
\mathsf{e}=2
case. The same relations hold for
i
and
j
exchanged, as well as analogous relations for
\mathsf{e}=3\,
according to the computations in
[
47
]
.
The respective relations for the
F_{i}
generators are obtained by application of the
\Omega
involution, completing the proof in the rank 2 case.

The proof of the statement for higher ranks extends the induction argument in the length
l(w)
in the proof of Proposition 1.8 of
[
45
]
to all Lie types.
Let
s=\mathscr{r}(w^{\flat})
and
i=\tau(w)
so that
s(\alpha_{i})=\gamma(w)\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
by Lemma
2.2
and
E_{w}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}(E_{i})\,
. Also
l(s\cdot s_{i})=l(w)=l(w^{\flat})+1=l(s)+1\,
.

Following Lemma
2.13
we next write
s=t\cdot r
with
r\in\mathscr{W}\mkern-4.0mu\raise-0.39993pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle(i,j)$}\,
. Since
l(s)=l(t)+l(r)
we may infer from (
4.22
) that
\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}(E_{i})=\mathit{\Gamma}_{t}\circ\mathit{\Gamma}_{r}(E_{i})=\mathit{\Gamma}_{t}(E_{z})
where

E_{z}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{r}(E_{i})
. Here
z=y\cdot w_{i}
with
y\in\mathscr{W}^{*}\mkern-4.0mu\raise-0.59998pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle(i,j)$}
and
r=\mathscr{r}(y)
as in Lemma
2.13
. Now
l(s)=l(t)+l(r)
and
l(s\cdot s_{i})=l(s)+1
also imply

l(r\cdot s_{i})=l(r)+1
so that
z
is indeed a reduced word. The statement above for the rank 2 case now implies that
E_{z}\in{U}_{\ \mkern-9.0muq}\mkern-1.5mu\raise 0.80002pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle(i,j)$}^{+}
and, thus, can be written as a
\Lambda_{q,{\mathsf{e}^{*}}}
combination of monomials in
E_{i}
and
E_{j}\,
.

Let now
x\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
be a reduced word presenting
t=\mathscr{r}(x)
. With
t(\alpha_{i}),t(\alpha_{j})\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
implied by Lemma
2.13
, we also know that
u_{i}=x\cdot w_{i}
and
u_{j}=x\cdot w_{j}
are reduced words. Since
l(r)\geq 1
we have
l(t)<l(s)
and, hence,
l(u_{i}),l(u_{j})<l(w)\,
. Thus, by induction hypothesis, we have that

E_{u_{i}}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{t}(E_{i}),\,E_{u_{j}}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{t}(E_{j})\in U_{q}^{+}\,
. Since
E_{z}
is a combination of monomials in
E_{i}
and
E_{j}
we conclude that
E_{w}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{t}(E_{z})
is the same combination of monomials in
E_{u_{i}}
and
E_{u_{j}}
. In particular,
E_{w}\in U_{q}^{+}
as desired.

Suppose, further, that
\gamma(w)=s(\alpha_{i})=\alpha_{k}\in\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}\,
. By Lemma
2.13
we then have
r\cdot s_{i}=\mathchoice{{s}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{s}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{s}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{s}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}}
, meaning that
z=y\cdot w_{i}\in\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}\mkern-2.5mu\raise-0.59998pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle(i,j)$}\,
and
r(\alpha_{i})\in\{\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j}\}\,
. The rank 2 results above assure that
E_{z}=E_{m}
where
m\in\{i,j\}
and
r(\alpha_{i})=\alpha_{m}
. Also,
t(\alpha_{m})=t(r(\alpha_{i}))=s(\alpha_{i})=\alpha_{k}\,
. The induction hypothesis, therefore, implies that

\mathit{\Gamma}_{t}(E_{m})=E_{k}
so that also
\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}(E_{i})=\mathit{\Gamma}_{t}(\mathit{\Gamma}_{r}(E_{i}))=\mathit{\Gamma}_{t}(E_{m})=E_{k}\,
as claimed.

The respective statements for the
F_{i}
follow by applications of the
\Omega\,
involution.
∎

An important special case of Proposition
5.1
are words
z\in\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}
of maximal length.
If
j=\tau(z)\,
, recall from (
2.22
) that
q_{j}=\mathscr{r}(z^{\flat})={s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}\cdot s_{j}=s_{\eta(j)}\cdot{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}\,
, where

is the involution of the Dynkin diagrams as defined at the start of Section

.
As noted in the proof of Lemma

,
this yields

. Thus,

(5.8)

E_{z}=E_{\eta(\tau(z))}\qquad\mbox{for all}\quad z\in\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}\,.

The next formulae summarize notations for two relevant renormalizations of a generator
E_{w}
for some word
w\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
with
\alpha=\gamma(w)\,
. The quantities
d_{\alpha}
,
q_{\alpha}
, and
[n]_{\alpha}
are as defined in (
3.1
) and
k\in\mathbb{N}\,
.

(5.9)

\displaystyle E^{(k)}_{w}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\,[k]!_{\alpha}\!\!}E_{w}^{k}

(5.10)

\displaystyle\breve{E}_{w}

\displaystyle=(q_{\alpha}^{-1}-q_{\alpha})E_{w}=(q^{-1}-q)[d_{\alpha}]E_{w}

The first extends Lusztig’s
divided power generators
, already mention in Section
3.2
for simple roots, to all positive roots and
a priori

requires the ground ring to contain the reciprocals of all quantum numbers, such as for
\Lambda_{q,\infty}
or
\mathbb{Q}(q)
.

The
singularized generators

\breve{E}_{w}
coincide,
for appropriate ordering and up to signs, with the generators
\overline{E}_{\beta}
introduced in
[
22
, Sec 12.1]
. In calculations, this renomalization often removes the
(q-q^{-1})
denominators, such as in
(
3.13
), and avoids the use of the extended ground rings such as
\Lambda_{q}^{\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{0.87694pt}{\scalebox{.47}{$\blacktriangledown$}}}
or
\Lambda_{q,n}^{\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{0.87694pt}{\scalebox{.47}{$\blacktriangledown$}}}
.

5.2.
Garside Automorphisms and Dictionary between Generators

In this section, we aim to provide precise correspondences between Lusztig’s and our definition of generators, which entails various useful identities. For a reduced word

w=w_{i_{1}}\ldots w_{i_{k}}\,
, the
T_{i}
-analog of (
5.1
) is defined as

(5.11)

\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{w}=T_{w^{\flat}}(E_{\tau(w)})=T_{i_{1}}\ldots T_{i_{k-1}}(E_{i_{k}})\,,

with the analogous formula for
\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$F$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$F$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.59727pt}{\hskip-20.59727pt}{\hskip-16.38411pt}{\hskip-14.0245pt}{F}_{w}\,
. As in (
5.3
), for a positive root
\alpha\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
, we set
\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{\alpha}=\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{z[\alpha]}
, matching the definition of generators in
[
45
,
46
]
for an adequately chosen reduced word
z\in\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}
of maximal length. They can be related to our convention using the
\mho
involution as well as the notion of complementary words defined in Section
2.4
.

Proposition 5.2
.

For non-empty reduced words
v,w\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
, assume that
w\dualmap v
. Then

\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-21.24713pt}{\hskip-21.24713pt}{\hskip-17.27788pt}{\hskip-11.93614pt}{E}_{w}=\mho(E_{w})=E_{v}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$F$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$F$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-21.10828pt}{\hskip-21.10828pt}{\hskip-17.17026pt}{\hskip-11.84933pt}{F}_{w}=\mho(F_{w})=F_{v}\,.

Proof.

The first equality is immediate from (
4.23
) expressed as
\mho\circ\mathit{\Gamma}_{i_{1}}\circ\ldots\circ\mathit{\Gamma}_{i_{k-1}}=T_{i_{1}}\circ\ldots\circ T_{i_{k-1}}\circ\mho\,
.
For the second equality set
s=\mathscr{r}(v^{\flat})
,
t=\mathscr{r}(w^{\flat})
, and

j=\tau(v)\,
.
As in (
2.22
) we have
t^{-1}\cdot s=q_{j}
with
l(q_{j})=l(t^{-1})+l(s)
so
\mathit{\Gamma}_{q_{j}}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{t^{-1}}\circ\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}
by
(
4.22
).
With
\mathit{\Gamma}_{q_{j}}(E_{j})=E_{\eta(j)}
implied by (
5.8
) as well as
(
4.23
), we thus compute

\mho(E_{w})=\mho(\mathit{\Gamma}_{t}(E_{\eta(j)}))=\mathit{\Gamma}_{t^{-1}}^{-1}(\mho(E_{\eta(j)}))=\mathit{\Gamma}_{t^{-1}}^{-1}(E_{\eta(j)})=\mathit{\Gamma}_{t^{-1}}^{-1}(\mathit{\Gamma}_{q_{j}}(E_{j}))=\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}(E_{j})=E_{v}\,
. The assertion for
F_{w}
follows again by application of
\Omega\,
, which commutes with
\mho\,
.
∎

As a second application of Proposition
5.1
we are able to explicitly compute the Lusztig automorphism
\mathit{\Gamma}_{\boldsymbol{\partial}}

associated to the Garside element
\boldsymbol{\partial}=\mathscr{s}({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}})\in\mathscr{A}^{+}

as in (
2.7
).
In our conventions as explained in Section
4.3
,
we may also write
\mathit{\Gamma}_{{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{\boldsymbol{\partial}}
, where
{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}\in\mathscr{W}
is the longest element.

The relation also involves the automorphism
\mbox{\hskip-12.80373pt
I}:U_{q}\rightarrow U_{q}\,
that implements the involution

\eta
on Dynkin diagrams defined at the beginning of Section
2.4
.
It is given on generators by

(5.12)

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip-12.80373pt
I}(E_{i})=E_{\eta(i)}\,,

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip-12.80373pt
I}(F_{i})=F_{\eta(i)}\,,

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip-12.80373pt
I}(K_{i})=K_{\eta(i)}\,.

The maps
\boldsymbol{\iota},\varpi\in\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}},\Lambda^{\star})
are as in
(
4.9
) and (
4.16
) and the remaining automorphisms are as defined in Section
4
.

Corollary 5.3
.

The Gardside automorphism and its square are given by the following composites of elementary automorphisms:

(5.13)

\mathit{\Gamma}_{\boldsymbol{\partial}}=\mbox{\hskip-12.80373pt
I}\circ\Pi\circ\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{\mathsfit i\!d}_{\boldsymbol{\iota}}=\mbox{\hskip-12.80373pt
I}\circ\Pi\circ\mho\circ S\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\mathit{\Gamma}_{\boldsymbol{\partial}}^{2}=\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{2\mathsfit i\!d}_{\varpi^{-1}}\;.

Proof.

As explained above, we express
\mathit{\Gamma}_{{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{\boldsymbol{\partial}}
in terms of the longest Weyl element. With the same notation as in (
4.23
) or the proof of Proposition
5.2
we have
{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}=s_{\eta(i)}\cdot q_{i}
with
l({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}})=l(q_{i})+1
and
\mathit{\Gamma}_{q_{i}}(E_{i})=E_{\eta(i)}\,
for given
i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\,
. Hence,

(5.14)

\displaystyle\mathit{\Gamma}_{{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}}(E_{i})

\displaystyle=\mathit{\Gamma}_{\eta(i)}(\mathit{\Gamma}_{q_{i}}(E_{i}))=\mathit{\Gamma}_{\eta(i)}(E_{\eta(i)})=-K_{\eta(i)}^{-1}F_{\eta(i)}=

\displaystyle=\mbox{\hskip-12.80373pt
I}(-K_{i}^{-1}F_{i}))=\mbox{\hskip-12.80373pt
I}\circ\Pi(-K_{i}E_{i}))=\mbox{\hskip-12.80373pt
I}\circ\Pi\circ\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{\mathsfit i\!d}_{\boldsymbol{\iota}}(E_{i})\,,

which proves the first identity (
5.13
) on
E_{i}\,
. The verification for
F_{i}
follows, as usual, by application of
\Omega
to (
5.14
), and the automorphisms on both ends of (
5.14
) clearly map
K^{\nu}
to
K^{-\eta(\nu)}
, where
\eta
is the obvious extension to
\mathbb{Z}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}\,
. The formula for the square of the Garside automorphism is readily derived from the first identity and the commutation relations in (
4.15
).
∎

Aside from
\mho
and
\Omega
introduced in Section
4.2
we also record here the action of
the conjugation automorphism
\Upsilon
on the generators. The formula contains an additional factor in
\Lambda^{\star}
, which only depends on the root associated with the word label.

Lemma 5.4
.

Let
w\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
be a non-empty, reduced word and
\beta=\gamma(w)
the associated root. Then

(5.15)

\Upsilon(E_{w})=(-1)^{0pt(\beta)-1}q^{\mathchoice{\left(\rho|\beta\right)}{(\rho|\beta)}{(\rho|\beta)}{(\rho|\beta)}-d_{\beta}}E_{w}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\Upsilon(F_{w})=(-1)^{0pt(\beta)-1}q^{-\mathchoice{\left(\rho|\beta\right)}{(\rho|\beta)}{(\rho|\beta)}{(\rho|\beta)}+d_{\beta}}F_{w}\,.

Proof.

Let
s=\gamma(w^{\flat})
and
i=\tau(w)
so that
E_{w}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}(E_{i})\,
and
\beta=s(\alpha_{i})\,
.
Relation (
4.33
) implies

\Upsilon(E_{w})=\Upsilon(\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}(E_{i}))=(\mbox{\hskip-11.38109pt
Ch}^{0}_{\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{s}})^{-1}(\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}(\Upsilon(E_{i})))=(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{s}(\beta))^{-1}\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}(E_{i})=(-1)^{\mathchoice{\left(\breve{\theta}(s)|\beta\right)}{(\breve{\theta}(s)|\beta)}{(\breve{\theta}(s)|\beta)}{(\breve{\theta}(s)|\beta)}}q^{\mathchoice{\left(\theta(s)|\beta\right)}{(\theta(s)|\beta)}{(\theta(s)|\beta)}{(\theta(s)|\beta)}}E_{w}\,
. Now, by (
2.27
),

\mathchoice{\left(\theta(s)|\beta\right)}{(\theta(s)|\beta)}{(\theta(s)|\beta)}{(\theta(s)|\beta)}=\mathchoice{\left(\rho-s(\rho)|\beta\right)}{(\rho-s(\rho)|\beta)}{(\rho-s(\rho)|\beta)}{(\rho-s(\rho)|\beta)}=\mathchoice{\left(\rho|\beta\right)}{(\rho|\beta)}{(\rho|\beta)}{(\rho|\beta)}-\mathchoice{\left(s(\rho)|s(\alpha_{i})\right)}{(s(\rho)|s(\alpha_{i}))}{(s(\rho)|s(\alpha_{i}))}{(s(\rho)|s(\alpha_{i}))}=\mathchoice{\left(\rho|\beta\right)}{(\rho|\beta)}{(\rho|\beta)}{(\rho|\beta)}-\mathchoice{\left(\rho|\alpha_{i}\right)}{(\rho|\alpha_{i})}{(\rho|\alpha_{i})}{(\rho|\alpha_{i})}=\mathchoice{\left(\rho|\beta\right)}{(\rho|\beta)}{(\rho|\beta)}{(\rho|\beta)}-d_{i}=\mathchoice{\left(\rho|\beta\right)}{(\rho|\beta)}{(\rho|\beta)}{(\rho|\beta)}-d_{\beta}\,
since
d_{\beta}
is
\mathscr{W}
-invariant. Also,
(
2.28
) implies
\mathchoice{\left(\breve{\theta}(s)|\beta\right)}{(\breve{\theta}(s)|\beta)}{(\breve{\theta}(s)|\beta)}{(\breve{\theta}(s)|\beta)}=0pt(\beta)-0pt(\alpha_{i})=0pt(\beta)-1\,
. The relation for
F_{w}
follows by application of
\Omega
and
(
5.5
).
∎

In the remainder of this section,
we discuss the generators and actions more explicitly in the rank 2 case.
As in the proof of Proposition
5.1
, let
{U}_{\ \mkern-9.0muq}\mkern-1.5mu\raise 0.80002pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle(i,j)$}^{+}
be the subalgebra generated by
E_{i}
and
E_{j}

for two indices
i
and
j
. We assume
A_{ji}=-1\,
, implying
d_{i}=1
and

-A_{ij}=d_{j}=\mathsf{e}\in\{1,2,3\}\,
, corresponding to Lie type
\mathsf{A}_{2}
,
\mathsf{B}_{2}
, or
\mathsf{G}_{2}\,
, respectively, for
{U}_{\ \mkern-9.0muq}\mkern-1.5mu\raise 0.80002pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle(i,j)$}^{+}
.
As before, let
m=m_{ij}\in\{3,4,6\}
be the length of the longest element in
\mathscr{W}\mkern-4.0mu\raise-0.39993pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle(i,j)$}\,
.

For
r\in\{1,\ldots,m\}
let
a_{r}=w_{i}w_{j}\ldots
and
b_{r}=w_{j}w_{i}\ldots
be the two possible reduced words of length
r
in
\mathscr{W}^{*}\mkern-4.0mu\raise-0.59998pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle(i,j)$}\,
as in (
2.32
). Combining Lemma
2.12
and Proposition
5.2
now yields the identities

(5.16)

\mho(E_{a_{r}})=E_{b_{m-r+1}}=\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{a_{r}}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\mho(F_{a_{r}})=F_{b_{m-r+1}}=\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$F$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$F$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.59727pt}{\hskip-20.59727pt}{\hskip-16.38411pt}{\hskip-14.0245pt}{F}_{a_{r}}\,.

Since later proofs will refer to and invoke several commutation relations in
[
46
]
, we provide here a dictionary from the notation used there for generators in a rank 2 system to our conventions. Specifically, in Section 5.1 of
[
46
]
Lusztig uses subscripts of the form
1\ldots 12\ldots 2
for the
E
-generators. Replacing
i\leftrightharpoons 1
to index the short root and
j\leftrightharpoons 2
for the (possibly) long root, the definition there can be summarized in the formula

(5.17)

\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{\underbracket{\scriptstyle i\ldots i}_{k}\underbracket{\scriptstyle j\ldots j}_{p}}=\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.39304pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.39304pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.22911pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-0.90138pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ji$}}[\alpha]}\qquad\mbox{ with}\quad\alpha=k\alpha_{i}+p\alpha_{j}\,\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\mkern-2.0mu{\scriptstyle(ij)}\;.

That is, the frequency of
i
’s and
j
’s determined the coefficients of the root
\alpha
in the root sublattice. This is identified with the unique word
b_{r}\leq_{R}\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ji$}}
as in (
2.32
) for which
\alpha=\gamma(b_{r})
, with
r
determined by the position of the root in the ordering in (
2.33
). The respective
E
-generator in our convention is then obtained via (
5.16
), which, in turn, can be expressed in the notation from (
5.2
).

For example, in the
\mathsf{G}_{2}
(
\mathsf{e}=3
,
m=6
) case,
\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{iiijj}
indicates in
[
46
]
the generator associated to root
3\alpha_{i}+2\alpha_{j}
. In the ordering for
\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ji$}}
in
(
2.33
) it appears in position
r=3
so that
\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{iiijj}=\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{b_{3}}=\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{w_{j}w_{i}w_{j}}=\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{(jij)}=T_{j}T_{i}(E_{j})\,
. From (

) we next obtain
that
\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{b_{3}}=E_{a_{6+1-3}}=E_{a_{4}}=E_{w_{i}w_{j}w_{i}w_{j}}=E_{(ijij)}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{i}\mathit{\Gamma}_{j}\mathit{\Gamma}_{i}(E_{j})\,
.
Similarly, the generators associated to simple roots are readily identified as

(5.18)

\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{j}=\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{w_{j}}=E_{\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.39304pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.39304pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.22911pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-0.90138pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}}}=E_{(\underbracket{\scriptstyle ij\ldots}_{m})}=E_{j}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{i}=\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.39304pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.39304pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.22911pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-0.90138pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ji$}}}=\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{(\underbracket{\scriptstyle ji\ldots}_{m})}=E_{(i)}=E_{i}\,.

The associated simple roots appear either as maximal or minimal elements in the two total orders on
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\mkern-2.0mu{\scriptstyle(ij)}
.

The full dictionary translating between the notation in
[
46
]
and our conventions is as follows. Here, generators are ordered by the roots and
\prec_{\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.39304pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.39304pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.22911pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-0.90138pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ji$}}}
as in (
2.33
), omitting the first and last terms given in (
5.18
) for even

. For

the identity
is
\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{i}=E_{i}=E_{(iji)}\,
.

(5.19)

\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathsf{e}=1\quad&\left\{{\quad\begin{aligned} \rule[-5.69054pt]{0.0pt}{14.22636pt}\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{ij}=\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{(ji)}=E_{(ij)}\,\;\end{aligned}}\right.\\

5.3.
Monomial Expressions, Exponent Sets, and Their Spans

The PBW type bases of interest for us are given by monomials whose exponents are labeled by positive roots. To describe these more formally, we introduce
exponents sets

(5.20)

\mathcal{E}(s)=\mathrm{Maps}\left({\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s),\mathbb{N}_{0}}\right)=\mathbb{N}_{0}^{\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\mathcal{E}^{\scalebox{.45}{$\star$}}\mkern-1.2mu(s)=\mathrm{Maps}\left({\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s),\mathbb{Z}}\right)=\mathbb{Z}^{\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)}\,,

where the inversion sets
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)
are as in (
2.9
).
Additionally, we use the more compact notation for the maximal sets

(5.21)

\mathcal{E}_{\bullet}=\mathcal{E}({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}})=\mathrm{Maps}\left({{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}},\mathbb{N}_{0}}\right)=\mathbb{N}_{0}^{{{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}}}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\mathcal{E}^{\scalebox{.45}{$\star$}}_{\bullet}\mkern-1.2mu=\mathcal{E}^{\scalebox{.45}{$\star$}}\mkern-1.2mu({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}})=\mathrm{Maps}\left({{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}},\mathbb{Z}}\right)\,.

Suppose
s=t_{1}\cdot t_{2}
with
l(s)=l(t_{1})+l(t_{2})
. Recall from Corollary
2.4
that
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)
is then the disjoint union of
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(t_{1})
and
t_{1}\!\left({\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(t_{2})}\right)
, which, correspondingly, implies the following bijections of exponent sets:

\displaystyle\hskip 34.1433pt\mathcal{E}(t_{1})\times\mathcal{E}(t_{2})

\displaystyle\rightarrow\mathcal{E}(s)\,

\displaystyle:

\displaystyle\quad(\psi_{1},\psi_{2})\,

\displaystyle\mapsto\,\psi=\psi_{1}\sqcup(t_{1}^{-1})^{*}(\psi_{2})\,,\hskip 34.1433pt

(5.22)

\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(s)

\displaystyle\rightarrow\mathcal{E}(t_{1})\times\mathcal{E}(t_{2})\,

\displaystyle:

\displaystyle\quad\psi\,

\displaystyle\mapsto\,(\iota_{1}^{*}\psi,\iota_{2}^{*}t_{1}^{*}(\psi)))\,.

Here,
s^{*}(\psi)=\psi\circ s
denotes the usual pull-back, the disjoint union of maps indicates the respective definition on the two sets, and
\iota_{i}^{*}
is the restriction to
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s_{i})
.

Suppose
w\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
,
s=\mathscr{r}(w)\in\mathscr{W}\,
with
L=l(w)=|\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)|\,
, and
\psi\in\mathcal{E}(s)\,
.
Following (
2.15
) and the explanations in Section
2.3
, we write
\beta_{j}=\gamma(w[1,j])
for the ordered root sequence implied by
w
as well as
w^{j}=w[1,j]=w[\beta_{j}]
for the words
\leq_{R}w
. Given these conventions, we define the following monomials, expressed in two equivalent notations and for each of two opposing directions of multiplication.

(5.23)

\displaystyle{E}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle}

\displaystyle=E_{w^{1}}^{\psi(\gamma(w^{1}))}\ldots E_{w^{L}}^{\psi(\gamma(w^{L}))}=E_{w[\beta_{1}]}^{\psi(\beta_{1})}\ldots E_{w[\beta_{L}]}^{\psi(\beta_{L})}\vskip 5.69054pt

\displaystyle{E}\mkern 1.3mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}w$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-16.46146pt}{\hskip-11.75818pt}}{\scriptstyle}

\displaystyle=E_{w^{L}}^{\psi(\gamma(w^{L}))}\ldots E_{w^{1}}^{\psi(\gamma(w^{1}))}=E_{w[\beta_{L}]}^{\psi(\beta_{L})}\ldots E_{w[\beta_{1}]}^{\psi(\beta_{1})}\,

Generators
{F}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 25.90247pt}
and
{F}\mkern 1.3mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}w$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-16.46146pt}{\hskip-11.75818pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 26.7191pt}
are defined by the same formulae (
5.23
) with
E
replaced by
F
. Using that
\Omega
is an anti-homomorphism we find from (
5.5
) the direction reversing relations

(5.24)

\Omega({E}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 25.90247pt})={F}\mkern 1.3mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}w$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-16.46146pt}{\hskip-11.75818pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 26.7191pt}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\Omega({F}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 25.90247pt})={E}\mkern 1.3mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}w$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-16.46146pt}{\hskip-11.75818pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 26.7191pt}\;.

Similarly, from Lemma
5.4
we find that the conjugation automorphism reverses
the direction for the same type of monomial up to a unit factor. Specifically, if we denote
\vec{\psi}=\sum_{\alpha}\psi(\alpha)\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}
,
d(\psi)=\sum_{\alpha}\psi(\alpha)d_{\alpha}\in\mathbb{N}_{0}
, and
n(\psi)=\sum_{\alpha}\psi(\alpha)\in\mathbb{N}_{0}
the following formulae hold for the
\Upsilon
anti-involution.

(5.25)

\displaystyle\Upsilon({E}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 25.90247pt})

\displaystyle=(-1)^{0pt(\vec{\psi})-n(\psi)}q^{\mathchoice{\left(\rho|\vec{\psi}\right)}{(\rho|\vec{\psi})}{(\rho|\vec{\psi})}{(\rho|\vec{\psi})}-d(\psi)}{E}\mkern 1.3mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}w$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-16.46146pt}{\hskip-11.75818pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 26.7191pt}\vskip 11.38109pt

\displaystyle\Upsilon({F}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 25.90247pt})

Proposition 5.5
.

For a non-empty
w\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
, let

and

as in
(

). Moreover, let

and

. Then

(5.27)

\mho({E}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-26.68861pt}{\hskip-26.68861pt}{\hskip-16.1402pt}{\hskip-11.52873pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 26.68861pt})\,=\,{\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-21.24713pt}{\hskip-21.24713pt}{\hskip-17.27788pt}{\hskip-11.93614pt}{E}}\mkern 1.3mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}w$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-27.50525pt}{\hskip-27.50525pt}{\hskip-16.71185pt}{\hskip-11.93704pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 27.50525pt}\,=\,\mathit{\Gamma}_{r}\left({{E}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\phi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-3.64168pt}{\hskip-3.64168pt}{\hskip-2.10294pt}{\hskip-1.50209pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w^{\dagger}\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-29.3664pt}{\hskip-29.3664pt}{\hskip-18.19576pt}{\hskip-13.58429pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 29.3664pt}}\right)\,.

The analogous relation holds with directions flipped in all terms as well as with
E
generators replaced by
F
generators.

Proof.

As noted in Section
2.2
, we can find
u\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
such that
z=w\cdot u
is a reduced word of maximal length. So, with
N=l(z)
and
L=l(w)
we have
l(u)=N-L\,
. Moreover,
g=\mathscr{r}(u)=t^{-1}\cdot{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}={s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}\cdot\eta(t)^{-1}={s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}\cdot t^{\dagger}\,
and, hence,
\mathscr{r}(u^{\dagger})=g^{\dagger}=t\cdot{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}=t^{\llcorner}=r\,
. Now, Lemma
2.7
vi)
implies
r(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(t^{\dagger}))=t^{\llcorner}(\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(t^{\dagger}))=\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(t)
so that, indeed,

r_{*}
maps
\mathcal{E}(t)
to
\mathcal{E}(t^{\dagger})\,
.

Assume that
j\leq L\,
, and let
y=z^{\dagger}=u^{\dagger}\cdot w^{\dagger}
. Then we have
z[1,j]=w[1,j]
and

y[1,N+1-j]=u^{\dagger}\cdot(w^{\dagger}[1,L+1-j])
. Thus,
Lemma
2.8
implies

w[1,j]\dualmap u^{\dagger}\cdot(w^{\dagger}[1,L+1-j])\,
, which entails together with
Proposition
5.2
and (
5.4
) that
\mho(E_{w[1,j]})=\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}_{w[1,j]}=E_{u^{\dagger}\cdot(w^{\dagger}[1,L+1-j])}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{u^{\dagger}}(E_{w^{\dagger}[1,L+1-j]})=\mathit{\Gamma}_{r}(E_{w^{\dagger}[1,L+1-j]})\,
.
From Lemma
2.8
we also find that
\beta_{j}=\gamma(w[1,j])=\gamma(u^{\dagger}\cdot(w^{\dagger}[1,L+1-j]))=r(\delta_{L+1-j})
where
\delta_{i}=\gamma(w^{\dagger}[1,i])\,
. Thus,

(5.28)

\displaystyle\mho({E}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 25.90247pt})

\displaystyle=\mho\left({E_{w[1,1]}^{\psi(\beta_{1})}\ldots E_{w[1,L]}^{\psi(\beta_{L})}}\right)

\displaystyle=\mho\left({E_{w[1,L]}^{\psi(\beta_{L})}}\right)\ldots\mho\left({E_{w[1,1]}^{\psi(\beta_{1})}}\right)

\displaystyle=\mathit{\Gamma}_{r}\left({E_{w^{\dagger}[1,1]}}\right)^{\psi(\beta_{L})}\ldots\mathit{\Gamma}_{r}\left({E_{w^{\dagger}[1,L]}}\right)^{\psi(\beta_{1})}

\displaystyle=\mathit{\Gamma}_{r}\left({E_{w^{\dagger}[1,1]}^{\psi(r(\delta_{1}))}}\right)\ldots\mathit{\Gamma}_{r}\left({E_{w^{\dagger}[1,L]}^{\psi(r(\delta_{L}))}}\right)

\displaystyle=\mathit{\Gamma}_{r}\left({E_{w^{\dagger}[1,1]}^{\phi(\delta_{1})}\ldots E_{w^{\dagger}[1,L]}^{\phi(\delta_{L})}}\right)

\displaystyle=\mathit{\Gamma}_{r}({E}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\phi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-3.64168pt}{\hskip-3.64168pt}{\hskip-2.10294pt}{\hskip-1.50209pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w^{\dagger}\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-28.58025pt}{\hskip-28.58025pt}{\hskip-17.94536pt}{\hskip-13.40543pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 28.58025pt})\,,

which shows equality of the first and third term in (

). Furthermore, the last expression in the first line of (

) is readily identified with

\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}^{\psi(\beta_{L})}_{w[1,L]}\ldots\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}^{\psi(\beta_{1})}_{w[1,1]}={\phantom{\scalebox{.65}{$E$}}\accentset{\bullet\mkern-1.1mu\bullet}{\scalebox{.82}{\vphantom{$E$}}}\mathchoice{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-20.73613pt}{\hskip-16.49173pt}{\hskip-14.11131pt}{E}}\mkern 1.3mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}w$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-16.46146pt}{\hskip-11.75818pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 26.7191pt}\,
.
Identities for reversed directions follow analogously. The respective statements for

∎

1.3mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{S},+\hskip-3.01389pt$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-8.11118pt}{\hskip-8.11118pt}{\hskip-4.9681pt}{\hskip-3.54861pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}w$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-16.46146pt}{\hskip-11.75818pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 26.7191pt}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{t_{1}}\bigl({{\scalebox{.96}{${\mathfrak{B}}\mkern-1.0mu$}}\mkern 1.3mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}_{2},+\hskip-3.01389pt$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-11.06117pt}{\hskip-11.06117pt}{\hskip-7.2181pt}{\hskip-5.79861pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}u_{2}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-28.42375pt}{\hskip-28.42375pt}{\hskip-17.87665pt}{\hskip-13.4119pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 28.42375pt}}\bigr)\mkern-1.8mu\centerdot\mkern-1.8mu{\scalebox{.96}{${\mathfrak{B}}\mkern-1.0mu$}}\mkern 1.3mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}_{1},+\hskip-3.01389pt$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-11.06117pt}{\hskip-11.06117pt}{\hskip-7.2181pt}{\hskip-5.79861pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}u_{1}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-28.42375pt}{\hskip-28.42375pt}{\hskip-17.87665pt}{\hskip-13.4119pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 28.42375pt}.\end{split}

The above splitting property
\mathsf{S}\cong\mathsf{S}_{1}\times\mathsf{S}_{2}
may be rephrased as the condition
that
\psi\in\mathsf{S}
if and only if
\iota_{1}^{*}(\psi)\in\iota_{1}^{*}(\mathsf{S})
and

\iota_{2}^{*}(t_{1}^{*}(\psi))\in\iota_{2}^{*}(t_{1}^{*}(\mathsf{S}))
, independently. Although very restrictive in general, the property
applies to several useful situations below.

Assume now that
\Lambda
is an integral domain with a ring homomorphism
f\!:\Lambda_{q,{\mathsf{e}^{*}}}\rightarrow\Lambda
, and set
U_{q,\Lambda}^{\pm}=U_{q}^{\pm}\otimes_{f}\!\Lambda
to be the respective quantum algebra over
\Lambda
. We denote the respective
\Lambda
-spans of the above sets in

U_{q,\Lambda}^{\pm}
by

(5.38)

{\scalebox{.96}{${\mathfrak{S}}\mkern-1.0mu$}}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{S},\pm\hskip-3.01389pt$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-8.22227pt}{\hskip-8.22227pt}{\hskip-4.9681pt}{\hskip-3.54861pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 25.90247pt}\,=\,\bigl\langle{\scalebox{.96}{${\mathfrak{B}}\mkern-1.0mu$}}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{S},\pm\hskip-3.01389pt$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-8.22227pt}{\hskip-8.22227pt}{\hskip-4.9681pt}{\hskip-3.54861pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 25.90247pt}\bigr\rangle_{\Lambda}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad{\scalebox{.96}{${\mathfrak{S}}\mkern-1.0mu$}}\mkern 1.3mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{S},\pm\hskip-3.01389pt$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-8.22227pt}{\hskip-8.22227pt}{\hskip-4.9681pt}{\hskip-3.54861pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}w$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-16.46146pt}{\hskip-11.75818pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 26.7191pt}\,=\,\bigl\langle{\scalebox{.96}{${\mathfrak{B}}\mkern-1.0mu$}}\mkern 1.3mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{S},\pm\hskip-3.01389pt$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-8.22227pt}{\hskip-8.22227pt}{\hskip-4.9681pt}{\hskip-3.54861pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}w$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-16.46146pt}{\hskip-11.75818pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 26.7191pt}\bigr\rangle_{\Lambda}\,.

As before, we write

{\mathfrak{S}}\mkern-1.0mu

\scriptstyle\pm\hskip-3.01389pt
\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}
or

{\mathfrak{S}}\mkern-1.0mu

\scriptstyle\pm\hskip-3.01389pt
\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}w
if
\mathsf{S}=\mathcal{E}(s)
. Additional identities for the action
of
\mho
on either basis sets or spans, such as
\mho\bigl({\scalebox{.96}{${\mathfrak{B}}\mkern-1.0mu$}}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{S},+\hskip-3.01389pt$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-8.11118pt}{\hskip-8.11118pt}{\hskip-4.9681pt}{\hskip-3.54861pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 25.90247pt}\bigr)=\mathit{\Gamma}_{r}\bigl({\scalebox{.96}{${\mathfrak{B}}\mkern-1.0mu$}}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle r^{*}(\mathsf{S}),+\hskip-3.01389pt$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-21.23946pt}{\hskip-21.23946pt}{\hskip-13.37598pt}{\hskip-10.19711pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w^{\dagger}\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-28.58025pt}{\hskip-28.58025pt}{\hskip-17.94536pt}{\hskip-13.40543pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 28.58025pt}\,\bigr)
, follow from Proposition
5.5
.

5.4.
Some Commutation Relations

We collect next various commutation relations among the
E_{w}
generators that are useful in establishing integral PBW bases and also support later computations of ideal properties. The most basic commutation relation for
a pair of generators
(A,B)
is that they
skew-commute
, meaning that
BA=zAB
where
z
is a unit in the ground ring. An important skew-commutation relation among the
E_{w}
generators is given by the following.

Lemma 5.6
.

Suppose
w\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
with reduced decomposition
w=u\cdot v
for non-empty
u,v\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
. Denote
j=\tau(u)
,
\alpha=\gamma(u)
, and
\beta=\gamma(w)
. Assume further that
w_{j}
does not occur as a letter in
v
. Then

(5.39)

E_{w}E_{u}=q^{\mathchoice{\left(\alpha|\beta\right)}{(\alpha|\beta)}{(\alpha|\beta)}{(\alpha|\beta)}}E_{u}E_{w}\,.

Proof.

Since
w_{j}
is not a letter in
v
,
E_{v}
is an expression in
\{E_{i}\}_{i\neq j}
and, hence, commutes with
F_{j}
. Also, by (
5.6
) and (
4.2
) we find

E_{v}K_{j}=q^{-\mathchoice{\left(\nu|\alpha_{j}\right)}{(\nu|\alpha_{j})}{(\nu|\alpha_{j})}{(\nu|\alpha_{j})}}K_{j}E_{v}
where
\nu=\gamma(v)\,
. Observe further that by (
5.26
)
E_{w}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{u}(E_{v})
and

E_{u}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{u^{\flat}}(E_{j})=\mathit{\Gamma}_{u}(\mathit{\Gamma}_{j}^{-1}(E_{j}))=\mathit{\Gamma}_{u}(-F_{j}K_{j})\,
. Thus

E_{w}E_{u}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{u}(E_{v}(-F_{j}K_{j}))=q^{-\mathchoice{\left(\nu|\alpha_{j}\right)}{(\nu|\alpha_{j})}{(\nu|\alpha_{j})}{(\nu|\alpha_{j})}}\mathit{\Gamma}_{u}((-F_{j}K_{j})E_{v})=q^{-\mathchoice{\left(\alpha_{j}|\nu\right)}{(\alpha_{j}|\nu)}{(\alpha_{j}|\nu)}{(\alpha_{j}|\nu)}}E_{u}E_{w}\,
. Now, let
s=\mathscr{r}(u)
and
t=\mathscr{r}(u^{\flat})
so that

s=t\cdot s_{j}\,
. Then
s(\alpha_{j})=t(s_{j}(\alpha_{j}))=-t(\alpha_{j})=-\gamma(u)=-\alpha\,
. Moreover, we have
\beta=\gamma(u\cdot v)=s(\gamma(v))=s(\nu)\,
.
\mathscr{W}
-invariance of the form now implies
\mathchoice{\left(\alpha_{j}|\nu\right)}{(\alpha_{j}|\nu)}{(\alpha_{j}|\nu)}{(\alpha_{j}|\nu)}=-\mathchoice{\left(\alpha|\beta\right)}{(\alpha|\beta)}{(\alpha|\beta)}{(\alpha|\beta)}\,
, from which we infer the assertion.
∎

The most basic case is given by
v=w_{k}
, when
l(w)=l(u)+1
already implies the requirement
k\neq j\,
of the lemma. It encompasses, for example, 2.3.(d3,d4) in
[
45
]
and several skew-commutation relations in Section 5.2 of
[
45
]
. The same references also contain strict commutation relations
E_{\alpha}E_{\beta}=E_{\beta}E_{\alpha}
in special situations when
\alpha+\beta\not\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\,
and, hence,
\mathchoice{\left(\alpha|\beta\right)}{(\alpha|\beta)}{(\alpha|\beta)}{(\alpha|\beta)}=0
. We will see, however, in the proof of Proposition
5.11
below that for non-simply laced Lie type
B
we may have weakly orthogonal pairs of roots
\alpha,\beta\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
, meaning
\alpha+\beta\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
but
\mathchoice{\left(\alpha|\beta\right)}{(\alpha|\beta)}{(\alpha|\beta)}{(\alpha|\beta)}=0
, for which the associated generators do not commute.

We next reformulate the commutation relations for divided and ordinary powers of simple root generators derived in (c), (i), and (a1) from Section 5.2 in
[
46
]
into our conventions and a more compact formalism.
As in Section
2.7
, assume
-A_{ji}=d_{i}=1
and

-A_{ij}=d_{j}=\mathsf{e}\in\{1,2,3\}\,
depending on Lie type. The translation utilizes the dictionary of generators from (
5.19
) as well as additional notation as follows.

To begin with, define for a root lattice vector
\vec{n}=M\alpha_{i}+N\alpha_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}
the set

(5.40)

S_{\mathsf{e}}(\vec{n})=\left\{\psi\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}}:\vec{\psi}=M\alpha_{i}+N\alpha_{j}\right\}\,,

where
\vec{\psi}=\sum_{\alpha}\psi(\alpha)\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}
as in Section
5.3
.
Note that the ordering of generators from right to left is the one determined by
\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}}

as discussed in Section
2.7
, opposite to the one displayed in (
2.33
)
for
\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ji|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ji$}}
. As before, set
\beta_{s}=\gamma(\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.69998pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.49994pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-1.1pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}}[1,s])
so that
\beta_{1}=\alpha_{i}
,

\beta_{2}=s_{i}(\alpha_{j})=\mathsf{e}\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{j}
and so forth.

For a given
\psi\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}}

define
k_{s}=\psi(\beta_{s})
. So, explicitly, for
\mathsf{e}=1
we have
k_{1}=\psi(\alpha_{i})
,
k_{2}=\psi(\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{j})
, and
k_{3}=\psi(\alpha_{j})
, and for
\mathsf{e}=2
we have
k_{1}=\psi(\alpha_{i})
,
k_{2}=\psi(2\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{j})
,
k_{3}=\psi(\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{j})
and
k_{4}=\psi(\alpha_{j})
. Moreover, if
\mathsf{e}=3
, we have
k_{1}=\psi(\alpha_{i})
,
k_{2}=\psi(3\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{j})
,
k_{3}=\psi(2\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{j})
,
k_{4}=\psi(3\alpha_{i}+2\alpha_{j})
,
k_{5}=\psi(\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{j})
, and
k_{6}=\psi(\alpha_{j})\,
. The explicit forms of the associated root lattice vectors are thus

(5.41)

\displaystyle\vec{\psi}

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\;\;(k_{1}+k_{2})\alpha_{i}+(k_{2}+k_{3})\alpha_{j}&\;\mathsf{e}=1\\
\;\;(k_{1}+2k_{2}+k_{3})\alpha_{i}+(k_{2}+k_{3}+k_{4})\alpha_{j}&\;\mathsf{e}=2\\
\;\;(k_{1}+3k_{2}+2k_{3}+3k_{4}+k_{5})\alpha_{i}+(k_{2}+k_{3}+2k_{4}+k_{5}+k_{6})\alpha_{j}&\;\mathsf{e}=3\,.\end{cases}\,

With these conventions we also define a quadratic function
f_{\mathsf{e}}:\mathbb{N}_{0}^{{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}_{0}\,
as

(5.42)

\displaystyle f_{\mathsf{e}}(\psi)

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\;\;k_{1}k_{3}\,+\,k_{2}&\mathsf{e}=1\\
\;\;2k_{4}(k_{1}+k_{2})+k_{3}k_{1}\,+\,2k_{2}+2k_{3}&\mathsf{e}=2\\
\begin{array}[]{l}3k_{6}(k_{1}+2k_{2}+k_{3}+k_{4})\,+\,k_{5}(2k_{1}+3k_{2}+k_{3})\,+\,3k_{4}(k_{1}+k_{2})\,+\,k_{3}k_{1}\\
\,\;\;+\,3k_{2}+4k_{3}+6k_{4}+3k_{5}\end{array}&\mathsf{e}=3\;.\end{cases}\,

Suppose
\hat{\chi}_{i},\hat{\chi}_{j}\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}}
are the indicator functions for the simple roots
\alpha_{i}
and
\alpha_{j}
respectively. That is,
(k_{1},\ldots,k_{m})
is equal to
(1,0,\ldots,0)
for the former and

(0,\ldots,0,1)
for the latter. The variation of
f_{\mathsf{e}}
with respect to the simple root exponents can then be expressed as

(5.43)

\displaystyle f_{\mathsf{e}}(\psi+s\hat{\chi}_{j})

\displaystyle=\,f_{\mathsf{e}}(\psi)\,+\,s\mathsf{e}\left({\psi(\alpha_{j})+\mathscr{u}_{j}(\vec{\psi})}\right)

\displaystyle\mbox{and}\rule{0.0pt}{8.0pt}\quad\qquad f_{\mathsf{e}}(\psi+s\hat{\chi}_{i})

\displaystyle=\,f_{\mathsf{e}}(\psi)\,+\,s\left({\psi(\alpha_{i})+\mathscr{u}_{i}(\vec{\psi})}\right)\,.

Here
\mathscr{u}_{i},\mathscr{u}_{j}\in(\mathbb{Z}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}})^{*}
are defined for
\vec{\psi}=M\alpha_{i}+N\alpha_{j}
as

(5.44)

\displaystyle\mathscr{u}_{j}(\vec{\psi})

\displaystyle=M-N=\begin{cases}k_{1}-k_{3}&\mathsf{e}=1\\
k_{1}+k_{2}-k_{4}&\mathsf{e}=2\\
k_{1}+2k_{2}+k_{3}+k_{4}-k_{6}&\mathsf{e}=3\end{cases}

(5.45)

\displaystyle\mathscr{u}_{i}(\vec{\psi})

\displaystyle=\mathsf{e}N-M=\begin{cases}-k_{1}+k_{3}&\mathsf{e}=1\\
-k_{1}+k_{3}+2k_{4}&\mathsf{e}=2\\
k_{1}+k_{3}+3k_{4}+2k_{5}+3k_{6}&\mathsf{e}=3\,.\end{cases}

Using the basis elements from (
5.33
), the mentioned equations in
[
46
]
can thus be written in the following form, which applies to all Lie types.

(5.46)

E_{i}^{(M)}E_{j}^{(N)}=\sum_{\psi\in S_{\mathsf{e}}(\vec{n})}q^{f_{\mathsf{e}}(\psi)}{E}\mkern 1.3mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle(\psi)$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-10.37508pt}{\hskip-10.37508pt}{\hskip-6.18626pt}{\hskip-4.41876pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.39304pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.39304pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.22911pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-0.90138pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-119.56487pt}{\hskip-119.56487pt}{\hskip-72.8805pt}{\hskip-52.68301pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 119.56487pt}

For convenience, we provide the explicit forms of the basis elements

(5.47)

\displaystyle{E}\mkern 1.3mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle(\psi)$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-10.37508pt}{\hskip-10.37508pt}{\hskip-6.18626pt}{\hskip-4.41876pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.39304pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.39304pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.22911pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-0.90138pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-119.56487pt}{\hskip-119.56487pt}{\hskip-72.8805pt}{\hskip-52.68301pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 119.56487pt}

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\;\;E_{j}^{(k_{3})}E_{(ij)}^{(k_{2})}E_{i}^{(k_{1})}&\mathsf{e}=1\\
\;\;E_{j}^{(k_{4})}E_{(iji)}^{(k_{3})}E_{(ij)}^{(k_{2})}E_{i}^{(k_{1})}&\mathsf{e}=2\\
\;\;E_{j}^{(k_{6})}E_{(ijiji)}^{(k_{5})}E_{(ijij)}^{(k_{4})}E_{(iji)}^{(k_{3})}E_{(ij)}^{(k_{2})}E_{i}^{(k_{1})}&\mathsf{e}=3\;.\end{cases}\,

Multiplying both sides of (
5.46
) by respective quantum factorials, we obtain the commutation relation of ordinary powers,

(5.48)

E_{i}^{M}E_{j}^{N}=\sum_{\psi\in S_{\mathsf{e}}(\vec{n})}q^{f_{\mathsf{e}}(\psi)}\lBrack\psi\rBrack_{\mathsf{e}}{E}\mkern 1.3mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}\mathchoice{{z}\mkern-1.0mu\raise-1.39304pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.8mu\raise-1.39304pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}\mkern-0.77mu\raise-1.22911pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.46}{$|ij|$}}}{{z}^{\circ}\mkern-7.0mu\raise-0.90138pt\hbox{\small$\scriptscriptstyle ij$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-119.56487pt}{\hskip-119.56487pt}{\hskip-72.8805pt}{\hskip-52.68301pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 119.56487pt}\,,

where all coefficients are in
\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]\,
. Explicitly, these are expressed in terms of quantum factorials and quantum multinomial coefficients as follows.

(5.49)

\displaystyle\lBrack\psi\rBrack_{\mathsf{e}}

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\;\;[k_{2}]!\begin{bmatrix}\vskip-1.99168pt\raise 2.84526pt\hbox{$k_{1}+k_{2}$}\vskip-1.99168pt\\
k_{2}\vskip-2.27621pt\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\vskip-1.99168pt\raise 2.84526pt\hbox{$k_{2}+k_{3}$}\vskip-1.99168pt\\
k_{2}\vskip-2.27621pt\end{bmatrix}\ &\mathsf{e}=1\\
\;\;[2k_{2}]![k_{3}]!_{j}\begin{bmatrix}\vskip-1.99168pt\raise 2.84526pt\hbox{$k_{1}+2k_{2}+k_{3}$}\vskip-1.99168pt\\
k_{1}\,,\,2k_{2}\,,\,k_{3}\vskip-2.27621pt\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\vskip-1.99168pt\raise 2.84526pt\hbox{$k_{2}+k_{3}+k_{4}$}\vskip-1.99168pt\\
k_{2}\,,\,k_{3}\,,\,k_{4}\vskip-2.27621pt\end{bmatrix}_{j}&\mathsf{e}=2\\
\begin{array}[]{l}[3k_{2}]![k_{3}]![k_{3}]!_{j}[3k_{4}]![k_{4}]!_{j}[k_{5}]!_{j}\begin{bmatrix}\vskip-1.99168pt\raise 2.84526pt\hbox{$2k_{3}$}\vskip-1.99168pt\\
k_{3}\vskip-2.27621pt\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\vskip-1.99168pt\raise 2.84526pt\hbox{$2k_{4}$}\vskip-1.99168pt\\
k_{4}\vskip-2.27621pt\end{bmatrix}_{j}\!\!\cdot\\
\,\;\;\cdot\!\begin{bmatrix}\vskip-1.99168pt\raise 2.84526pt\hbox{$k_{1}+3k_{2}+2k_{3}+3k_{4}+k_{5}$}\vskip-1.99168pt\\
k_{1}\,,\,3k_{2}\,,\,2k_{3}\,,\,3k_{4}\,,\,k_{5}\vskip-2.27621pt\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\vskip-1.99168pt\raise 2.84526pt\hbox{$k_{2}+k_{3}+2k_{4}+k_{5}+k_{6}$}\vskip-1.99168pt\\
k_{2}\,,\,k_{3}\,,\,2k_{4}\,,\,k_{5}\,,\,k_{6}\vskip-2.27621pt\end{bmatrix}_{j}\end{array}&\mathsf{e}=3\end{cases}\,

As usual, the
j
subscripts at the quantum numbers and quantum multinomial coefficients indicate that
q_{j}=q^{\mathsf{e}}
is used instead of
q_{i}=q
. The resummation formulae in the next lemma are an important
tool for relating bases in later sections.

Lemma 5.7
.

Suppose
\,N,M\in\mathbb{N}_{0}\,
and
\,\vec{n}=M\alpha_{i}+N\alpha_{j}\,
. Then, for an indeterminate
z
,

(5.50)

\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{N}z^{k}q_{j}^{k(\mathscr{u}_{j}(\vec{n})-1)}E_{j}^{(k)}E_{i}^{(M)}E_{j}^{(N-k)}
