\scriptstyle{\;\mathrm{id}_{J}\otimes\mathscr{m}^{+}_{z}\;}
\textstyle{J\otimes_{\Lambda}U_{\zeta}^{{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}}}
\textstyle{{\widehat{J}}}
\scriptstyle{\mathscr{m}_{J}}

∎

An important special family of
\mathscr{G}
-invariant ideals are those generated by augmentation ideals of the
subalgebra
\mathcal{Z}^{+}_{w}
for some reduced word
w\in\mathscr{W}
and
{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}=+
,
{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}={\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}
, or
\scriptscriptstyle\Box
omitted for the full algebra. They are defined as

(6.63)

\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(w)$}}^{{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}}=\left(A_{w}^{+}\right)=A_{w}^{+}\cdot\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}^{{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}}\qquad\mbox{ where }\qquad A_{w}^{+}=\mathrm{ker}\left(\varepsilon:\mathcal{Z}^{+}_{w}\rightarrow\Lambda\right)\,.

It is clear from the PBW bases that

\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(w)$}}^{+}
is identical to the ideal generated by
\{X_{v}:\scalebox{.9}{$\emptyset$}\neq v\leq_{R}w\}\,
.
Assume some
z\in\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}
with
w\leq_{R}z
and let
s=\mathscr{r}(w)\,
.
It is then not hard to see that, as a
free
\Lambda
-module,
\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(w)$}}^{+}
is spanned by all
{X}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle z\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-24.03674pt}{\hskip-24.03674pt}{\hskip-14.74419pt}{\hskip-10.53159pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 24.03674pt}
in

{\mathfrak{B}}\mkern-1.0mu

\scriptstyle{(\mathfrak{l},s)},+\hskip-3.01389pt
\scriptstyle z\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}

for which the restriction of
\psi
to the inversion set
\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)\subseteq{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
is non-zero.

For a more concise description of the ideals in the full quantum algebras, we
introduce abbreviated notation for exponent subsets complementary to the
[0,\mathfrak{l})_{s}
from (
6.37
), namely,

(6.64)

[\mathfrak{l},\infty)^{s}=\left\{\psi\in\mathcal{E}(s):\,\exists\alpha\in\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(s)\;\mbox{ for which }\;\psi(\alpha)\geq\ell_{\alpha}\right\}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad[\mathfrak{l},\infty)^{\bullet}=[\mathfrak{l},\infty)^{{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}}\;.

It is clear from the isomorphism in (
6.38
) and with notation as in (
5.38
) that
the associated ideals in
U_{\zeta}^{+}
may also be written as the two-sided ideals
generated by the spans corresponding to these exponent sets. That is,

(6.65)

\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(w)$}}^{+}\,=\,U_{\zeta}^{+}\cdot{\scalebox{.96}{${\mathfrak{S}}\mkern-1.0mu$}}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle[\mathfrak{l},\infty)^{s},+\hskip-3.01389pt$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-26.27383pt}{\hskip-26.27383pt}{\hskip-16.64113pt}{\hskip-12.88829pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 25.90247pt}\!=\,U_{\zeta}^{+}\cdot{\scalebox{.96}{${\mathfrak{S}}\mkern-1.0mu$}}\mkern 1.3mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle[\mathfrak{l},\infty)^{s},+\hskip-3.01389pt$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-26.27383pt}{\hskip-26.27383pt}{\hskip-16.64113pt}{\hskip-12.88829pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 1.3mu\blacktriangleleft\mkern 3.8mu$}}w$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-26.7191pt}{\hskip-16.46146pt}{\hskip-11.75818pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 26.7191pt}\!.

Observe that for a maximal word
z\in\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}
we have
\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(z)$}}^{+}=A^{+}_{z}\,
, as defined in
(
6.63
), and
\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(z)$}}^{{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}}=A^{+}_{z}\cdot\mathcal{Z}^{0}\,
.
Correspondingly, (
6.65
) reduces to

\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(z)$}}^{+}\,=\,{\scalebox{.96}{${\mathfrak{S}}\mkern-1.0mu$}}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle[\mathfrak{l},\infty)^{\bullet},+\hskip-3.01389pt$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-26.42697pt}{\hskip-26.42697pt}{\hskip-16.7505pt}{\hskip-12.99767pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle z\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-24.03674pt}{\hskip-24.03674pt}{\hskip-14.74419pt}{\hskip-10.53159pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 24.09366pt}\!
.

Note that
since the automorphisms from Corollary
6.11
preserve the counit, the analogs of
the identities in (
6.35
) also hold for the respective ideals. Applied to the
induced ideals in the quantum algebras one finds

(6.66)

\Omega\bigl(\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(w)$}}^{\pm}\bigr)=\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(w)$}}^{\mp}\,,\qquad\mho\bigl(\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(z)$}}^{\pm}\bigr)=\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(z^{\dagger})$}}^{\pm}\,,\quad\mbox{and}\quad S\bigl(\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(z)$}}^{{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}({\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\leq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\leq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\leq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\leq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}})}\bigr)=\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(z^{\dagger})$}}^{{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}({\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\leq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\leq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\leq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\leq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}})}\,.

Similarly, Theorem
6.19

and the fact that the definition in (
6.63
) does not refer to choices of bases
imply the next remark.

Corollary 6.26
.

Assume the Lie type is not
\mathsf{G}_{2}
,
\mathscr{k}
as before, and
s=\mathscr{r}(w)=\mathscr{r}(w^{\prime})
for two reduced
words
w,u\in\mathscr{W}^{*}
. Then
\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(w)$}}^{{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}}=\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(u)$}}^{{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}}\,
.

We may thus write
\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(s)$}}^{{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}}
for Lie types different from
\mathsf{G}_{2}\,
.
We then adopt the abbreviated notation for a maximal reduced word
z\in\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}\,

(6.67)

\mathcal{K}_{\bullet}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}=\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(z)$}}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}=\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}})$}}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\widehat{\mathcal{K}}_{\bullet}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}=\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(z)$}}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}=\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}})$}}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}\,,

where the first equalities also apply to the
\mathsf{G}_{2}
case (for which
\mathcal{K}_{\bullet}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}
may be
ambiguous). Furthermore,

\mathscr{A}
-invariance of
\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}
, as asserted in Theorem
6.22
, the recursion (
6.19
), and the basis
generators for
\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(s)$}}
imply the following recursion for ideals.

Lemma 6.27
.

Suppose
\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(s)$}}
is the ideal of the full algebra
\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}
,
l(s\cdot t)=l(s)+l(t)
for
s,t\in\mathscr{W}
, and Lie type
\neq\mathsf{G}_{2}\,
. Then

(6.68)

\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(s\cdot t)$}}=\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(s)$}}+\mathit{\Gamma}_{s}(\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(t)$}})\,.

Analogous augmentation ideals
\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\leq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\leq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\leq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\leq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}
and
\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}^{-}
are defined in using

A_{s}^{-}=\mathrm{ker}\left(\varepsilon:\mathcal{Z}^{-}_{s}\rightarrow\Lambda\right)
as generators. For a pair
s,t\in\mathscr{W}
, combined ideals in the full algebra
\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}
are given
as

(6.69)

\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(s,t)$}}\,=\,\left(A_{s}^{+},A_{t}^{-}\right)\,=\,(A_{s}^{+}+A_{t}^{-})\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}\;.

Observe also that
A_{1}^{\pm}=0
and than (
6.58
) implies
\Omega(A^{+}_{s})=A^{-}_{s}\,
, which yields the identity

(6.70)

\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(s)$}}=\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(s,1)$}}=\Omega(\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(1,s)$}})\;.

For later convenience, we introduce compact notation for the ideals in
\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}
corresponding to the longest element
{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}}\in\mathscr{W}
as

(6.71)

\mathcal{K}_{\scalebox{.97}{$\bullet$}\mkern-1.6mu\raise 0.49164pt\hbox{\scalebox{.7}{$\circ$}}}=\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}},1)$}}\,,\qquad\mathcal{K}_{\raise 0.49164pt\hbox{\scalebox{.7}{$\circ$}}\mkern-1.6mu\scalebox{.97}{$\bullet$}}=\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(1,{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}})$}}\,,\quad\mbox{and}\quad\mathcal{K}_{\scalebox{.95}{$\bullet$}\mkern-1.4mu\scalebox{.95}{$\bullet$}}=\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}},{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}})$}}\,.

Also for Lie types different from
\mathsf{G}_{2}
(or keeping in mind the aforementioned possible
ambiguity for
\mathsf{G}_{2}
) we use the suggested notation from Proposition
6.25
for the
entailed ideals in
U_{\zeta}
such as, for example,

(6.72)

\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(s)$}}\,,\quad\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(s,t)$}}\,,\quad\widehat{\mathcal{K}}_{\scalebox{.97}{$\bullet$}\mkern-1.6mu\raise 0.49164pt\hbox{\scalebox{.7}{$\circ$}}}=\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}},1)$}}\,,\quad\mbox{or}\quad\widehat{\mathcal{K}}_{\scalebox{.95}{$\bullet$}\mkern-1.4mu\scalebox{.95}{$\bullet$}}=\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$({s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}},{s\mkern-1.0mu_{\bullet}})$}}\,.

More generally, any subset
M\subset{\scalebox{.96}{${\mathfrak{B}}\mkern-1.0mu$}}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle{(\mathfrak{l},s)},+\hskip-3.01389pt$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-20.14017pt}{\hskip-20.14017pt}{\hskip-11.07605pt}{\hskip-7.91145pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 25.90247pt}
generates a
\mathscr{G}
-invariant ideal

J=(M)
of
\mathcal{Z}^{+}_{w}
since all monomials in

{\mathfrak{B}}\mkern-1.0mu

\scriptstyle{(\mathfrak{l},s)},+\hskip-3.01389pt
\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}
are homogeneous in the
sense that
g\raise-2.0pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$\smalltriangleright$}}{X}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 25.90247pt}=\pm{X}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 25.90247pt}\,
for all
g\in\mathscr{G}\,
.
So, if
M=\left({{X}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi_{1}$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-6.77988pt}{\hskip-6.77988pt}{\hskip-4.49924pt}{\hskip-3.85658pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 25.90247pt},\ldots,{X}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi_{K}$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-8.84195pt}{\hskip-8.84195pt}{\hskip-5.97214pt}{\hskip-5.32948pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 25.90247pt}}\right)
a PBW basis for
\mathcal{Z}^{+}_{w}/M

is given by the set of all
{X}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 25.90247pt}
for which
\psi\not\geq\chi_{i}
for any
i=1,\ldots,K\,
. The
partial order used here is defined as

\psi\geq\chi
iff
\psi(\alpha)\geq\chi(\alpha)
for all
\alpha\in\mkern 0.4mu\boldsymbol{\mathscr{N}}\mkern-1.0mu(w)\,
. Consequently, a PBW basis
of
U_{\zeta}^{+}/\widehat{M}
if given by the set of all
{E}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\phi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-3.64168pt}{\hskip-3.64168pt}{\hskip-2.10294pt}{\hskip-1.50209pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 25.90247pt}
for which
\phi\not\geq\mathfrak{l}\cdot\chi_{i}
for any
i=1,\ldots,K\,
.

We briefly elaborate here on the caution expressed in the introduction to this monograph regarding quotients by only the

X_{i}
for simple roots. Let
M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}
be ideal in
\mathcal{Z}_{z}^{+}
generated by the set

\{X_{i}:i=1,\ldots,n\}=\{X_{v}:\gamma(v)\in\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}\,,\;v\leq_{R}z\}
, see Proposition
5.1
. Considering only the positive part, a PBW basis of
U_{\zeta}^{+}/\widehat{M}_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}
is given by
{X}\mkern 1.5mu\raisebox{5.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\psi$}\mkern-2.8mu{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-4.12505pt}{\hskip-2.37517pt}{\hskip-1.69653pt}}\raisebox{-2.7pt}{$\scriptstyle w\raisebox{0.8pt}{\scalebox{.33}{$\mkern 2.0mu\blacktriangleright\mkern 1.0mu$}}$}{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-25.90247pt}{\hskip-15.8898pt}{\hskip-11.34987pt}}{\scriptstyle\hskip 25.90247pt}
with
\psi(\alpha_{i})<\ell_{i}
on simple roots
but
\psi
unbounded on
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\setminus\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}\,
, so that
U_{\zeta}^{+}/\widehat{M}_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}
is of
infinite
rank if
n>1\,
.

Even more concretely, for Lie type
\mathsf{A}_{2}\,
and
\mathscr{k}=2\ell
, the algebra obtained by imposing only relations
E_{1}^{\ell}=0
and

E_{2}^{\ell}=0
(but not
E_{(12)}^{\ell}=0
) has PBW basis
\{E_{1}^{i_{1}}E_{(12)}^{j}E_{2}^{i_{2}}:\,0\leq i_{1},i_{2}<\ell\mbox{ and }j\in\mathbb{N}_{0}\,\}\,
. The observations for the full quantum groups are analogous, leading to algebras without the desired properties of a restricted quantum group.

We mention also a natural
\mathscr{G}
-grading
\mathbb{z}^{*}
on any of the
\mathcal{Z}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}_{w}
algebras, which provides a dual picture to
\mathscr{G}
-invariance and which is analogous to
\mathbb{o}^{*}
on
U_{q}\,
. Given
\alpha=\gamma(v)

we set
\,\mathbb{z}^{*}(X_{v})=(\bar{\alpha},0)\,
and
\,\mathbb{z}^{*}(Y_{v})=(0,\bar{\alpha})\,
where
\bar{\alpha}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}
is the image of the canonical lattice map
{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}
that assigns
\alpha_{i}\mapsto\alpha_{i}
. Similarly, we set

\mathbb{z}^{*}(L^{\mu})=(\bar{\mu},\bar{\mu})\,
for
\mu\in\mathbb{Z}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}
and
L
as in (
6.16
). By Proposition
6.10
the grading extends uniquely to all
of
\mathcal{Z}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}_{w}
, yielding a decomposition

(6.73)

\mathcal{Z}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}_{w}\,=\,\bigoplus_{g\in\mathscr{G}}\left(\mathcal{Z}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}_{w}\right)_{g}\;.

A pairing of
\mathscr{G}
with itself is now given by the symmetric bihomomorphism

(6.74)

\raise 0.70007pt\hbox{$\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\upsilon}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\upsilon}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\upsilon}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\upsilon}$}}}$}:\mathscr{G}\times\mathscr{G}\longrightarrow\{+1,-1\}\qquad\mbox{with}\qquad\raise 0.09995pt\hbox{$\raise 0.70007pt\hbox{$\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\upsilon}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\upsilon}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\upsilon}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\upsilon}$}}}$}$}\mkern 0.15mu\hbox{\scalebox{0.92}{$((\bar{\mu},\bar{\nu}),(\bar{\mu}^{\prime},\bar{\nu}^{\prime}))$}}=\raise 0.09995pt\hbox{$\raise 0.70007pt\hbox{$\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\varepsilon}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\varepsilon}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\varepsilon}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\varepsilon}$}}}$}$}\mkern 0.0mu\hbox{\scalebox{0.92}{$(\bar{\mu},\bar{\mu}^{\prime})$}}\cdot\raise 0.09995pt\hbox{$\raise 0.70007pt\hbox{$\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\varepsilon}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\varepsilon}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\varepsilon}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\varepsilon}$}}}$}$}\mkern 0.0mu\hbox{\scalebox{0.92}{$(\bar{\nu},\bar{\nu}^{\prime})$}}\,,

where

\mathsf{\varepsilon}

is as defined in (
6.11
).

Suppose now
that
\mathscr{k}=2\ell\,
and that

\mathsf{\Phi}

is of oddly laced Lie type (
\mathsf{ADEG}
). Then
Lemma
6.5
implies that (
6.60
) can be expressed more compactly.
Namely, for any
g,h\in\mathscr{G}
and
W\in\left(\mathcal{Z}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}_{w}\right)_{g}

(6.75)

h\raise-2.0pt\hbox{\scalebox{0.6}{$\smalltriangleright$}}W=\raise 0.09995pt\hbox{$\raise 0.70007pt\hbox{$\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\upsilon}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\upsilon}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\upsilon}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\upsilon}$}}}$}$}\mkern 0.15mu\hbox{\scalebox{0.92}{$(g,h)$}}\cdot W\,.

Assume, further, that the Lie type is
\mathsf{A}_{2k}
,
\mathsf{E}_{6}
,
\mathsf{E}_{8}
, or
\mathsf{G}_{2}
. For each of these,

\mathsf{\varepsilon}

and, hence,

\mathsf{\upsilon}

are non-degenerate pairings of respective
\mathbb{F}_{2}
lattices. So,
in these cases a submodule
J\subseteq\mathcal{Z}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}_{w}
is
\mathscr{G}
-invariant if and only if it respects
the decomposition in (
6.73
), meaning that for
J_{g}=J\cap(\mathcal{Z}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}_{w})_{g}
we have

(6.76)

J\,=\,\bigoplus_{g\in\mathscr{G}}J_{g}\,.

The decomposition in (
6.73
) can be described in more concrete terms under further assumptions.
Aside from the restriction to
\{\mathsf{A}_{2k}\,,\mathsf{E}_{6}\,,\mathsf{E}_{8}\,,\mathsf{G}_{2}\}\,
, suppose further
\ell
is even (
\mathscr{k}\equiv 0\mod 4
) and
w\in\mathscr{W}^{*}_{\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{m}}
is maximal so that, by Corollary
6.14
,
\mathcal{Z}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Box$}}_{w}
can be identified with a polynomial algebra as in (
6.41
). There is a natural epimorphism from the former with indeterminates labeled by all
positive roots to the polynomial algebra with inderminates given by only the simple roots.

\textstyle\Lambda\left[\{x_{\alpha}:\,\alpha\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\}\right]\,\rightarrow\,\Lambda\left[z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}\right]\,:\;x_{\alpha}\mapsto\prod_{i}z_{i}^{c_{i}}\quad\mbox{for }\;\alpha=\sum_{i}c_{i}\alpha_{i}\,.

Given
\mu\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Delta}$}}}}
we say that a polynomial
f\in\Lambda\left[z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}\right]
has parity

\mu
if

f(z_{1},\ldots,z_{i-1},-z_{i},z_{i+1},\ldots,z_{n})=(-1)^{\mu_{i}}f(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n})\;\qquad\forall i=1,\ldots,n\,.

Thus, a polynomial
p\in\Lambda\left[\{x_{\alpha}:\,\alpha\in{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}\}\right]
represents an element
in
(\mathcal{Z}_{w}^{+})_{(\bar{\mu},0)}
with
\bar{\mu}=(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{n})
precisely if it is mapped to a polynomial in
\Lambda\left[z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}\right]
of
parity
\mu\,
, in which case we assign the parity
\bar{\mu}
also to
p\,
and well as the respective element in

\mathcal{Z}_{w}^{+}\,
.

Thus, for example for type
\mathsf{A}_{2}\,
, the element
X_{(12)}^{3}+X_{1}^{5}X_{2}
is of parity
(1,1)
in
(\mathcal{Z}_{w}^{+})_{((1,1),0)}
, while the element
X_{1}+X_{2}
is not of any fixed parity since

X_{1}\in(\mathcal{Z}_{w}^{+})_{((1,0),0)}
but
X_{2}\in(\mathcal{Z}_{w}^{+})_{((0,1),0)}\,
.
Thus,
(X_{(12)}^{3}+X_{1}^{5}X_{2})
is a
\mathscr{G}
-invariant ideal of
\mathcal{Z}_{w}^{+}
but
(X_{1}+X_{2})
is not.
The smallest
\mathscr{G}
-invariant ideal the latter is contained in is
(X_{1}+X_{2},2X_{1})\,
.

Any finite collection of elements with fixed parity in
\mathcal{Z}_{w}^{+}
thus generates a

\mathscr{G}
-invariant ideal. For a converse statement, suppose
\mathbb{L}
is a Noetherian integral domain in which 2 is a unit, suppose
\mathscr{j}:\Lambda\rightarrow\mathbb{L}
is a ring epimorphism, and let

\mathcal{Z}_{w,\mathbb{L}}^{+}=\mathcal{Z}_{w}^{+}\otimes_{\mathscr{j}}\mathbb{L}\,
.
Then, in fact,
all

\mathscr{G}
-invariant ideals of
\mathcal{Z}_{w,\mathbb{L}}^{+}

are given as ideals generated by a finite collection of elements of fixed parity.

7.
Hopf Ideals for
U_{\zeta}(\mathfrak{sl}_{n+1})
from Solvable Linear Algebraic Groups

The
\mathsf{A}_{n}
case is computationally more accessible than other Lie types, allowing
explicit descriptions of the correspondence between the skew-central subalgebras discussed in the previous chapter and the (semi) classical coordinate rings of Borel subgroups. We start by providing
basic background
on linear algebraic groups and their coordinate rings in Section
7.1
.

In Section
7.2
we construct specific generators of
U_{\zeta}(\mathfrak{g})

for both
\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{sl}_{n+1}
and
\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{gl}_{n+1}\,
.
They are used in Section
7.3
to establish

\mathcal{Z}^{{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}}_{\bullet}
as a Hopf subalgebra with explicit forms for
the coproduct. The latter are used for identifications with centrally extended
quantum matrix algebras,
whose complexifications for
\mathscr{k}\not\equiv 2\mod 4
, coincide with the coordinate rings
of upper triangular matrices.

Recall from Section
6.3

that for
\mathscr{k}\equiv 0\mod 4
the algebra
\mathcal{Z}^{{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}}_{\bullet}
is
commutative but
not
central in
U_{\zeta}(\mathfrak{g})
.
The remainder and Section
7.4
discuss the construction of Hopf ideals from
subgroups and the relation of the
\mathcal{K}\raise 0.7pt\hbox{\scalebox{.82}{$(s)$}}^{{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}}
ideals from
(
6.63
) to respective Bruhat subgroups.

7.1.
Basic Background and Elementary Examples

We provide here some basic vocabulary and elementary examples as preparation and motivation for
the correspondences between Hopf ideals and algebraic subgroups discussed in
Sections
7
and
8
. Most of the material reviewed here
can be found, for example, in the early chapters of
[
67
]
and
[
50
]
.

Suppose
G
is any algebraic set
and
M
some ring of functions on
G
. Further, assume
H
is any subset of
G
and
I
some
ideal in
M
. We denote the
vanishing ideal
of
H
in
M
as well as the

vanishing locus
of
I
in
G
as

(7.1)

\mathcal{I}(H)=\left\{f\in M:\,f(h)=0\;\forall h\in H\right\}\quad\mbox{ and }\quad\mathcal{V}(I)=\left\{g\in G:f(g)=0\;\forall f\in I\right\}\,,

respectively. We, trivially, have inclusions
H\subseteq\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{I}(H))
and

I\subseteq\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{V}(I))
. Suppose
\mathbb{k}
is an algebraically closed field,

G=\mathbb{k}^{m}
, and
M=\mathbb{k}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}]
the ring of polynomials viewed as functions
on
G
. In this case, Hilbert’s Nullstellensatz and the definition of the Zariski topology imply that

(7.2)

\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{V}(I))=\raise 0.8pt\hbox{\scalebox{.85}{$\surd$}}\mkern-1.0mu{I}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{I}(H))=\mathrm{Zcl}(H)\,,

where
\raise 0.8pt\hbox{\scalebox{.85}{$\surd$}}\mkern-1.0mu{I}
denotes the radical of
I
and
\mathrm{Zcl}(H)
the usual Zariski closure, establishing
a one-to-one correspondence between Zariski closed subsets and radical ideals. This correspondence
generalizes from
\mathbb{k}^{n}
to any algebraic set
G
.

Recall that a linear algebraic group is an affine algebraic set
G\subseteq\mathbb{k}^{N}
with
group operations that are morphisms of
varieties. The coordinate ring on
G
, customarily denoted by

\mathbb{k}[G]=\mathbb{k}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}]/\mathcal{I}(G)
, admits for each
g\in G
a well-defined
algebraic evaluation map
\mathscr{e}_{g}:\mathbb{k}[G]\rightarrow\mathbb{k}
with
\mathscr{e}_{g}([p])=p(g)\,
where

p
is a polynomial in
\{x_{i}\}\,
.

Importantly, these admit a natural Hopf algebra structure, see for example
[
67
, Ch 2]
,
[
50
, Ch 3]
.
The coproduct
\Delta:\mathbb{k}[G]\rightarrow\mathbb{k}[G\times G]\cong\mathbb{k}[G]\otimes\mathbb{k}[G]

is the dual of the product morphism on
G
such that

(\mathscr{e}_{a}\otimes\mathscr{e}_{b})\circ\Delta=\mathscr{e}_{ab}\,
or, more informally,

\Delta([p])(a,b)=p(ab)\,
. An antipode is obtained similarly from inversion on
G\,
.

As a central example, consider
\mathbb{k}[\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{k})]\cong\mathbb{k}[\{x_{ij}\},\tau]/\mathcal{I}\,
, where

\mathcal{I}=(\tau\cdot\det(x)-1)\,
. The presentation implies that any element
[p]\in\mathbb{k}[\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{k})]

can be represented by a polynomial
p\in\mathbb{k}[\{x_{ij}\},\tau]
in
N=n^{2}+1
indeterminates.
The coalgebra structure is readily worked out as

(7.3)

\Delta([x_{ij}])=\sum_{k=1}^{n}[x_{ik}]\otimes[x_{kj}]\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\Delta([\tau])=[\tau]\otimes[\tau]

and it is immediate that
\mathcal{I}\,
is a Hopf ideal.

As usual, for a Hopf algebra
A
, denote the subgroup of
group-like
elements as
Gr(A)=\{a\in A:\Delta(a)=a\otimes a\}\,
. Applied to a coordinate ring
A=\mathbb{k}[G]
this group is
naturally identified with the algebraic character group
\mathrm{Spec}_{\mathfrak{m}}(G)=\mathrm{Hom}_{alg}(G,\mathbb{k}^{\times})=Gr(\mathbb{k}[G])

consisting of group homomorphisms
\sigma:G\rightarrow\mathbb{k}^{\times}\,
that are also morphisms of algebraic sets. For algebraically closed
\mathbb{k}
with
\mathrm{char}(\mathbb{k})=0
the character group
of
\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{k})
is infinite cyclic generated by the determinant function. That is,

(7.4)

\mathrm{Spec}_{\mathfrak{m}}(\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{k}))=\mathbb{Z}_{(\mathrm{det})}\,.

Closely related is the fact that
\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{k})
is linearly reductive or, equivalently, that

\mathbb{k}[\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{k})]
is cosemisimple for such
\mathbb{k}\,
.

Next, let
\delta:\mathbb{k}[\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{k})]\rightarrow\mathbb{N}_{0}
be the function assigning the minimal degree of representatives
\delta(f)=\min\{\deg(p):f=[p]\}\,
, where
\deg(p)
denotes the total degree of
p
as a polynomial in the
n^{2}+1
variables.
Observe that the finite-dimensional linear subspaces
D_{m}=\{f\in\mathbb{k}[\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{k})]:\,\delta(f)\leq m\}
form an ascending chain of subcoalgebras. Indeed, if
f=[p]
and
p
is of minimal degree
d=\delta(f)
, it is clear from the formulae in (
7.3
) that
\Delta(f)
can be written as a summation of pure tensors of monomials, each of which with degree
\leq d\,
.

It is a basic fact that for any linear algebraic group
H
over
\mathbb{k}
there exists a (Zariski) closed monomorphism

j_{H}:H\hookrightarrow\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{k})\,
of algebraic groups for some
n\,
, e.g.
[
67
, 2.3.7]
.
Given such an embedding, we may define an ascending sequence of finite-dimensional linear spaces
D_{m}(H)=j^{*}_{H}(D_{m})
, each of which is clearly a subcoalgebra of
\mathbb{k}[H]\,
.

The next lemma establishes a one-to-one correspondence between Hopf ideals and (Zariski) closed algebraic subgroups in characteristic zero. It is easy to find examples in positive characteristic for which

ii)
does not hold.

Lemma 7.1
.

Let
G
be a linear algebraic group over an algebraically closed
\mathbb{k}
with
\mathrm{char}(\mathbb{k})=0
.

i)

If
J\subset\mathbb{k}[G]
is a Hopf ideal, then
H=\mathcal{V}(J)
is a closed algebraic subgroup in
G
.

ii)

Further,
J
is a radical ideal so that
J=\mathcal{I}(H)=\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{V}(J))\,
.

iii)

If
H\leq G
is any subgroup, then
\mathcal{I}(H)
is a Hopf ideal in
\mathbb{k}[G]\,
.

iv)

In this case
\mathcal{I}(H)=\mathcal{I}(\mathrm{Zcl}(H))\,
.

v)

If
I
and
J
are Hopf ideals in
\mathbb{k}[G]
, then
\mathcal{V}(I+J)=\mathcal{V}(I)\cap\mathcal{V}(J)\,
.

vi)

If
H
and
K
are closed algebraic subgroups of
G
, then
\mathcal{I}(H\cap K)=\mathcal{I}(H)+\mathcal{I}(K)\,
.

Proof.

For
i)
note that
a\in\mathcal{V}(J)
iff
J\subseteq\mathrm{ker}(\mathscr{e}_{a})
.
So, for
a,b\in\mathcal{V}(J)
and
J
a bi-ideal we have

\mathscr{e}_{ab}(J)=\mathscr{e}_{a}\otimes\mathscr{e}_{b}(\Delta(J))\subseteq\mathscr{e}_{a}\otimes\mathscr{e}_{b}(J\otimes\mathbb{k}[G]+\mathbb{k}[G]\otimes J)=\{0\}
and hence
ab\in\mathcal{V}(J)
. The argument for the antipode is analogous.
Given that
\mathrm{char}(\mathbb{k})=0
and using the fact that
\mathbb{k}[G]/J
is a commutative Hopf algebra, Theorem 13.1.2 in
[
69
]
states that
\mathbb{k}[G]/J
is a reduced
\mathbb{k}
-algebra.
This, in turn, means that

J=\raise 0.8pt\hbox{\scalebox{.85}{$\surd$}}\mkern-1.0mu{J}
is a radical ideal. The statements in
ii)
follow now from
(
7.2
) as

J=\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{V}(J))=\mathcal{I}(H)\,
.

For
iii)
use the chain of finite-dimensional coalgebras
D_{0}\subset D_{1}\subset\ldots

with
\mathbb{k}[G]=\bigcup_{j}D_{j}\,
described above. Set
\mathcal{I}_{m}=\mathcal{I}(H)\cap D_{m}\,
, let

D_{m}=\mathcal{I}_{m}\oplus R_{m}
for some complementary space, and pick a basis
\{g_{\nu}\}
for
R_{m}\,
with

\dim(R_{m})=M
. Let
\vec{g}:G\rightarrow\mathbb{k}^{M}
be given by
\vec{g}(a)=(g_{1}(a),\ldots,g_{M}(a))
.
Thus, if
\vec{v}\,^{\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.63}{$\mathsf{T}$}}\vec{g}(a)=0
for all
a\in H
then
\vec{v}\,^{\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.63}{$\mathsf{T}$}}\vec{g}\in\mathcal{I}(H)

and hence
\vec{v}=0
by linear independence. Given
f\in\mathcal{I}_{m}\,
, there are now unique coefficients
b_{\nu,\mu}\in\mathbb{k}
such that
\Delta(f)=\sum_{\nu\mu}b_{\nu,\mu}g_{\nu}\otimes g_{\mu}+T
with

T\in\mathcal{I}_{m}\otimes D_{m}+D_{m}\otimes\mathcal{I}_{m}\,
. Evaluating at
(a,b)
for
a,b\in H
so that
ab\in H

we have

0=f(ab)=\mathscr{e}_{a}\otimes\mathscr{e}_{b}\Delta(f)=\sum_{\nu\mu}b_{\nu,\mu}g_{\nu}(a)g_{\mu}(b)+\mathscr{e}_{a}\otimes\mathscr{e}_{b}(T)=\vec{g}(a)^{\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.63}{$\mathsf{T}$}}B\vec{g}(b)
, where
B=(b_{\nu,\mu})\,
and
\mathcal{I}_{m}\subseteq\mathrm{ker}(\mathscr{e}_{a})\,
.

As
\vec{g}(a)^{\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.63}{$\mathsf{T}$}}B\vec{g}(b)=0
holds for all
a,b\in H
, the previous remarks imply

B=0
and, hence,
\Delta(f)=T\in\mathcal{I}_{m}\otimes D_{m}+D_{m}\otimes\mathcal{I}_{m}\subseteq\mathcal{I}(H)\otimes\mathbb{k}[G]+k[G]\otimes\mathcal{I}(H)\,
, proving that
\mathcal{I}(H)
is a bi-ideal. Invariance under the antipode is clear
from
S(f)(a)=f(a^{-1})=0\,
if
a\in H
and
f\in\mathcal{I}(H)\,
.
Finally, combining
iii)
with
ii)
and (
7.2
) we find

\mathcal{I}(H)=\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{I}(H)))=\mathcal{I}(\mathrm{Zcl}(H))\,
.

The last two statements follow from the standard correspondence between algebraic sets and radical ideals. The only additional observation needed is that the sum of two Hopf ideals is again a Hopf ideal so that by

ii)

\mathcal{I}(H\cap K)=\raise 0.8pt\hbox{\scalebox{.85}{$\surd$}}\mkern-1.0mu{(\mathcal{I}(H)+\mathcal{I}(K))}=\mathcal{I}(H)+\mathcal{I}(K)\,
.
∎

The most elementary example is the additive group
\mathbb{k}_{a}
, for which
\mathbb{k}[\mathbb{k}_{a}]=\mathbb{k}[x]
with
\Delta(x)=x\otimes 1+1\otimes x\,
and
S(x)=-x\,
.
The vanishing locus of any polynomial in
\mathbb{k}[x]
is finite so that a non-trivial Hopf ideal needs to correspond to a finite subgroup of
\mathbb{k}_{a}
. In
\mathrm{char}(\mathbb{k})=0
the only such subgroup is
\{0\}
. Thus,
by Lemma
7.1
, the only proper Hopf ideal of
\mathbb{k}[x]
is the augmentation ideal
\boldsymbol{\left(\right.}x\boldsymbol{\left.\right)}=\mathcal{I}(\{0\})\,
.
In characteristic
p>0
we, additionally, have that the principal ideal
\boldsymbol{\left(\right.}x^{p}\boldsymbol{\left.\right)}
generated by

x^{p}
is a Hopf ideal.

For the multiplicative group
\mathbb{k}_{m}=(\mathbb{k}^{\times},\cdot)
, we have
\mathbb{k}[\mathbb{k}_{m}]=\mathbb{k}[\lambda,\lambda^{-1}]=\mathbb{k}[\lambda,\tau]/(\lambda\tau-1)\,
with
\Delta(\lambda)=\lambda\otimes\lambda\,
. Recall any finite subgroup of

\mathbb{k}_{m}
is cyclic and, thus, of the form
\mathsf{Z}_{r}=\langle\xi\rangle\,
where
\xi
a primitive
r
-th root of unity. We denote
\mathsf{Z}_{1}=\{1\}
and use the convention
\mathsf{Z}_{0}=\mathbb{k}^{\times}\,
.
The
\mathsf{Z}_{r}
are algebraic subgroups with
vanishing ideal
F_{r}=\mathcal{I}({\mathsf{Z}}_{r})=\boldsymbol{\left(\right.}\lambda^{r}-1\boldsymbol{\left.\right)}\,
so that
\{F_{r}:r\in\mathbb{N}\}
is the complete set of
non-trivial Hopf ideals of
\mathbb{k}[\lambda,\lambda^{-1}]\,
.

A somewhat more involved example is the semidirect product
P=\mathbb{k}^{\times}\ltimes\mathbb{k}
with group
product given by
(\lambda,x)(\lambda^{\prime},x^{\prime})=(\lambda\lambda^{\prime},x\lambda^{\prime}+x^{\prime})\,
. It may be viewed as the closed algebraic subgroup of the upper
triangular matrices in
\mathrm{GL}_{2}
with 1 in the upper left entry.
Alternatively,
P
may be viewed as
\mathrm{PGL_{2}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}}
, given by
the image of the upper triangular matrices in the projective linear group
\mathrm{PGL}_{2}
.
Denote abelian algebraic subgroups as

\bar{\mathsf{Z}}_{r}=\mathsf{Z}_{r}\times\{0\}
and
U=\{1\}\times\mathbb{k}=[P,P]\cong\mathbb{k}_{a}\,
.

Lemma 7.2
.

Any closed algebraic subgroup of
P
is of the form
g\bar{\mathsf{Z}}_{r}g^{-1}
or
\bar{\mathsf{Z}}_{r}U

with
g\in U
and
r\in\mathbb{N}_{0}
.

Proof.

Suppose
H
is an algebraic subgroup in
P
. Let
\sigma:P\rightarrow\mathbb{k}^{\times}
be
the abelianization map and note that
S=\sigma(H)\leq\mathbb{k}^{\times}
is an abelian (
a priori
only constructible) subgroup.
Suppose
\rho\in S\setminus\{1\}
is a non-trivial element, meaning
(\rho,y)\in H
for some
y\in\mathbb{k}
.
It is then easy to check that
g(\rho,0)g^{-1}=(\rho,y)
for
g=(1,(\rho-1)^{-1}y)\in U\,
.

Note that
H\cap U=\mathrm{ker}(\sigma|_{H})
is an algebraic subgroup of
\mathbb{k}_{a}
and, hence, either
\mathbb{1}=(1,0)
or
U
. If
H\cap U=\{\mathbb{1}\}
the map
\sigma:H\rightarrow S
is a group isomorphism
so that
H
is abelian. If
S\neq\{1\}
there are, by the previous remark,
g\in U
and
\rho\in\mathbb{k}^{\times}
with
\rho\neq 1
and
g(\rho,0)g^{-1}\in H
. Since
H
is abelian it has to be in the centralizer
of
g\bar{\mathsf{Z}}_{0}g^{-1}=C(g(\rho,0)g^{-1})\cong\mathbb{k}_{m}\,
. Thus,
H=g\bar{\mathsf{Z}}_{r}g^{-1}
for some
r\in\mathbb{N}\,
. If
S=\{1\}
clearly
H=\{\mathbb{1}\}\,
.

Finally, assume
H\cap U=U
and
S\neq\{1\}
. By the observation above we have that
(\rho,y)\in H

implies
(\rho,0)\in H
as now
g\in H\,
. Hence,
H=S\ltimes\mathbb{k}
so that
S\cong H\cap\bar{\mathsf{Z}}_{0}
is
an algebraic group. It follows that
H=K_{r}\ltimes\mathbb{k}=\bar{\mathsf{Z}}_{r}U\,
. If also
S=\{1\}
, clearly

H=U=\bar{\mathsf{Z}}_{1}U\,
.
∎

For a clearer formal distinction between coordinates of and functions on
G
denote
by
\hat{t},\hat{x}:G\rightarrow\mathbb{k}
the projections given by
\hat{\lambda}(g)=\lambda

and
\hat{x}(g)=x
if
g=(\lambda,x)\,
. Similar to the previous examples, we have

\mathbb{k}[\mathrm{PGL_{2}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}}]\cong\mathbb{k}[P]=\mathbb{k}[\hat{\lambda},\hat{\lambda}^{-1},\hat{x}]
as a commutative algebra. The coproducts are easily
worked out from the product rule on
P
as

(7.5)

\Delta(\hat{\lambda}\,)=\hat{\lambda}\otimes\hat{\lambda}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\Delta(\hat{x})=\hat{x}\otimes\hat{\lambda}+1\otimes\hat{x}\,,

with
S(\hat{\lambda})=\hat{\lambda}^{-1}
and
S(\hat{x})=-\hat{x}\hat{\lambda}^{-1}\,
.

Assuming
\mathrm{char}(\mathbb{k})=0
and using Lemma
7.1
, we obtain a complete list of
Hopf ideals for
\mathbb{k}[P]
as the vanishing ideals of the subgroups classified in
Lemma
7.2
. For example, for
g=(1,\nu)
with
\nu\in\mathbb{k}
we find
J_{\nu}=\mathcal{I}(g\bar{\mathsf{Z}}_{0}g^{-1})=\boldsymbol{\left(\right.}\hat{x}-\nu(\hat{\lambda}-1)\boldsymbol{\left.\right)}
and for any
r\in\mathbb{N}
we have
F_{r}=\mathcal{I}(\bar{\mathsf{Z}}_{r}U)=\boldsymbol{\left(\right.}\hat{\lambda}^{r}-1\boldsymbol{\left.\right)}
.
For the remaining subgroups, the respective Hopf ideals are no longer principal, since for
r\in\mathbb{N}

\mathcal{I}(g\bar{\mathsf{Z}}_{r}g^{-1})=\mathcal{I}(g\bar{\mathsf{Z}}_{0}g^{-1}\cap\bar{\mathsf{Z}}_{r}U)=F_{r}+J_{\nu}=\boldsymbol{\left(\right.}\hat{\lambda}^{r}-1,\hat{x}-\nu(\hat{\lambda}-1)\boldsymbol{\left.\right)}\,
. Note, finally, that the augmentation ideal is given by
\mathrm{ker}(\varepsilon)=F_{1}+J_{0}=J_{\nu}+J_{\mu}
for
\nu\neq\mu
and that
F_{s}+F_{r}=F_{\gcd(s,r)}\,
, providing a full description of the additive semigroup of Hopf ideals of
\mathbb{k}[P]\,
.

The discussion of
\mathbb{k}[P]
now directly applies to quantum groups
U_{\zeta}
or
U_{\zeta}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}
at a root of unity
\zeta\,
. For a simple root
\alpha_{i}
, denote by
\mathcal{Z}_{i}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}
the subalgebra
generated by
L_{i}=K_{i}^{\ell_{i}}
and
X_{i}=E_{i}^{\ell_{i}}
.

Corollary 7.3
.

The algebra
\mathcal{Z}_{i}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}
is a commutative Hopf subalgebra of
U_{\zeta}^{({\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}})}
.

The semigroup of possible Hopf ideals of
\mathcal{Z}_{i}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}\otimes\mathbb{C}
is given by
the principal ideals

\ddot{F}_{r}=\boldsymbol{\left(\right.}L_{i}^{r}-1\boldsymbol{\left.\right)}
with
r\in\mathbb{N}
and
\ddot{J}_{\nu}=\boldsymbol{\left(\right.}X_{i}-\nu(L_{i}-1)\boldsymbol{\left.\right)}

with
\nu\in\mathbb{C}
as well as the sums of ideals
\ddot{F}_{r}+\ddot{J}_{\nu}\,
.

Proof.

Note first
X_{i}L_{i}=\zeta_{i}^{2\ell_{i}^{2}}L_{i}X_{i}=L_{i}X_{i}
by definition of
\zeta_{i}

and
\ell_{i}
. So,
\mathcal{Z}_{i}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}
is commutative, as also stated in Corollary
6.14
.
Clearly,
L_{i}
is group-like since
K_{i}
is. Moreover, we find from (
3.17
) and
Corollary
6.2

the coproduct formula

(7.6)

\displaystyle\Delta(X_{i})=\sum_{s=0}^{\ell_{i}}\begin{bmatrix}\vskip-1.99168pt\raise 2.84526pt\hbox{$\ell_{i}$}\vskip-1.99168pt\\
s\vskip-2.27621pt\end{bmatrix}_{i}\zeta_{i}^{n(\ell_{i}-s)}E_{i}^{s}\otimes E_{i}^{\ell_{i}-s}K_{i}^{s}=E_{i}^{\ell_{i}}\otimes K_{i}^{\ell_{i}}+1\otimes E_{i}^{\ell_{i}}=X_{i}\otimes L_{i}+1\otimes X_{i}\,.

Thus,
\mathcal{Z}_{i}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}\otimes\mathbb{C}\cong\mathbb{C}[P]
as Hopf algebras over
\mathbb{C}\,
. The claim now follows from the previously discussed classification of Hopf ideals of
\mathbb{C}[P]\,
.
∎

Non-trivial Hopf ideals in
\mathcal{Z}_{i}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}
for a general ground ring
\Lambda
containing
\Lambda_{\zeta}
can be found as preimages of the extension of scalars map
\mathcal{Z}_{i}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}_{i}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}\otimes\mathbb{C}
, provided that
\nu\in\Lambda\,
.
All of these are readily seen to be free and complemented
\Lambda
-submodules of
\mathcal{Z}_{i}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}
.

The classification in Corollary
7.3
underscores the need to choose the minimal exponents

\ell_{i}=\ell/\gcd(d_{i},\ell)
in the definition of the
X_{i}
generators.
Specifically, suppose
\alpha_{i}
is a long root in the doubly laced Lie type case, meaning
d_{i}=2
, and
\ell
is even. Then
\ell=2\ell_{i}
so that

E_{i}^{\ell}=X_{i}^{2}\,
, generating an ideal
\boldsymbol{\left(\right.}E_{i}^{\ell}\boldsymbol{\left.\right)}=\boldsymbol{\left(\right.}X_{i}^{2}\boldsymbol{\left.\right)}
that is not even radical and hence not Hopf. The latter is also obvious from the coproduct

\Delta(X_{i}^{2})=X_{i}^{2}\otimes L_{i}^{2}+2X_{i}\otimes L_{i}X_{i}+1\otimes X_{i}^{2}\;\;\not\in\;\;\boldsymbol{\left(\right.}X_{i}^{2}\boldsymbol{\left.\right)}\otimes U_{\zeta}+U_{\zeta}\otimes\boldsymbol{\left(\right.}X_{i}^{2}\boldsymbol{\left.\right)}\,.

Since restricted groups are occasionally defined in the literature with such generators
we add the above observation as a more formal remark, which has an obvious analogue for
\mathsf{G}_{2}\,
.

Remark 7.4
.

Assume
U_{\zeta}^{({\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}})}
is of Lie type
\mathsf{B}_{n}
,
\mathsf{C}_{n}
, or
\mathsf{F}_{4}
with
n\geq 2
as well as
\mathscr{k}\equiv 0\mod 4
.
Then the ideal generated by

\{E_{\alpha}^{\ell}:\,\alpha\in\mathsf{R}\}
is
not
a Hopf ideal if
\mathsf{R}\subseteq{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\scalebox{1.18}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}{\raisebox{-0.15pt}{\scalebox{0.8}{$\mathsf{\Phi}$}}}^{+}}
contains a long root.
∎

Recall that any reductive algebraic subgroups over an algebraically closed field admits a Borel subgroup, unique up to conjugation.
The fundamental example of such a Borel subgroup is the subgroup
\mathrm{T}_{n}<\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{k})
of upper triangular matrices with non-zero diagonal entries. Denote also by
\mathrm{D}_{m}
the subgroup of diagonal matrices and
\mathrm{U}_{n}

the subgroup of upper triangular matrices with 1’s on the diagonal so that
\mathrm{T}_{n}=\mathrm{D}_{m}\ltimes\mathrm{U}_{n}\,
.
As algebraic sets,
\mathrm{U}_{n}\cong\mathbb{k}^{\binom{n}{2}}
and
\mathrm{D}_{m}\cong(\mathbb{k}^{\times})^{n}
, where the latter is realized as either
\{(x_{1,1},\ldots,x_{n,n},\tau)\in\mathbb{k}^{n}\times\mathbb{k}:x_{1,1}\ldots x_{n,n}\tau=1\}
or, equivalently, as

(D_{1})^{n}
. The former is commensurable with the embedding in
\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{k})
, while the latter yields the
coordinate rings as Laurent polynomials.

The coordinate ring is, thus, given as

\mathbb{k}[\mathrm{T}_{n}]=\mathbb{k}\bigl[\{\hat{x}_{i,j}:i\leq j\},\{\hat{x}_{i,i}^{-1}\}\bigr]

so that the set of functions
that are polynomials in off-diagonal entries and Laurent polynomials in the diagonal entries. As before,
we notationally distinguish coordinates and coordinate functions. The group of group-like elements in
\mathbb{k}[\mathrm{T}_{n}]
, corresponding to algebraic characters on

\mathrm{T}_{n}
, are given

(7.7)

\mathrm{Spec}_{\mathfrak{m}}(\mathrm{T}_{n})\cong\mathbb{Z}^{n}\qquad\mbox{ with generators }\quad\{\hat{x}_{i,i}:i=1,\ldots n\}\,.

The counit is simply
\varepsilon(\hat{x}_{i,j})=\delta_{ij}
. The coproduct and antipode for the remaining generators
i<j
are readily
derived from (
7.3
) as

(7.8)

\Delta(\hat{x}_{i,j})=\sum_{i\leq k\leq j}\hat{x}_{i,k}\otimes\hat{x}_{k,j}\quad\mbox{ and }\quad S(\hat{x}_{i,j})=\mkern-18.0mu\mathop{\textnormal{\hbox{\hbox to15.83pt{\vbox to16.44pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.0pt\lower-10.00012pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{{}{}{}{}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@discardpath@clipped{M 0 -13.84 L 0 8.92 L 21.9 8.92 L 21.9 -13.84 Z} {{{}{}{{}}{}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}}_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq m\leq j-i\\
i=k_{0}<k_{1}<\ldots<k_{m}=j\end{subarray}}\mkern-18.0mu(-1)^{m}\hat{x}_{i,i}^{-1}\hat{x}_{i,k_{1}}\hat{x}_{k_{1},k_{1}}^{-1}\hat{x}_{k_{1},k_{2}}\ldots\hat{x}_{k_{m-1},j}\hat{x}_{j,j}^{-1}\;.

We finally mention the notion of a
cosolvable
Hopf algebra
H
following
[
51
]
. In the case
of a commutative Hopf algebra
H
, it starts from a finite ascending series of

\mathbb{k}1=H_{0}\subset H_{1}\subset\ldots\subset H_{n}=H
Hopf subalgebras.
From the augmentation ideals
H_{s}^{\circ}=H_{s}\cap\mathrm{ker}(\varepsilon)
one obtains for each
s

a Hopf ideal
H_{s-1}^{\circ}H_{s}
in
H_{s}
and, thus, a Hopf algebra

\bar{H}_{s}=H_{s}/H_{s-1}^{\circ}H_{s}
, called the
s
-th
factor
of the series.
H
is said to be
cosolvable if all of the factors are cocommutative for some such series.

In the case
H=\mathbb{k}[\mathrm{T}_{n}]
, these properties can be easily verified if we define
H_{s}

as the polynomial subalgebra generated by
\{\hat{x}_{i,j}:\,j-i<s\}
and 1.
It is immediate from (
7.8
) that each
H_{s}
defines a Hopf subalgebra.
Moreover, it is clear that
\bar{H}_{1}=\mathbb{k}[\mathrm{D}_{m}]
, generated by group-like elements.
For
s>1
, one readily verifies that
\bar{H}_{s}\cong\mathbb{k}[\{\bar{x}_{i,j}:i-j=s-1\}]

is a polynomial algebra, for which all generators are strictly primitive. Hence, each

H_{s}
is cocommutative and
\mathbb{k}[\mathrm{T}_{n}]
is cosolvable.

Recall, further, that by the Lie-Kolchin Theorem every closed,
connected
, and
solvable
linear
algebraic group
B
is conjugate to a subgroup of
\mathrm{T}_{n}
, see
[
67
, 6.3.1.]
. The images of the
H_{s}

under restriction and conjugation map
\mathbb{k}[\mathrm{T}_{n}]\rightarrow\mathbb{k}[B]
give rise to a respective series with the same properties as the one for
\mathbb{k}[\mathrm{T}_{n}]\,
.

Corollary 7.5
.

Suppose
B
is a closed, connected, solvable algebraic subgroup of
\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{k})
over an algebraically closed field
\mathbb{k}
. Then
\mathbb{k}[B]
is cosolvable in the sense of
[
51
]
.

In particular,
the coordinate ring of
\mathbb{k}[\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{k})]
is fundamentally different from that of a (connected) Borel subgroup. The former is cosemisimple and thus not cosolvable and its character group
in (
7.4
) also differs from that in (
7.7
).

7.2.
Standard Presentation of
U_{q}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}
for
\mathsf{A}_{n}

We provide next detailed relations and coproduct formulae for generators
E_{w}
of
U_{q}^{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.86}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}{\scalebox{.5}{$\mkern 1.0mu\geq\mkern-4.3mu0$}}}(\mathfrak{sl}_{n+1})
with respect to a particularly convenient choice of a maximal word.
It is given by
the conjugate
z_{n}=w_{\mathsf{A}_{n}}^{\dagger}
of the one mentioned in Section
5.5
and inductively defined as

(7.9)

z_{n}=z_{n-1}c_{n,1}\quad\mbox{ with }\quad c_{n,k}=w_{n}\ldots w_{n+1-k}\quad\mbox{ so that }\quad c_{n,k}^{\flat}=w_{n}\ldots w_{n+2-k}=c_{n,k-1}\,.

Observe that
z_{m}
is the word of maximal length in the canonically embedded
\mathsf{A}_{m}
subsystem in
\mathsf{A}_{n}
for
n>m
with

l(z_{m})=\binom{m+1}{2}
.
Denote by
\bar{z}_{n}=\mathscr{r}(z_{n})
and
\bar{c}_{n,k}=\mathscr{r}(c_{n,k})
the respective elements in the Weyl group
\mathscr{W}
.
In the standard Euclidean realization of the
\mathsf{A}_{n}
root system in
\mathbb{R}^{n+1}=\langle\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{n+1}\rangle
, simple roots are given as

\alpha_{i}=\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{i+1}
and
\mathscr{W}
acts as the group of permutations in
n+1
letters
via
s(\epsilon_{i})=\epsilon_{s(i)}\,
, with
generators
s_{i}=(i,i+1)\,
. Specifically,
\bar{c}_{n,k}=(n+1,n,\ldots,n+1-k)
is a cyclic permutation
and
\bar{z}_{m}(\epsilon_{i})=\epsilon_{m+2-i}
for
1\leq i\leq m+1
and
\bar{z}_{m}(\epsilon_{i})=\epsilon_{i}
for
i>m+1\,
.

Suppose
N=\binom{m}{2}+k
for
1\leq k\leq m
. We have then
z_{n}[1,N]=z_{m-1}c_{m,k}\,
for the first
N
letters in
z_{n}
. The

N
-th term in the ordering sequence is now computed as

(7.10)

\displaystyle\beta_{N}

\displaystyle=\gamma(z_{n}[1,N])=\gamma(z_{m-1}c_{m,k})=\bar{z}_{m-1}\bar{c}_{m,k-1}(\alpha_{m+1-k})

\displaystyle=\bar{z}_{m-1}(m+1\ldots m+2-k)(\epsilon_{m+1-k}-\epsilon_{m+2-k})

\displaystyle=\bar{z}_{m-1}(\epsilon_{m+1-k}-\epsilon_{m+1})=\epsilon_{k}-\epsilon_{m+1}=\alpha_{k}+\ldots+\alpha_{m}\,.

Hence, the ordering
\prec_{z}
defined in Section
2.3
is simply the lexicographic ordering.
Namely, for
i<j
and
r<s
we have

(7.11)

\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{j}\prec_{z}\epsilon_{r}-\epsilon_{s}\qquad\mbox{ iff }\quad j<s\;\;\mbox{ or }\;(j=s\;\mbox{ and }\;\;i<r)\,.

Consider next for
1\leq k\leq m
the reduced words

(7.12)

b_{m,k}=w_{k}\ldots w_{m}=c_{m,m+1-k}^{*}\,\quad\mbox{ so that }\quad b_{m,k}^{\flat}=w_{k}\ldots w_{m-1}=b_{m-1,k}\,.

As before, we denote the respective element in the Weyl group as
\bar{b}_{m,k}=(k,\ldots,m,m+1)\,
and compute

(7.13)

\gamma(b_{m,k})=\bar{b}_{m-1,k}(\alpha_{m})=(k,\ldots,m)(\epsilon_{m}-\epsilon_{m+1})=\epsilon_{k}-\epsilon_{m+1}\,.

Note next that
\bar{b}_{m,k}
is in the
\mathsf{A}_{m}
subsystem and thus
\bar{b}_{m,k}\leq_{R}\bar{z}_{m}\,
. Thus, there exists
some
\bar{u}_{m,k}
in the Weyl group of the subsytem such that

(7.14)

\bar{z}_{m}=\bar{b}_{m,k}\cdot\bar{u}_{m,k}\quad\mbox{with }\;\;l(\bar{z}_{m})=l(\bar{b}_{m,k})+l(\bar{u}_{m,k})\,.

In fact, it is easy to verify that a representative reduced word is given by
u_{m,k}=z_{m-1}\cdot c_{m,k-1}\,
.
The calculations in (
7.10
) and (
7.13
) show that

\bar{b}_{m-1,k}(\alpha_{m})=\bar{z}_{m-1}\bar{c}_{m,k-1}(\alpha_{m+1-k})=\bar{b}_{m-1,k}\bar{u}_{m-1,k}\bar{c}_{m,k-1}(\alpha_{m+1-k})\,.

Together with length comparisons we find

(7.15)

\displaystyle\alpha_{m}

\displaystyle=\bar{u}_{m-1,k}\bar{c}_{m,k-1}(\alpha_{m+1-k})

\displaystyle\mbox{and}

\displaystyle l(z_{m-1}c_{m,k-1})=l(b_{m-1,k})+l(u_{m-1,k})+l(c_{m,k-1})\,.

For
1\leq i<j\leq n+1
, denote now the generators of
U_{q}^{+}
as follows.

(7.16)

E_{i,j}=E_{z_{n}[\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{j}]}=E_{z_{n}[1,N]}\qquad\mbox{ with }\ N=\mbox{$\binom{j-1}{2}$}+i

Proposition 7.6
.

For a given
j\in\{2,\ldots,n+1\}
, the elements in (
7.16
) are determined by
the identity
E_{j-1,j}=E_{j-1}
and the recursive relation

(7.17)

E_{i,j}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{i}(E_{i+1,j})=q^{-1}E_{i}E_{i+1,j}-E_{i+1,j}E_{i}\qquad\mbox{for}\quad i<j-1\;.

Proof.

Set
m=j-1
and
k=i
. We have
\gamma(z_{n}[1,N])=\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{j}
for
N=\binom{j-1}{2}+i\,
by (
7.10
). Thus, by definition,
E_{z_{n}[1,N]}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{z_{j-2}c_{j-1,i-1}}(E_{j-i})=\mathit{\Gamma}_{b_{j-2,i}u_{j-2,i}c_{j-1,i-1}}(E_{j-i})=\mathit{\Gamma}_{b_{j-2,i}}(\mathit{\Gamma}_{u_{j-2,i}c_{j-1,i-1}}(E_{j-i}))
since
the
\mathit{\Gamma}
only depend on the Weyl element and
l(b_{j-2,i}u_{j-2,i}c_{j-1,i-1})=l(b_{j-2,i})+l(u_{j-2,i}c_{j-1,i-1})
by (
7.15
).

Note, further, that by (
7.15
) we have that the weight of
E_{u_{j-2,i}c_{j-1,i}}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{u_{j-2,i}c_{j-1,i-1}}(E_{j-i})
is
\alpha_{j-1}\,
. It, therefore, follows from Proposition
5.1
that
E_{u_{j-2,i}c_{j-1,i}}=E_{j-1}\,
. Plugging this into the previous expression for
E_{z_{n}[1,N]}
we find

(7.18)

E_{i,j}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{b_{j-2,i}}(E_{j-1})=\mathit{\Gamma}_{i}\ldots\mathit{\Gamma}_{j-2}(E_{j-1})=\mathit{\Gamma}_{i}(E_{i+1,j})\,.

In particular,
E_{j-1,j}=E_{j-1}\,
. The recursion in (
7.17
) follows by induction, decreasing in
i
. Assuming the identity for
i+1
, one can express
E_{i+1,j}
by
E_{i+1}
and
E_{i+2,j}
. Since the latter is in the subalgebra

\langle E_{i+2},\ldots,E_{j-1}\rangle
generated by

\{E_{i+2},\ldots,E_{j-1}\}
,
\mathit{\Gamma}_{i}
acts as identity on
E_{i+2,j}
and
E_{i}
commutes with
E_{i+2,j}
. The resulting expression
in
E_{i}
,
E_{i+1}
, and
E_{i+2,j}
can now be worked out and identified with the left side of (
7.17
).
∎

A full set of commutation relations as well as nested subalgebras of
\mathsf{A}
-types are derived in the next proposition. Most of these can be found in other references, with the possible exception of the relation in Item
iii)
below.

Proposition 7.7
.

For
1\leq i<s<j<t\leq n+1
the following commutation relations hold.

i)

E_{i,t}=q^{-1}E_{i,j}E_{j,t}-E_{j,t}E_{i,j}

ii)

E_{i,t}E_{s,j}=E_{s,j}E_{i,t}

iii)

E_{i,j}E_{s,t}-E_{s,t}E_{i,j}=-(q-q^{-1})E_{s,j}E_{i,t}

iv)

E_{i,s}E_{j,t}=E_{j,t}E_{i,s}

v)

E_{i,t}E_{i,j}=qE_{i,j}E_{i,t}

vi)

E_{j,t}E_{i,t}=qE_{i,t}E_{j,t}

More generally, suppose
\hat{j}=(j_{1},\ldots,j_{m+1})
is a sequence with

1\leq j_{1}<j_{2}<\ldots<j_{m+1}\leq n+1
. Then there exists an injective algebra homomorphism

\phi_{\hat{j}}:U_{q}^{+}(\mathfrak{sl}_{m+1})\rightarrow U_{q}^{+}(\mathfrak{sl}_{n+1})
with

(7.19)

\phi_{\hat{j}}(E_{r,s})=E_{j_{r},j_{s}}\,.

Proof.

The relation in
i)
is obtained by applying

\mathit{\Gamma}_{b_{i-1,k}}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{k}\ldots\mathit{\Gamma}_{i-1}
to (
7.17
), using that
\mathit{\Gamma}_{b_{i-1,k}}
acts trivially on
E_{i+1,j}\in\langle E_{i+1},\ldots,E_{j-1}\rangle\,
, and substituting indices. Item
iv)
is clear,
since
E_{i,s}\in\langle E_{i},\ldots,E_{s-1}\rangle
and
E_{j,t}\in\langle E_{j},\ldots,E_{t-1}\rangle
are in algebras for which the generators of one commute with the generators of the other.

Next note that, by (
7.18
), we can write
E_{i,j}=E_{w_{ij}}
, where
w_{ij}=w_{i}\ldots w_{j-1}\,
.
Clearly,
w_{it}=w_{ij}w_{jt}
with
l(w_{it})=l(w_{ij})+l(w_{jt})
. Further,
the index of
\tau(w_{ij})=j-1
does not occur
w_{jt}\,
. We also have

\alpha=\gamma(w_{ij})=\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{j}
and

\beta=\gamma(w_{it})=\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{t}\,
, so that
\mathchoice{\left(\alpha|\beta\right)}{(\alpha|\beta)}{(\alpha|\beta)}{(\alpha|\beta)}=1
. The relation in

v)
follows now directly from Lemma
5.6
, with

w=w_{it}
,
u=w_{ij}
, and
v=w_{jt}\,
.

Alternatively, we find from (
7.10
) and (
7.16
) that
E_{it}=E_{z_{t-2}c_{t-1,i}}\,
.
From (
7.9
) we have
c_{t-1,j}=c_{t-1,i}v\,
, where
v=w_{t-1-i}\ldots w_{t-j}\,
. So, if we
set
w=z_{t-2}c_{t-1,j}
and
u=z_{t-2}c_{t-1,i}
we find
w=uv
with
l(w)=l(u)+l(v)\,
.
As before
\tau(u)=t-j
does not occur as an index in
v\,
. Moreover,
\alpha=\gamma(u)=\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{t}

and
\beta=\gamma(w)=\epsilon_{j}-\epsilon_{t}\,
, so that
\mathchoice{\left(\alpha|\beta\right)}{(\alpha|\beta)}{(\alpha|\beta)}{(\alpha|\beta)}=1
.
Lemma
5.6
, therefore, implies the relation in Item
vi)
.

Combining relation
i)
with
v)
as well as
combining relation
i)
with
vi)
we obtain respective Serre relations

E_{ij}^{2}E_{jt}-[2]E_{ij}E_{jt}E_{ij}+E_{jt}E_{ij}^{2}=0\quad\mbox{ and }\quad E_{jt}^{2}E_{ij}-[2]E_{jt}E_{ij}E_{jt}+E_{ij}E_{jt}^{2}=0\,.

Together with the relation in
v)
we observe that, for a sequence
j_{1}<\ldots<j_{m+1}
as above,
the elements
\tilde{E}_{r}=E_{j_{r},j_{r+1}}
fulfill the relations of the standard generators of
U_{q}^{+}(\mathfrak{sl}_{m+1})
.
Hence, we have a well-defined algebra homomorphism
\phi_{\hat{j}}
that maps the
E_{r}
generator in
U_{q}^{+}(\mathfrak{sl}_{m+1})

to
\tilde{E}_{r}
in
U_{q}^{+}(\mathfrak{sl}_{n+1})
. Setting
(i,j,t)=(j_{k},j_{k+1},j_{m})

and denoting
\tilde{E}_{k,m}=E_{j_{k},j_{m}}
relation
v)
can be written as

\tilde{E}_{k,m}=q^{-1}\tilde{E}_{k}\tilde{E}_{k+1,m}-\tilde{E}_{k+1,m}\tilde{E}_{k}
. Since this is the same recursion
(
7.17
) for the generators in
U_{q}^{+}(\mathfrak{sl}_{m})
and
\phi_{\hat{j}}
is a homomorphism,
(
7.19
) follows inductively. This also means that the PBW basis elements given by ordered monomials
in the
E_{i,j}
in
U_{q}^{+}(\mathfrak{sl}_{m+1})
are mapped to elements of standard PBW basis of
U_{q}^{+}(\mathfrak{sl}_{n+1})
, which, in turn, implies that
\phi_{\hat{j}}
is injective.

Given the
\mathsf{A}_{m}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{A}_{n}
inclusions, it now suffices for the remaining relations to consider the

\mathsf{A}_{3}
case, using
\phi_{\hat{j}}
with
\hat{j}=(j_{1},j_{2},j_{3},j_{4})=(i,s,j,t)\,
. The relation in

ii)
is then implied by
E_{1,4}E_{2}=E_{2}E_{1,4}
. To see this, observe
E_{1,4}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{1}\mathit{\Gamma}_{2}(E_{3})

and
E_{2}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{1}\mathit{\Gamma}_{2}(E_{1})
as in Proposition
5.1
. Thus,
[E_{1,4},E_{2}]=[\mathit{\Gamma}_{1}\mathit{\Gamma}_{2}(E_{3}),\mathit{\Gamma}_{1}\mathit{\Gamma}_{2}(E_{1})]=\mathit{\Gamma}_{1}\mathit{\Gamma}_{2}([E_{1},E_{3}])=0

as desired.

To derive the last relation
iii)
, we set
\theta_{2}=\mathit{\Gamma}_{2}^{-1}(E_{2})=-F_{2}K_{2}
and compute from the relations in Section
3.2
the following equations in the full quantum group
U_{q}
.

\theta_{2}E_{i}=q^{-1}E_{i}\theta_{2}\quad\mbox{for }i\in\{1,3\}\qquad\mbox{and }\qquad\theta_{2}E_{2}=\tfrac{q^{2}}{q-q^{-1}}(K_{2}^{2}-1)+q^{2}E_{2}\theta_{2}

Letting
c=\tfrac{q^{2}}{q-q^{-1}}
and
i,j\in\{1,3\}
, these entail commutators

(7.20)

\displaystyle=c(qK_{2}^{2}-q^{-1})E_{i}E_{j}\,,

\displaystyle[\theta_{2},E_{2}E_{i}E_{j}]

\displaystyle=c(K_{2}^{2}-1)E_{i}E_{j}\,,

\displaystyle[\theta_{2},E_{i}E_{j}E_{2}]

\displaystyle=c(q^{2}K_{2}^{2}-q^{-2})E_{i}E_{j}\,.

Using the braid relations for the
\mathit{\Gamma}_{i}
as well as
\mathit{\Gamma}_{2}\mathit{\Gamma}_{3}(E_{2})=E_{3}
we, further, compute

(7.21)

\displaystyle\mathit{\Gamma}_{2}^{-1}\mathit{\Gamma}_{1}^{-1}\mathit{\Gamma}_{2}(E_{3})

\displaystyle=\mathit{\Gamma}_{1}\mathit{\Gamma}_{2}^{-1}\mathit{\Gamma}_{1}^{-1}(E_{3})=\mathit{\Gamma}_{1}\mathit{\Gamma}_{2}^{-1}(E_{3})=\mathit{\Gamma}_{1}\mathit{\Gamma}_{3}(E_{2})

\displaystyle=q^{-2}E_{3}E_{1}E_{2}-q^{-1}(E_{3}E_{2}E_{1}+E_{1}E_{2}E_{3})+E_{2}E_{1}E_{3}\;.

Combining (
7.20
) and (
7.21
) we arrive at

[\mathit{\Gamma}_{2}^{-1}(E_{2}),\mathit{\Gamma}_{2}^{-1}\mathit{\Gamma}_{1}^{-1}\mathit{\Gamma}_{2}(E_{3})]=-(q-q^{-1})E_{1}E_{3}\;,

which yields, after application of
\mathit{\Gamma}_{1}\mathit{\Gamma}_{2}
and using
\mathit{\Gamma}_{1}\mathit{\Gamma}_{2}(E_{1})=E_{2}=E_{2,3}\,
, the desired form

[E_{1,3},E_{2,4}]=[\mathit{\Gamma}_{1}(E_{2}),\mathit{\Gamma}_{2}(E_{3})]=-(q-q^{-1})\mathit{\Gamma}_{1}\mathit{\Gamma}_{2}(E_{1})\mathit{\Gamma}_{1}\mathit{\Gamma}_{2}(E_{3})=-(q-q^{-1})E_{2,3}E_{1,4}\,.

∎

To express the coproducts of these elements we introduce notations
K_{i,j}=K_{i}\ldots K_{j-1}
and
E_{i,i}=E_{j,j}=1
.

Lemma 7.8
.

For
i<j
, the coproduct of
E_{i,j}
is

(7.22)

\Delta(E_{i,j})=\sum_{k=i}^{j}c_{k}E_{i,k}\otimes K_{i,k}E_{k,j}

where
c_{i}=c_{j}=1
and
c_{k}=-(q-q^{-1})
for
i<k<j
.

Proof.

The formula is immediate for the coproduct of
E_{j-1}
when
i=j-1
. The assertion for
i<j-1
is then obtained by descending induction in
i
, using the recursion (
7.17
). For
T^{i,j}_{k}=E_{i,k}\otimes K_{i,k}E_{k,j}

a basic calculation yields

q^{-1}\Delta(E_{i})T^{i+1,j}_{k}-T^{i+1,j}_{k}\Delta(E_{i})=\begin{cases}T^{i,j}_{k}&\mbox{ for }\ k>i+1\\
-(q-q^{-1})T^{i,j}_{i+1}+T^{i,j}_{i}&\mbox{ for }\ k=i+1\,.\end{cases}

Assuming (
7.22
) for
\Delta(E_{i+1,j})
we then use this computation to derive
(
7.22
) for the coproduct as
\Delta(E_{i,j})=q^{-1}\Delta(E_{i})\Delta(E_{i+1,j})-\Delta(E_{i+1,j})\Delta(E_{i})\,
.
∎

The coproduct for powers of these generators is derived from commutation relations for the elements
T^{i,j}_{k}
defined in the proof above.
First, observe that the identities
v)
and
vi)
in Proposition
7.7
imply that

(7.23)

T^{i,j}_{r}T^{i,j}_{s}=q^{-2}T^{i,j}_{s}T^{i,j}_{r}\qquad\mbox{ for all }\;i\leq r<s\leq j\,.

Thus, if
D_{m}=\sum_{k=i}^{m}c_{k}T^{i,j}_{k}
we find from (
7.23
) that also
D_{m-1}T^{i,j}_{m}=q^{-2}T^{i,j}_{m}D_{m-1}\,
. We may now write

D_{m}=V+U
where
V=D_{m-1}
and
U=c_{m}T^{i,j}_{m}\,
. Applying
(
3.3
), this allows us to infer
D_{m}^{N}=\sum_{r}q^{r(N-r)}\begin{bmatrix}\vskip-7.68222pt\raise 3.1298pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{N}$}\\
\scriptstyle{r}\vskip-3.1298pt\end{bmatrix}D_{m-1}^{N-r}\left(c_{m}T^{i,j}_{m}\right)^{r}\,
. Iterating this formula, we arrive at the following expression,

(7.24)

\Delta(E_{i,j}^{N})=\mathop{\textnormal{\hbox{\hbox to15.83pt{\vbox to16.44pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.0pt\lower-10.00012pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{{}{}{}{}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@discardpath@clipped{M 0 -13.84 L 0 8.92 L 21.9 8.92 L 21.9 -13.84 Z} {{{}{}{{}}{}
